x: apkpack Builds and signs Android APKs with no Java, no Android SDK and no SDK licence: one native C++ tool for the squared SDK https://squared netizen.github.io/squared netizen/ in place of keytool, apksigner, aapt2, zipalign and android.jar. Status: planned, not yet built. What it will be One program with subcommands, so the build can move to it a step at a time: Command Replaces Does apkpack keygen keytool an ECDSA P 256 key and a self signed certificate; an existing debug key can be imported apkpack sign , apkpack verify apksigner APK Signature Scheme v2 Android 7.0 and later apkpack add zip, zipalign lib/ and classes.dex, stored entries aligned 4 bytes, 16 KB for a stored .so apkpack link aapt2, android.jar the manifest and XML resources as binary XML, resources.arsc, assets apkpack dump aapt2 dump the binary manifest as text apkpack explain none what a dex shim does, its bytecode and spec references, as JSON The framework attribute IDs android.jar supplied come from AOSP's public tables Apache 2.0 , pinned as a source. Dex code is never compiled here: dexgen writes squared's shims, and apkpack packs them. The plan 1. Sign : keygen, sign, verify. The build no longer needs Java. 2. Package : the zip writer with alignment. 3. Link : binary XML, resources.arsc, the attribute table. No aapt2 or android.jar. 4. Switch : squared's template calls apkpack. No SDK at all. Each phase is checked against the tool it replaces, and on the phone by installing and launching the APK. Licence MIT: see LICENSE LICENSE . Security issues: see SECURITY.md SECURITY.md .

Manuals Documentation for the squared SDK https://squared netizen.github.io/squared netizen/ , found first and read second: a fuzzy search across every manual installed, then a reader that moves through a page by its headings and links, in a terminal or as a squared screen. Status: designed, not yet built. What it will be Pages are Obsidian style markdown : frontmatter title, aliases, tags , wikilinks , callouts. Command pages share one shape TLDR first, then synopsis, description, parameters , so every command reads alike. Manuals come in cartridges sqcart 3.0, kind manual , and installing a package with sqterm's pkg installs its manual through a hook. Search is fuzzy : letters in order with gaps cartdg finds "cartridge" , typos forgiven, over titles, aliases, headings, tags and text. Commands that have no page still show which package installed them. Better navigation than man : headings that fold, a header window, and between headings, links with back and forward history, marks, and a : command line as in neovim. Two faces, one core : manuals in a terminal character cells, works over ssh , and a reader screen any squared app can show. Web pages come in too : a saved site converts to a manual with its internal links still working, through squared/data's converter. Inspired by the Linux Command Library https://github.com/SimonSchubert/LinuxCommandLibrary . Licence MIT: see LICENSE LICENSE . Security issues: see SECURITY.md SECURITY.md .

x: Squared Cartridge Specification, Version 2.0 Status: Draft Format identifier: squared cartridge format version : 2 File extension: .sq Media type: application/vnd.squared.cartridge+zip provisional Supersedes: version 1.0. See §0.2. 0. Scope and relationship to squared pg This document specifies a container format. It does not specify the generator, the engine, or the Squared framework runtime. The container is the single physical representation for every named, versioned, manifest identified resource in the Squared ecosystem: generator resources consumed by squared pg — templates, kits, packages, asset bundles; generator extensions — plugins; distributable applications produced by the Squared framework — cartridges. This specification satisfies the resource identity model required by §2.4.4 of the Generator Architecture: a resource is identified by its manifest, never by its filesystem path. 0.1 Independence requirement The Squared framework MUST NOT depend on squared pg §2.7.6 . Both systems need to read this format. Therefore: This specification is normative and standalone. Neither implementation may treat the other as its reference. The reader is expected to be a small standalone component sqcart depending only on a ZIP codec and a JSON parser, vendored independently by each consumer. Nothing in this document permits a cartridge to carry generator implementation details into a generated project. 0.2 Relationship to version 1.0 Version 2.0 is not backward compatible and no compatibility path is provided. A conforming reader implements exactly one format version and MUST refuse any other, in either direction §12.1 step 4 . Three changes account for the break: Kind bodies are replaced by consumers §5.6 . Version 1.0 defined six typed bodies — template , kit , package , asset bundle , plugin , cartridge — and every field in every one of them was a squared pg or Squared framework concept. A reader implementing this specification therefore had to know the generator's vocabulary, which made §0.1 false in practice: a framework runtime linking a conforming reader acquired integration areas and project types whether it wanted them or not. Version 2.0 moves all of it into namespaced sections a reader carries and never opens. kind is an opaque token §5.2 . It was a closed set of six. A closed set obliges a reader to know the ecosystem's roles, which is the same defect one level up. tree is a required envelope member §5.1 . Version 1.0 gave the payload root to templates only, as a kind body field, and left every other kind to a convention the reader could not see. The break is deliberate and was taken while the ecosystem was small enough for the migration to be mechanical. tree is required rather than defaulted because a defaulted field is invisible in the manifests an author learns the format from. What this costs is worth stating plainly. Version 1.0 could check that a cartridge's entry module named a present entry, that an asset bundle's declared paths existed, and that a template's ownership globs classified every file exactly once. Those were useful checks and they are gone, because none of them can be made without knowing a consumer's schema. They belong to the consumer now, which can give a better diagnostic anyway — it knows what the reference was for. Readers MUST NOT attempt to upgrade a version 1.0 manifest in place. The correct response to one is cartridge.format unsupported , naming the version found and the version implemented. 1. Design rationale The format is modelled on the Java Archive specification, which solved this problem correctly in outline and incorrectly in several specific places. Hindsight lets us keep the outline and discard the mistakes. 1.1 Retained from JAR Property Rationale Ordinary ZIP container Universal tooling. Inspectable with unzip , mountable, streamable, random access. Reserved metadata directory A well known root directory tells a reader how to interpret the rest without out of band knowledge. Explicit declared entry point The equivalent of Main Class . A container that runs must say what runs. Forward compatibility by ignoring unknown metadata Lets v1 readers survive v1.x additions. Per entry digests as the integrity primitive Integrity attaches to content, not to the container envelope. One container serving many roles jar / war / ear / apk are one format. Role belongs in metadata. 1.2 Corrected from JAR JAR behaviour Consequence Correction here Bespoke manifest grammar with 72 byte continuation lines Hand parsing, subtle encoding bugs, poor tooling JSON, UTF 8, parsed with a conventional parser Class Path pulls dependencies by relative filesystem path Fragile, non relocatable, unresolvable offline Dependencies declared by manifest identity only; resolution is the Package/Kit/Template Service's job Signed archives accept unsigned added entries Signature bypass by injection The content digest covers the complete entry set; any addition, removal or modification invalidates it Entry order, timestamps and compression unspecified Reproducible builds impossible; hashes unstable Canonical ordering and fixed timestamps for writers; reproducibility defined over content , not archive bytes Multi Release added a decade late as versioned directories Retrofit with awkward precedence rules Target overlay mechanism reserved from v1; base payload must always be complete Path safety unspecified "Zip slip" traversal, duplicate name confusion, zip bombs Strict, normative path and limit rules in §3 Role encoded in the file extension .war vs .jar divergence, extension based trust Single .sq extension; role is kind in the manifest and nothing is trusted by name Sealed packages, trusted library attributes Complex trust semantics few implemented correctly Deferred entirely; no trust semantics in v1 1.3 Non goals for v1 Native executable code loading. Signature verification and trust policy layout reserved, behaviour undefined . Delta or patch cartridges. Network resolution of any kind. The format is offline first by construction. 2. Terminology The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. Cartridge — an instance of this format, in either archived or exploded form. Reader — an implementation that opens and validates a cartridge. Writer — an implementation that produces a cartridge. Payload — every entry not under SQ INF/ . Kind — the declared role of a cartridge §6 . 3. Container format 3.1 ZIP profile A cartridge in archived form MUST be a ZIP archive conforming to PKWARE APPNOTE 6.3.x, restricted as follows. Writers MUST: use only compression method 0 Stored or 8 Deflate ; set general purpose bit 11 UTF 8 filename encoding on every entry; record accurate CRC 32, compressed size and uncompressed size in both the local header and the central directory; emit no encrypted entries general purpose bit 0 MUST be clear ; emit no data descriptors general purpose bit 3 MUST be clear ; emit no extra fields other than the ZIP64 extended information field; omit directory entries. Readers MUST: treat the central directory as authoritative; reject an entry whose local header disagrees with the central directory on name, method, CRC 32 or sizes; support ZIP64; reject any compression method other than 0 or 8; ignore external file attributes, including Unix mode bits. Symbolic links, device nodes and executable bits carry no meaning in v1 and MUST NOT be materialised. If a writer emits directory entries anyway, they MUST be zero length, Stored, and end in / . Readers MUST NOT depend on their presence and MUST NOT infer structure from their absence. 3.2 First entry rule SQ INF/manifest.json MUST be the first entry in the archive and MUST use compression method 0 Stored . This allows a reader to identify and parse the manifest from the head of the file, without scanning to the end for the central directory. It matters on constrained hosts — reading a manifest off a Termux filesystem or an Android asset stream should not require a seek to EOF. A reader MAY additionally locate the manifest through the central directory, but a cartridge that violates the first entry rule is non conforming and MUST be rejected at strict conformance §12 . 3.3 Entry path rules An entry path is the ZIP entry name interpreted as UTF 8. A conforming entry path MUST: use / as its only separator; be relative — no leading / ; contain no . or .. segment; contain no NUL byte, no backslash, no : drive designator, and no C0 or C1 control character; be non empty and not end in / except a tolerated directory entry ; be valid, NFC normalised UTF 8. A conforming cartridge MUST NOT contain: two entries with byte identical paths; two entries whose paths differ only by ASCII case; two entries whose paths differ only by Unicode normalisation form. Logical paths are case sensitive . The two collision rules above exist so that a case sensitive logical model can be materialised safely onto a case insensitive host filesystem, which is the normal situation on Android and macOS. Readers MUST reject a cartridge violating any rule in this section before extracting or mapping any entry. Path validation is a precondition of access, not a step during extraction. 3.4 Resource limits Readers MUST enforce a default limit for each of the following, and MAY allow a host policy to raise them. They MUST NOT default to unbounded. Limit Default SQ INF/manifest.json uncompressed size 1 MiB Any single SQ INF/ file 4 MiB Entry path length 1024 bytes Path depth 32 segments Entry count 65 536 Total uncompressed size 2 GiB Per entry compression ratio 200:1 Whole archive compression ratio 100:1 Exceeding a limit MUST produce a structured error §13 and MUST NOT produce a partially materialised result. 3.5 Exploded form A cartridge MAY exist as a directory tree rather than an archive. A directory is an exploded cartridge if it contains a readable SQ INF/manifest.json . Exploded and archived forms are semantically equivalent. A reader that supports one SHOULD support both. The rules of §3.3 apply to the relative paths within an exploded cartridge. Symbolic links inside an exploded cartridge MUST NOT be followed outside the cartridge root, and SHOULD be rejected. This is the mechanism that reconciles the format with the repository layout required by §1.13. A development checkout stores generator resources exploded: Distribution and content addressed caching store them archived: Neither form is canonical. Identity comes from the manifest in both cases. The repository layout remains a maintenance convenience and does not become part of the public generator contract, exactly as §2.4.4 requires. 4. The SQ INF/ directory SQ INF/ is reserved. Payload MUST NOT be placed under it. Path Status Purpose SQ INF/manifest.json REQUIRED Identity, kind and metadata SQ INF/hashes.json OPTIONAL Per entry content digests §9 SQ INF/thumbnail.png OPTIONAL Presentation image SQ INF/icon.png OPTIONAL Presentation icon SQ INF/licenses/ OPTIONAL Licence texts and notices SQ INF/signatures/ RESERVED Signature material §10 SQ INF/targets/ RESERVED Target overlays §11 SQ INF/ other OPTIONAL Implementation defined Readers MUST ignore unrecognised files under SQ INF/ . Validators SHOULD report them as informational diagnostics. Names not listed above are reserved for future versions of this specification. Third parties SHOULD namespace their additions, for example SQ INF/x vendor name/ . 5. The manifest SQ INF/manifest.json is a JSON document encoded as UTF 8 without a byte order mark. It MUST be a JSON object. The manifest has a fixed envelope , common to every kind and fully defined here, and an optional consumers object carrying sections this specification does not define §5.6 . That division is the whole of version 2.0. The envelope is what any reader can act on without knowing who the cartridge is for; everything else is addressed to someone in particular and carried unopened. 5.1 Envelope Field Type Status Notes format string REQUIRED MUST equal "squared cartridge" format version integer REQUIRED MUST equal 2 for this specification kind string REQUIRED Opaque role token, §5.2.1 id string REQUIRED Resource identity, §5.2 version string REQUIRED Semantic version, §5.3 tree string REQUIRED Payload root, §5.1.1 title string OPTIONAL Human facing display name description string OPTIONAL Short prose description requires features array of string OPTIONAL Container features the READER must implement, §5.4 authors array of object OPTIONAL name , optional email , url license string OPTIONAL SPDX identifier where one applies presentation object OPTIONAL Paths to thumbnail, icon, and display hints provenance object OPTIONAL §5.5 consumers object OPTIONAL Consumer sections, §5.6 Members not listed here are ignored and preserved §5.4 . A reader MUST NOT reject a manifest for carrying a member it does not recognise, and MUST NOT ascribe meaning to one — in particular, a top level member named after a kind carries no significance in this version. format , format version and tree MUST be validated before any other member is read §12.1 . Every field after them is interpreted under the rules of the version the manifest claims, so that claim is not something a reader may defer. 5.1.1 tree — the payload root tree names the directory at which the cartridge's payload begins, relative to the cartridge root. It has exactly two legal shapes: "." — the payload begins at the cartridge root. A relative directory path ending in / , for example "tree/" or "a/b/" . A reader MUST refuse any other form. In particular it MUST refuse a path without the trailing separator: "tree" is not an accepted spelling of "tree/" , and a reader MUST NOT normalise one into the other. Accepting both spellings would put two ways of writing one path into the ecosystem and oblige every reader to canonicalise on the way out, or let the two forms diverge in indexes, error messages and provenance records. A reader MUST additionally refuse a tree that: is absolute, or contains a . or .. component, or contains an empty segment, or contains a character excluded from entry paths by §3.3. Entry paths are validated relative to this prefix, so a payload root that can escape the cartridge defeats every path check below it; begins with SQ INF/ . The reserved directory is never payload §4 . SQ INF/ is excluded from the payload regardless of tree , including when tree is "." . The exclusion is §4's, and does not depend on the payload root happening to point elsewhere. A tree naming a directory the cartridge does not contain is not an error. A manifest only cartridge is legal, and a reader that refused one could not represent an asset bundle awaiting its assets. A validator SHOULD report it as an informational diagnostic, because the far more common cause is a misspelling that would otherwise surface as a missing file error somewhere with nothing pointing back at the manifest. Why the envelope. A reader must be able to find the payload without knowing the kind, and must be able to do so for kinds this version has not defined — which, since §5.2.1 makes kind opaque, is all of them. Version 1.0 placed the field on templates alone and gave the other five kinds prose conventions bridge/ , platform/ , include/ , assets/ , lua/ that no reader could act on, so implementations guessed: look for entries under tree/ , otherwise assume the root. That guess was correct for every resource that then existed and silently wrong for any cartridge shipping an unrelated tree/ directory. The declaration replaces it. 5.2 Identity id is a dotted identifier. Each segment MUST match a z a z0 9 and segments are joined with . . There MUST be at least two segments and no more than eight. id is compared byte for byte; there is no case folding and no aliasing. 5.2.1 kind kind is a single identity segment: a z a z0 9 , no dots. This specification does not enumerate legal kinds, and a conforming reader MUST NOT reject a kind it does not recognise. A reader validates the token's shape and nothing else. Version 1.0 defined a closed set of six. The set was wrong to be closed for the same reason the kind bodies were wrong to exist: which roles the ecosystem has is the ecosystem's question, and a reader that answers it cannot open a cartridge for a role invented after it shipped. kind is closer to a media type than to a schema selector — it tells a human or a tool what a cartridge claims to be, without either needing to know the claim's contents. Consumers MAY require particular kinds, and MUST report an unusable one themselves rather than expecting the reader to have refused it. Kind tokens in use at the time of writing, listed as information and not as a constraint: cartridge , template , kit , package , asset bundle , plugin . 5.2.2 Identifier prefixes Prefix conventions — kit. for kits, template. for templates and so on — are ecosystem policy, not format rules . Version 1.0 made them normative here; enforcing them requires knowing which prefix belongs to which role, which is the coupling this version removes. A conforming reader MUST NOT require or infer any relationship between id and kind . Consumers MAY impose one. The pair id, version is the complete identity of a cartridge. Nothing else — not the filename, not the directory, not the archive hash — participates in identity. 5.3 Versioning version MUST be a Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 version string. Version ranges appear in compatibility fields and use a restricted comparator grammar: Clauses separated by spaces are conjunctive. Disjunction is expressed as an array of range strings. There is no wildcard syntax; ^1.2.0 and ~1.2.0 carry their usual SemVer meanings. format version is an integer owned by this specification and is unrelated to version . A reader MUST reject a cartridge whose format version it does not implement. 5.4 Compatibility model Two tiers, because "ignore what you don't recognise" is safe for additive metadata and unsafe for semantic changes. Default tier. A reader MUST ignore unrecognised members of any manifest object. This is what allows v1.1 to add fields without breaking v1.0 readers. Critical tier. requires features is an array of feature tokens. A reader MUST refuse to load the cartridge unless it implements every token listed. Tokens are opaque strings assigned by this specification. The rule is that a writer relying on behaviour a v1.0 reader does not have MUST declare it here. Silence means "everything I depend on is in v1.0". This replaces JAR's blanket ignore unknown rule, which had no way to say "this one actually matters". No feature tokens are defined by v1.0. 5.5 Provenance For kinds produced by generation rather than authored by hand, the manifest MAY record how it was produced. provenance MUST NOT contain machine specific paths, hostnames, usernames, or temporary filesystem locations §2.7.2 . It exists to support update workflows and debugging, not to describe a build machine. 5.6 consumers consumers is an OPTIONAL object carrying data addressed to consuming tools. Its keys are consumer identities; its values are sections whose contents this specification does not define and a conforming reader does not interpret. What a reader MUST check 1. consumers , if present, is an object. 2. Each key is a consumer identity: dotted segments matching a z a z0 9 , at most 128 characters. 3. Each value is an object. 4. The whole is within the reader's Limits §3.4 for nesting depth and size. What a reader MUST NOT do A reader MUST NOT interpret, validate, transform, reorder or reject a section's contents. It MUST NOT require any particular key to be present, and a section addressed to a consumer the reader has never heard of is not an error — it is the mechanism working. A reader MUST make each section retrievable by identity, and MUST preserve member order within a section. Insignificant whitespace need not be preserved. Why an object, and why namespaced The va

A hostile reading of the first 3.0 draft sq cartridge 3.0.md , commit b92935a , alongside the published problems of formats and stores that solve the same problems: LMDB and Bolt two slot commits , SQLite atomic commit , Electron's asar an indexed archive with integrity , Godot's PCK game data packs and patches , zstd frames and dictionaries , ZIP and its extractors zip bombs, Zip Slip , Android's APK signing Janus , git paths on case insensitive systems , and the crash consistency research on POSIX file systems. Every finding below has been fixed in the draft or written into it as a stated limit. The section numbers are the revised draft's. Severity: High means a reader can be made to return wrong data, lose a commit, or be compromised. Medium means a crash or a hostile file costs data or resources, or two implementations disagree. Low means a portability or usability fault. Summary Finding Severity Resolution R1 Both superblock slots in one 4096 byte page High slots on separate pages; header 8192 bytes §3.1 R2 Feature flags rewritten in place in the header High flags move into each commit record §3.9 R3 A sequence number can be reused after a fallback Medium next = higher slot + 1, valid or not §10.3 R4 Locking the cartridge file loses commits across compaction High lock a separate <file .lock §10.2 R5 zstd frame sizes and windows trusted High one frame, declared size required and checked, window capped §4.3 R6 Partial reads unverified; a big entry rewritten whole for any change High chunked entries and a tree hash §4.5, §9.1 R7 Dictionaries named by entry index High named by zstd dictionary ID, immutable §4.3 R8 Content digest depends on JSON serialisation Medium length prefixed framing, RFC 8785 canonical JSON §9.2 R9 Commit chain can loop or point anywhere High ordering and region checks per commit, overflow checks §3, §3.4 R10 Entries may share or overlap bytes Medium identical or disjoint runs only §3.6 R11 Unsigned trailing bytes make polyglots possible High trailing bytes ignored and reported; format chosen by magic only §3.3, §9.4, §13 R12 Symbolic links in pack and unpack Zip Slip High never followed; O EXCL creation §6.1 R13 Case collisions allowed, a regression from 2.0 High collisions forbidden under Unicode case folding §4.1 R14 A workspace's .squared/ would be packed Medium .squared/ and .git/ are never entries §6.1, §6.2 R15 mappable aligned to 4096 on 16 KiB page devices Medium 16384 alignment §3.6 R16 "fsync" underspecified Medium per system flush, folder flush, Windows rename §10.3, §10.4 R17 Android shared storage and FAT32 Medium private storage advised; 4 GiB refusal §10.6 R18 Titles can carry bidi and control characters Low shown visibly or stripped §4.2 R19 JSON duplicate members, big integers Medium I JSON everywhere §5 R20 Version ranges "as npm and Cargo write them" disagree Medium one grammar, defined §8 R21 Signatures: no algorithm field, unsigned signer name Medium algorithm per signature, name signed, strict Ed25519 §9.3 R22 Rollback to an older signed state Medium stated; consumers refuse downgrades §9.4 R23 Verification bypassed through another load path High runtimes load only verified cartridges §11 R24 A file changes after it was verified Medium stated; copy to private storage §9.1 R25 3.0 cannot be streamed Low stated §3.3 R26 Output not reproducible Low fixed layout order, SOURCE DATE EPOCH §3.10 R27 A metadata only change rewrites content Low records may name earlier runs §3.6 R28 Exploded form: no signatures, stale entries.json Low signatures carried across pack; orphans reported §6.1 R29 The Drive's staging beside the cartridge Low staging in the Drive's own storage §10.5 Findings R1. Both superblock slots in one page High The draft put slot A at offset 64 and slot B at 128, in the same 4096 byte page. Storage writes whole pages or sectors; a power cut during the write of slot B can leave that page torn, and slot A, in the same page, torn with it. The whole point of two slots is that one survives. LMDB keeps its two meta pages on separate pages for this reason, and has argued about the case anyway: its maintainers declined a meta page checksum as a format change, and a corrupted meta page there needs manual recovery from the other one. Bolt's developers rely on the meta fitting in one sector, page aligned. SQLite's documentation is explicit that its atomic commit depends on "powersafe overwrite", the assumption that a write does not damage bytes outside it, and that some storage does not provide it. Fix. Slot A on page 0, slot B on page 1; the header is 8192 bytes. The draft already had a checksum per slot, which LMDB lacks. R2. Feature flags in the header High The draft's header held the feature flags, and the zstd dictionaries bit was "set only when some entry uses a dictionary". The first commit to use a dictionary therefore had to rewrite the header in place, outside the slot protocol, with no crash safety: a torn write there destroys the magic. Fix. Feature flags live in each commit record, and describe that commit's state. Nothing in the header changes after creation except the two slots. R3. Sequence numbers after a fallback Medium If the newer slot names a commit whose bytes never reached storage, a reader falls back to the older one. The draft said the next commit takes "the next sequence number", which could be the same number as the invalid slot's. Two different commits with one sequence number make "the higher slot wins" ambiguous after the next crash. Fix. The next sequence number is one more than the higher of both slots, whether or not that slot was valid §10.3 . R4. Locking the file that compaction replaces High The draft allowed the writer's lock to be on the cartridge file itself. Compaction renames a new file over the old one. A second writer blocked on the old file's lock acquires it once the first releases, then appends to the old, now unlinked, file: its commit is reported durable and is gone. This is why SQLite and git use lock files rather than locks on the data file they replace. Fix. The lock is always <file .lock ; on systems without working flock some FUSE mounts the lock file records host, PID and start time, and a stale lock is taken over only when that process is gone §10.2 . R5. Trusting zstd's frame header High The draft compared nothing against the frame. A zstd frame may omit its content size, may declare a wrong one, may need a window of up to several GiB, and may be followed by skippable frames or another frame. The zstd manual warns that for untrusted input the declared size "could be wrong or intentionally modified"; RFC 9659 made a window limit a requirement for HTTP for the same reason; services such as Vector cap both the window and the output. Fix. A run is exactly one frame; its declared content size is required and must equal the record's; the reader sets ZSTD d windowLogMax and stops at the declared size; a window larger than 2^23 needs the required feature bit zstd window 27 §4.3 . R6. Partial reads, and big entries High This is the finding that changed the draft most, and it is the same question as the Virtual Cartridge Drive's. The draft verified an entry's SHA 256 "on the first full read". A reader that maps a big texture, or seeks inside a 4 GiB video, never does a full read, and so never verifies anything: a signed cartridge gave no assurance about the bytes actually used. Electron's asar has the same problem and solved it with a hash per block of blockSize bytes in its header. And because an entry was one zstd frame, a reader could not start in the middle, and a writer had to rewrite all 4 GiB to change one byte, which defeats "a commit costs what it changed" for exactly the big files the Drive exists for. Fix. Chunked entries codec 3, §4.5 : fixed 1 MiB chunks, each its own run with its own codec, listed in a chunk table with a SHA 256 per chunk. The entry's digest becomes a tree hash over 1 MiB leaves §9.1 , the same for chunked and unchunked entries, so chunking stays a storage choice the content digest ignores. A reader verifies the chunk table against the digest once and then each chunk as it reads it. A writer changes a range by writing the chunks it touches and a new table that names the old runs for the rest with R27 . Fixed size chunks favour in place edits; inserting bytes still rewrites what follows content defined chunking would avoid that, at a cost in complexity and in predictable offsets; not taken . R7. Dictionaries by entry index High The draft's record named its dictionary by "the index of the entry holding the dictionary", in whichever index the lookup ended in. With delta indexes the same number means different entries in different commits, and a later commit that replaced or deleted the dictionary silently broke every entry compressed with it. zstd itself has a mechanism for this: every frame carries the ID of its dictionary, and decoders that hold several dictionaries zstd jni, the kernel's pick by it, and reject a mismatch. Fix. The record holds the zstd dictionary ID; the dictionary is the entry SQ INF/dictionaries/<id .zdict ; the frame must carry the ID; dictionaries are immutable while used; IDs below 32768 reserved by zstd are not used §4.3 . R8. A digest over serialised JSON Medium The draft hashed lines of <path LF <hex LF <json LF , with the metadata as JSON "with no whitespace". Two correct serialisers still differ: number forms 1e3 , 1000 , string escapes é , é , and member order inside attributes . An entry's attributes travel through entries.json in exploded form and back, so a round trip through another tool could change the digest of an unchanged cartridge and break its signatures. Fix. Length prefixed fields instead of lines, and metadata in RFC 8785 canonical JSON; writers store attributes canonically and validators report those that are not §9.2 . R9. The commit chain High Commit records point back to their predecessors, and readers walk that chain. The draft said a record "never points forward" but did not make the reader check it, so a hostile file could loop a record pointing to itself , point into data, or claim regions that overlap another commit's. Offsets plus sizes in 64 bits can also wrap. Fix. §3.4 lists the checks a reader applies to every commit it walks: sequence numbers strictly increase, the previous record lies before this commit's regions, regions lie inside this commit and do not overlap, the chain length increases by one. §3 requires overflow checked arithmetic. R10. Overlapping entries Medium Nothing stopped two records from naming overlapping bytes. David Fifield's "better zip bomb" builds a 42 kB file that inflates to terabytes by overlapping ZIP entries; Info ZIP's fix CVE 2019 13232 detects and rejects overlap. Overlap is also how two readers can be made to disagree about what is where. Fix. Runs are either identical deliberate sharing: renames, metadata only changes, unchanged chunks or disjoint; a reader refuses partial overlap §3.6 . Total work stays bounded by §3.8's limits. R11. Trailing bytes and polyglots High The draft ignored bytes after the current commit and signed only the content digest. Anything can therefore be appended to a signed cartridge, including a ZIP central directory: ZIP readers find an archive from its end, so the file becomes a valid 3.0 cartridge and a valid ZIP with different contents. Since 3.0 readers may also read 2.0 ZIP cartridges, one tool could see one cartridge and another a different one, both "signed". This is the shape of Android's Janus flaw CVE 2017 13156 : extra bytes the v1 signature did not cover let one file be both a signed APK and a DEX. Fix. The format is decided by the first bytes alone and a 3.0 file is never tried as ZIP §3.3, §13 ; trailing bytes are reported by validators; §9.4 states that only the state is signed and that a distributed cartridge should be compacted. R12. Symbolic links, and Zip Slip High Exploded form packs "the folder's files". A symbolic link in the folder would pack whatever it points to a key, a password file into a cartridge someone then shares. In the other direction, extractors keep being caught writing through links: Snyk's Zip Slip research, the Rust zip crate's CVE 2025 29787 a link earlier in the archive used by a later entry , and extract zip and decompress advisories that bypassed their own earlier fixes. 3.0 has no link entries, but unpack can still meet a link already in the target folder. Fix. Pack refuses links and never reads through one; unpack refuses a non empty target unless merging, creates files with O EXCL and without following links §6.1 . R13. Case collisions High The draft said "two paths that differ only by case are distinct". 2.0 §3.3 forbade that, for good reason: Android's shared storage, macOS, Windows and FAT fold case, so two such entries unpack to one file, and which one wins is up to the extractor. git's CVE 2021 21300 turned a case collision on such a file system into code execution on clone. 2.0 folded ASCII only; those file systems fold far more É and é . Fix. Restore 2.0's rule and widen it to Unicode full case folding after NFC. Pack converts macOS's NFD names to NFC first git needed core.precomposeunicode for the same thing . Unpack also refuses names Windows cannot create §4.1 . Later 2026 11 19 : a case sensitive opt in. Linux's kernel headers hold names that differ only by case xt MARK.h , xt mark.h , and sqterm's sysroot package carries them. A manifest's "case sensitive": true lets such a cartridge be read. What made R13 dangerous does not come back with it: the danger was one file overwriting another on a file system that folds case, and §6.1's unpack never overwrites each file is created exclusively , so there the second of two colliding paths fails with an error, and nothing is lost or replaced. A cartridge without the member keeps the rule. R14. A workspace packs its own working state Medium A workspace is an exploded cartridge, and the draft kept square's journal, staging and lock in .squared/ inside it. Exploded form's entries were "the folder's files", so packing a workspace would have packed its lock and journal, and .git/ too. Fix. The top level .squared/ and .git/ are never entries §6.1 . R15. Mapping alignment on 16 KiB pages Medium mmap needs a file offset that is a multiple of the page size. Android 15 supports 16 KiB pages and sqterm already links with max page size=16384 ; a mappable entry aligned to 4096 could not be mapped there. Fix. 16384 alignment §3.6 . apkpack stores .sq assets uncompressed and 16384 aligned so the same holds inside an APK §10.6 . R16. What "fsync" means Medium Pillai et al.'s study of crash consistency OSDI 2014, "All File Systems Are Not Created Equal" found that applications' commit protocols broke on file systems that reorder appends and renames, and that a rename is not durable until its folder is flushed. On macOS fsync does not flush the drive's cache; SQLite uses F FULLFSYNC . On Windows, a file open without FILE SHARE DELETE cannot be renamed over. Fix. §10.3 defines flush per system and flushes the folder when a file is created; §10.4 flushes the folder after compaction's rename and says what happens on Windows. R17. Android shared storage and FAT32 Medium Since Android 11, /sdcard is a FUSE file system: slower than private storage Google's own guidance says so , writable by other apps with storage permission, case folding, and of uncertain flock support. A removable card may be FAT32, where a file cannot reach 4 GiB, and a growing cartridge would fail mid commit. Fix. §10.6: change cartridges in private storage; refuse a commit that would pass FAT32's limit. This bears on the planned /sdcard/sqterm/packages folder: fine for packages pkg reads, not for cartridges the Drive changes. R18. Deceptive titles Low Titles exist to be shown in place of paths. A title with bidirectional override characters can display reversed or hide text, as the "Trojan Source" attack did in code CVE 2021 42574 . Fix. Tools show such characters visibly or strip them; writers should refuse control characters in titles and authors §4.2 . R19. JSON that parses two ways Medium Records, attributes, the manifest and entries.json are JSON. Parsers disagree on duplicate member names first wins, last wins, error and on integers beyond 2^53. A cartridge that two parsers read differently can pass a check in one tool and act differently in another. Fix. I JSON RFC 7493 for every JSON text, refused rather than guessed; nesting limit of 64 §5, §3.8 . R20. Version ranges Medium "As npm and Cargo write them" is two different languages: a bare 1.2.3 is exact in npm and ^1.2.3 in Cargo, and they treat pre releases differently. Fix. §8 defines one grammar and its meaning, with npm's pre release rule. R21. Signature details Medium The draft's signature block had no algorithm field, so moving off Ed25519 later would be a format break; its signer name was not signed, so anyone could relabel a signature "Squared Netizen"; and Ed25519 implementations differ in which edge case signatures they accept. Fix. An algorithm number and key length per signature; the signer name inside the signed message, and still never shown without its key; RFC 8032 §5.1.7 verification with non canonical encodings rejected; at most 16 signatures §9.3, A.5 . R22. Rollback Medium A signature covers a state. An old signed cartridge, or this one cut back to an earlier commit, still verifies. Update systems call this a rollback or freeze attack TUF's threat model ; signatures alone cannot prevent it. Fix. Stated in §9.4: consumers that install or update compare id and version with what they have and refuse to go backwards. R23. A second, unverified load path High Electron's asar integrity could be bypassed CVE 2024 46992 , and its documentation says integrity checking is only meaningful with onlyLoadAppFromAsar , because otherwise the app loads code from a folder beside the archive. A squared runtime that accepts both packed and exploded cartridges has the same exposure. Fix. §11: code is loaded only through a verifying reader, and a runtime never falls back to an exploded folder when a packed cartridge fails verification. R24. Changed after verification Medium A cartridge on shared storage can be rewritten by another app after a reader has verified it, including under a mapping. Fix. Stated in §9.1: a runtime that relies on a cartridge being unchanged copies it to private storage and verifies the copy, or verifies every read. R25. No streaming Low A ZIP can be read from a pipe; a 3.0 cartridge needs its header and then its last commit. That is inherent in an indexed, appendable file. Fix. Stated §3.3, the summary table : tools store a stream whole first. R26. Reproducible output Low Godot's documentation warns that re exporting the same project can give a slightly different PCK, which breaks delta patches. The draft's commit time and unspecified layout order would have done the same. Fix. §3.10 fixes the layout order and takes the commit time from SOURCE DATE EPOCH . R27. Metadata only changes Low Retitling a 2 GiB entry had to rewrite 2 GiB, because records could only name data in their own commit. Fix. Records and chunk tables may name runs from earlier commits §3.6 . This is also what makes R6's range writes cheap. R28. Exploded form loose ends Low Where an exploded cartridge's signature goes was undefined, and a file renamed by another program left a record in entries.json describing nothing. Fix. Exploded cartridges carry no signature; pack signatures from copies one across since the digest is unchanged; orphan records are reported, and pack refuses them unless told to drop them §6.1 . R29. The Drive's staging Low The draft put staging in <file .vcd/ beside the cartridge. A cartridge inside an APK, or on read only storage, has nowhere beside it to write. Fix. Staging belongs in the Drive's own storage §10.5 . Th

10. Changing a cartridge, and the Virtual Cartridge Drive
x: Squared Cartridge Specification, Version 3.0 Status: draft, 2026 11 18, revised the same day after a red team review sq cartridge 3.0 red team.md , which explains every change and its evidence , and with the hash, signature library and chunk size decided Appendix B.1 . Nothing here is implemented. Version 2.0 sq cartridge 2.0.md stays the normative format until this one is accepted and sqcart reads and writes it. Version 3.0 replaces the container. A cartridge is no longer a ZIP archive: it is a single file in a format of its own, built for four things ZIP was never built for: fast reads of one entry among millions , by binary search over a memory mapped index, with no parsing and no allocation; changes without rewriting the file , by appending entries and a new index, which is what the Virtual Cartridge Drive §10.5 needs; big entries read and changed piece by piece : an entry of many gigabytes is stored as chunks, each compressed, verified and replaced on its own §4.5 ; metadata on every entry : a title independent of the file name, r/w/x flags, an author, created and updated times, a media type. The manifest, its envelope and consumers 2.0 §5 carry over almost unchanged, so most of what a consumer knows survives. What changes is listed below. Area 2.0 3.0 Container ZIP APPNOTE 6.3.x profile own format: header, data blocks, sorted index, commit records §3 Compression Stored or Deflate Stored, zstd, zstd with a shared dictionary, or chunked §4.3, §4.5 Entry metadata a path and a size path, title, flags r, w, x , author, created, updated, media type, attributes §4.2 Changing a cartridge rewrite the archive append a commit; compact later §10 Integrity SQ INF/hashes.json a SHA 256 tree hash per entry in the index; the content digest in each commit §9 Signatures reserved defined: Ed25519 over the content digest §9.3 Dependencies not defined requires in the envelope, resolved offline by consumers §8 Structured data files also record entries: flat JSON arrays of objects §5 Exploded form SQ INF/manifest.json the same, plus SQ INF/entries.json for entry metadata §6 Workspaces squared pg's .squared/metadata.json a workspace is an exploded cartridge of kind workspace §6.2 Streaming a ZIP can be read front to back a 3.0 cartridge needs random access: it cannot be read from a pipe §3.3 0. Scope This document specifies the container, the entries in it, the manifest envelope, integrity, signatures, dependencies as data, and the on disk rules for changing a cartridge. It does not specify any consumer's section, any kind's meaning, or a trust policy: those stay with the tools that read them 2.0 §5.6, kept . The Virtual Cartridge Drive is a separate tool built on sqcart; §10.5 says where the line between them runs. The independence requirement of 2.0 §0.1 stands: a cartridge is usable by any tool that implements this document, with no squared pg, square or framework present. 1. Design goals In priority order, where they conflict: 1. Correct and recoverable. A crash at any moment leaves a cartridge that opens as its last completed commit. Nothing a reader is given can make it read outside the file or allocate without bound. 2. Fast, small reads. Opening a cartridge reads a fixed header and one commit record. Finding an entry is a binary search in a mapped index. Reading part of an entry decompresses and verifies that part alone. 3. Small files. zstd at high levels, shared dictionaries for many small similar entries, and already compressed data PNG, JPEG, zstd stored as it is. 4. Cheap changes. A commit costs what it changed, not the size of the cartridge, and not the size of a big entry it changed a little of. 5. Reproducible. The content digest depends on entries and their metadata, never on compression or layout §9.2 , and one writer given the same inputs and settings writes the same bytes §3.10 . Non goals: concurrent writers one writer at a time, §10.2 , byte level in place writes a change to an entry replaces whole chunks, §4.5 , reading from a stream, and network resolution of anything. 2. Terminology RFC 2119 key words. Cartridge , reader , writer , payload and kind as in 2.0 §2, and: Entry : one named item in a cartridge: a path, metadata, and content or a tombstone, §3.5 . Commit : one append of data, an index and a commit record §3.4 . A cartridge is the state named by its latest valid commit. Live entry : an entry in the current state, after deltas and tombstones are applied. Chunk : one 1 MiB piece of a chunked entry's content §4.5 . Compaction : rewriting a cartridge as a single commit holding only live entries §10.4 . The Drive : the Virtual Cartridge Drive, a separate tool that gives applications a mutable view of a cartridge §10.5 . 3. Container format All integers are little endian. Offsets and sizes are unsigned 64 bit, counted in bytes from the start of the file. Appendix A gives every structure byte by byte. Every sum and product a reader forms from values in the file an offset plus a size, a count times a record size MUST be checked for overflow before it is compared or used. 3.1 Layout A cartridge grows only at its end, except for the superblock slots, which a commit rewrites last §10.3 . The two slots are on separate 4096 byte pages, so that a torn write of one page, the unit storage writes, can damage at most one slot. 3.2 Header The first 8192 bytes. Page 0 begins with the magic 89 53 51 43 0D 0A 1A 0A \x89SQC\r\n\x1a\n . Like PNG's, it catches a file mangled by a text mode transfer, and it is never valid UTF 8. The magic is followed by the format's major and minor version 3, 0 , the header size, and superblock slot A . Page 1 holds superblock slot B . Each slot names a commit: its sequence number, its record's offset and length, the file length when it was made, and a checksum over the slot. Nothing else in the header ever changes after the file is created. Feature flags live in each commit record §3.9 , not in the header, so that setting one is part of a commit and as crash safe as the rest of it. 3.3 Opening a cartridge A 3.0 cartridge needs random access: the reader starts at the header and then reads wherever the commit points. A reader MUST be given a file or a buffer it can seek in; a tool that receives a cartridge as a stream a pipe, a download in progress stores it whole first. A reader: 1. checks the magic at offset 0 and the major version it MUST refuse a major version it does not know, and MUST open any minor version of one it knows . A file whose first bytes are the 3.0 magic is a 3.0 cartridge and nothing else: a reader MUST NOT also try to read it as ZIP or as any other format §13 ; 2. reads both superblock slots and keeps the ones whose checksum is correct, whose sequence number is not zero, and whose commit record lies inside the file; 3. takes the slot with the higher sequence number, and reads and checks that commit record §3.4 ; if it is damaged its magic, checksum or bounds fail , it falls back to the other slot. A commit that is intact but that the reader cannot or may not read a required feature it lacks, a limit of §3.8 is refused as it is, never passed over: the older commit is a state the cartridge has replaced; 4. refuses the cartridge when neither slot names a valid commit. The slot the reader settles on is the current slot ; the other is the spare slot . Bytes after the end of the current commit are trailing bytes : a commit that did not finish, or something appended by another tool. A reader MUST ignore them and a validator MUST report them §12 ; a writer MUST truncate them before appending §10.3 . They are covered by no checksum, digest or signature §9.4 . 3.4 Commits A commit is written in this order: 1. its data blocks: the content of every entry, or every chunk, that it adds or replaces §3.6 ; 2. its index: one record for every entry it adds, replaces or deletes §3.5 ; 3. its string table §3.7 ; 4. its chunk tables, if it writes chunked entries §4.5 ; 5. its commit record: sequence number, the previous commit's offset, where its data, index, strings and chunk tables are, whether its index is full or a delta, the number of live entries, its feature flags §3.9 , the content digest §9.2 , an optional signature block §9.3 , and a SHA 256 over the record. Only then is the spare superblock slot overwritten to name it §10.3 . A reader checks a commit record before using it: its magic and its SHA 256; its sequence number is greater than its previous commit's, and its previous commit record lies before its own data; every region it names data, index, strings, chunk tables, signature block lies after the previous commit record's end and before its own record, and no two regions overlap; its delta chain length is 0 for a full index and the previous commit's plus one for a delta, and is at most the limit §3.8 . A reader that walks the chain of previous commits §3.5 applies the same checks to each, and so can neither loop nor run off the file. 3.5 The index: full and delta An index is an array of fixed size entry records 128 bytes, Appendix A.3 , sorted by path: byte wise ascending over the UTF 8 bytes. Because records are fixed size and sorted, a reader finds a path by binary search over the mapped array, reading strings only to compare. A commit's index is either: full : every live entry, and no tombstones. The first commit's index is always full, and so is every compaction's; delta : only what this commit added, replaced or deleted. A deletion is a tombstone , a record with the deleted flag §4.2 and no content. To find a path, a reader searches the newest commit's index, then the one before it, until it finds the path or reaches a full index. A tombstone ends the search: the entry does not exist. To list entries, a reader merges the indexes the same way. A chain of delta indexes MUST NOT be longer than 32. A writer MUST write a full index, or compact, before a 33rd delta. This bounds a lookup to 33 binary searches in the worst case and to one after compaction. 3.6 Data blocks An entry's content, or a chunk's §4.5 , is one contiguous run of bytes, compressed or stored as its codec says §4.3 . A run starts on a 64 byte boundary. An entry with the mappable flag is stored, not chunked, and starts on a 16384 byte boundary, so that a reader can map it straight into memory a font, a texture, an audio buffer on a system with 4 KiB or 16 KiB pages. Padding between runs is zero bytes and belongs to no entry. A record or a chunk table MAY name a run written by an earlier commit: renaming an entry, changing only its metadata, or changing some chunks of a big entry then costs no copy of the unchanged content. A run MUST lie inside the data region of its own commit or of an earlier one, never in an index, string table, chunk table or commit record, and never after its own commit. Two references to stored content either name exactly the same run the same offset and stored size or runs that do not overlap. A reader MUST refuse partial overlaps: an archive whose entries overlap is the "better zip bomb" construction red team R10 . Content belongs to the commit that wrote it. A replaced or deleted entry's old content stays in the file, unreachable, until compaction. 3.7 String table Paths, titles, authors, media types and attribute objects are stored in a commit's string table: each string is a 32 bit length and its UTF 8 bytes, with no terminator. An entry record names a string by its offset in the table. Offset 0xFFFFFFFF means "none". A string's length and bytes MUST lie inside the table. A string table belongs to its commit. A delta commit's records name strings in that commit's own table only. 3.8 Limits A reader enforces limits, for every cartridge, before it allocates or maps anything 2.0 §3.4, kept and extended : Limit Default Notes Entries in one index 2^32 − 1 fixed by the record format Path length 1024 bytes String length 1 MiB an attribute object larger than this belongs in an entry Entry size, uncompressed 64 GiB a reader MAY lower it Unchunked entry size 64 MiB anything larger is chunked §4.5 Chunk size 1 MiB fixed §4.5 zstd window 2^27 bytes 128 MiB readers MUST support up to 2^23; a writer MUST NOT exceed the window its profile allows §4.3 Delta chain 32 §3.5 JSON nesting 64 levels the manifest, entries.json , attributes and record entries §5 Signatures in one block 16 §9.3 A reader MUST refuse a cartridge whose index, strings, chunk tables or data reach outside the file or outside the regions of §3.4 and §3.6, before using them. 3.9 Feature flags Each commit record carries 64 feature bits for the state it names. A bit in the low 32 is required : a reader that does not implement the feature MUST refuse the cartridge. A bit in the high 32 is optional : a reader MAY ignore it. 3.0 defines: Bit Name Set when 0 zstd dictionaries some live entry or chunk uses codec 2 §4.3 1 chunked some live entry uses codec 3 §4.5 2 zstd window 27 some frame needs a window larger than 2^23 §4.3 Every other bit is reserved and MUST be zero. Compaction recomputes the bits from the live entries. This replaces 2.0's requires features for container features. The envelope member stays for features of the payload 2.0 §5.4 . 3.10 Reproducible output A writer given the same entries, metadata, settings and commit time SHOULD write the same bytes. To make that possible this specification fixes the order of everything a writer lays out: runs in index order, then chunks in content order; strings in order of first use while writing the index; chunk tables in index order. A writer takes the commit time from SOURCE DATE EPOCH when it is set, and zstd settings that change its output level, window, long distance matching, dictionary from the profile, not from the machine thread count, free memory . 4. Entries 4.1 Paths Paths follow 2.0 §3.3 unchanged: relative, / separated, no . or .. segment, no empty segment, no NUL, backslash, : or control character, at most 1024 bytes, UTF 8 in Normalization Form C. Logical paths are case sensitive, and, as in 2.0, a cartridge MUST NOT hold two live entries whose paths would collide on a case insensitive file system. 3.0 widens 2.0's ASCII only rule: two paths collide when they are equal after Unicode full case folding Unicode CaseFolding.txt , status C and F and NFC. Android's shared storage, exFAT, FAT, macOS and Windows all fold case, and fold more than ASCII. Case sensitive cartridges. A manifest with "case sensitive": true §7 says the cartridge is for case sensitive file systems only, and the rule above does not apply to it: its live paths MAY collide under case folding, and a reader MUST NOT refuse it for that. They stay distinct paths logical paths are case sensitive . Unpacking it onto a file system that folds case fails, at the second of two colliding paths, rather than losing the first: §6.1's unpack never overwrites. It is for content that holds such names already, as Linux's kernel headers do linux/netfilter/xt MARK.h and xt mark.h , in sqterm's sysroot package . case sensitive MUST be true or false when present; absent is false . A writer SHOULD warn about, and sqcart unpack MUST refuse, a path that cannot be created as a file on the target system: on Windows, a segment named CON , PRN , AUX , NUL , COM1 – COM9 or LPT1 – LPT9 with or without an extension , or ending in a dot or a space. SQ INF/ stays reserved 2.0 §4 . SQ INF/manifest.json MUST be a live entry in every commit's state. 4.2 Metadata Every entry record carries: Field Type Meaning path string the entry's name; the key title string or none a human title, independent of the path "Northern Province, 1802" ; readers SHOULD show it where they would show a name author string or none who made this entry; free text, by convention Name <email media type string or none an IANA media type image/png , application/json , text/markdown , or a vnd. one §5 created int64 milliseconds since 1970 01 01 UTC; 0 means unknown updated int64 the same, for the last change; 0 means unknown flags 16 bits below codec 16 bits §4.3 size uint64 uncompressed bytes stored size uint64 bytes of the run, or of the chunk table for codec 3 offset uint64 where the run or the chunk table starts §3.6, §4.5 dictionary uint32 for codec 2, the zstd dictionary ID §4.3 ; otherwise 0 digest 32 bytes the entry's tree hash §9.1 attributes string or none a JSON object of further metadata, defined by consumers Titles, authors and attribute values are text meant for people, and a tool that shows them MUST NOT let them deceive: it shows control characters and Unicode bidirectional controls U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069 visibly, or strips them, rather than letting them reorder or hide what is around them red team R18 . A writer SHOULD refuse titles and authors containing control characters. Flags. Bit Name Meaning 0 r readable: offered to the runtime and to consumers. An entry without r is kept for tools only sources, build notes and a runtime reader MUST NOT hand it to application code 1 w writable: the Drive and other writers may replace or delete it. A writer MUST refuse to change an entry without w unless it is rebuilding the cartridge from its sources 2 x executable: a runtime may run it Lua source, 2.0 §7 . It never makes a file executable on disk 2.0 §3.1, kept , and native code stays forbidden 2.0 §8 3 deleted a tombstone §3.5 4 mappable stored, 16384 aligned, for direct mapping §3.6 5 dictionary this entry is a zstd dictionary §4.3 ; it carries no r 6–15 reserved, zero The flags describe intent, not access control: a cartridge is a file, and anyone with the file can read every byte of it. They let readers, the Drive and tools agree on what an entry is for. r , w and x are covered by the content digest §9.2 , so changing one is a change a signature notices. created and updated are metadata like a title, not file times: a writer copies them from where the entry came from, or sets them from a caller supplied epoch for reproducible builds. They are covered by the content digest §9.2 . A tombstone has no title, author, media type or attributes, codec 0, offset, sizes and dictionary of 0, and a digest of zero bytes. An entry with no content size 0 has codec 0, offset 0 and stored size 0. 4.3 Codecs and compression Codec Name Content 0 stored the bytes as they are 1 zstd one zstd frame 2 zstd dict one zstd frame compressed with a dictionary; dictionary holds its ID 3 chunked a chunk table; the content is in chunks, each stored, zstd or zstd dict §4.5 Deflate is gone. zstd decompresses several times faster than Deflate and compresses smaller at its high levels, and squared already carries a zstd decoder sqterm's packages . Frames. A run of codec 1 or 2 is exactly one zstd frame RFC 8878 and nothing else: no skippable frames, no second frame, no bytes after it. The frame header MUST give the content size, and it MUST equal the entry's or the chunk's size. A reader checks that before it allocates, sets the decoder's window limit ZSTD d windowLogMax to what it supports, and stops decoding at the declared size: a frame header can lie, and an untrusted size must never drive an unbounded allocation red team R5 . A stored run's stored size equals its size. Choosing. A writer SHOULD store an entry whose content is already compressed, or would shrink by less than 5% PNG, JPEG, WebP, zstd, audio , and SHOULD compress everything else. Maximum compression. A writer offers profiles, as zstd does: Profile zstd level Window For fast 3 ≤ 2^23 the Drive's commits, development builds small default 19 ≤ 2^23 distributed cartridges max 22, with long distance matching ≤ 2^27 archives where size matters most and readers have memory to spare A reader MUST support windows up to 2^23 bytes 8 MiB and MAY refuse a larger one. A cartridge with a larger window sets the required feature bit zstd window 27 §3.9 , so a phone sized reader can refuse it cleanly before it decodes anything. Chunks are 1 MiB §4.5 , so a window larger than that gains a chunked entry nothing. Dictionaries. Many small, s
