x: section: "2.10" title: Assets and generator resources status: review tags: spec, architecture, resources, assets 2.10 Assets and generator resources !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.9 Kits · Next: 2.11 Packages !abstract Scope Defines what an asset is and how generator resources are stored and discovered. How assets are materialized is 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.7. Purpose Defines the asset resource and the storage, namespacing, and discovery rules for all generator owned resources. Outline x resource storage namespaces x generator internal resources x asset manifest block x asset type vocabulary x transformation declaration x platform placement x integrity x ownership x validation Content 2.10.1 Resource storage Generator resources live under resources/ 1.5 Resources : !note Resolution of Q 18 D 018 The earlier draft defined a "generator assets" category with no home. resources/generator/ is that home. Resources under it are generator owned and MUST NOT be materialized into a generated project . resources/assets/ remains project bound only. resources/assets/ is an Android style application asset tree, per the project vision: it holds the default application assets materialized into generated projects, including the default Android assets. Physical layout beneath any namespace is a maintainer convenience and MUST NOT be part of a contract. Every resource is addressed by identity. 2.10.2 Asset categories Category Provided by Ends up Owned after generation by Generator resources/generator/ never in a project generator Framework packages project project Kit kits project project Application resources/assets/ project user The generated project MUST distinguish these. A generator owned resource MUST NOT silently become a user editable application asset. 2.10.3 Asset manifest block 2.10.4 Asset type vocabulary asset type is drawn from a closed vocabulary so the engine can validate and route without interpreting file contents: binary is the escape hatch: an opaque payload copied without interpretation. It MUST NOT be used to smuggle a type that has a proper vocabulary entry. 2.10.5 Transformation A transformation is an engine capability token 2.14 Extensibility model . The manifest names a transformation per platform; copy is the identity transformation. Transformations MUST be deterministic: identical source, settings, and engine version MUST produce equivalent output, and SHOULD produce byte identical output where the transformation is not timestamp or ordering sensitive. A transformation whose capability is unavailable MUST fail at resolution , never at materialization — the workflow must learn it cannot proceed before anything is written. Pattern: Strategy, keyed by asset type and target platform. 2.10.6 Platform placement target maps platform to workspace relative destination. The template and applied kits determine which platforms are active; the Asset Service MUST NOT assume a universal layout. An asset with no target entry for an active platform is skipped, and the skip MUST be reported as a diagnostic rather than passing silently. 2.10.7 Integrity Assets SHOULD declare an integrity digest. Where declared, the Resource Service MUST verify it before the asset enters generation, and MUST fail with asset.integrity on mismatch. This is what makes an offline resource tree trustworthy after being copied, archived, or restored. 2.10.8 Ownership During generation the engine owns resolved asset state, transformation state, temporary files, and staging resources. After finalization the project owns materialized application assets. Materialized asset paths carry an ownership class exactly as template paths do. Application assets are seeded by default: the generator seeds them once and the user owns them thereafter. 2.10.9 Validation Assets MUST be validated for envelope correctness, identity and version syntax, asset type validity, source availability, integrity where declared, transformation availability, target declarations for active platforms, and package requirements. Invalid assets MUST NOT silently enter the pipeline. Related 1.5 Resources · 2.7 Project generation model · 2.11 Packages · 2.8 Templates · 2.14 Extensibility model

section: "2.11" title: Packages status: review tags: spec, architecture, resources, packages 2.11 Packages !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.10 Assets and generator resources · Next: 2.12 Generated project boundary !abstract Scope Defines what a package is . How a package is resolved and materialized is 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.6. Manifest envelope and identity grammar are 2.8 Templates §2.8.1–2.8.4. Purpose Defines the package resource: a versioned, identifiable unit of reusable Squared framework functionality, and the algorithm that resolves package graphs deterministically. Outline x what a package is x package manifest block x dependency resolution algorithm and complexity x conflict detection and reporting x compatibility declarations x build integration metadata x feature configuration x offline availability x integrity x validation x migrations x reference package set Content 2.11.1 What a package is A package provides reusable Squared framework functionality: C++ sources, public headers, libraries, build targets, configuration, framework services, runtime resources, tests, and documentation. A package MUST expose functionality through documented public interfaces and MUST NOT require the generator to understand its private implementation. A package MUST NOT redefine the architectural role of the selected template. 2.11.2 Package manifest block supported templates: " " means the package places no template constraint. 2.11.3 Dependency resolution Resolution MUST complete before any materialization. Algorithm — deterministic, and specified rather than promised: 1. Seed the constraint set from the workflow request, plus requirements declared by the resolved template and kits. 2. Maintain a work queue of unresolved identities, processed in sorted identity order. 3. For each identity, select the highest version satisfying all accumulated constraints 2.8 Templates §2.8.2 . 4. Add the selected version's dependencies as new constraints. 5. If a newly added constraint invalidates an already selected version, backtrack: reselect that identity at the next highest satisfying version, visiting candidates in descending order. 6. Terminate when the queue is empty success or when an identity has no satisfying candidate failure . Backtracking MUST be bounded. Implementations MUST impose a documented step limit and, on exceeding it, fail with package.resolution.exhausted rather than running unbounded — a generator that hangs on Termux is worse than one that refuses. Complexity: worst case exponential in the number of backtracking identities, as for any version solver. In practice the graph is small and shallow; the step limit bounds the pathological case. The developer docs MUST record the chosen limit and its rationale. The dependency graph MUST be acyclic. A cycle MUST be reported with the full cycle path, not merely detected. 2.11.4 Conflict reporting A resolution failure MUST identify: the identity that could not be satisfied; every constraint acting on it, and which resource declared each; the versions that were considered and why each was rejected. A conflict error that says only "no compatible version" is insufficient; the workflow and the user need the constraint set to act. 2.11.5 Compatibility Packages MAY declare compatibility against framework version, templates, kits, platforms, other packages, and engine capabilities. The engine validates and reports. Lua decides the response: another package, another kit, another template, amended configuration, or termination. The engine MUST NOT silently alter the requested project design. 2.11.6 Build integration Packages declare build integration as structured data , not as build system text. The engine emits build files for the target build system from that data. This keeps packages independent of any one build system and is what allows an Android project to consume the same package declaration as a desktop one. The generated project MUST contain enough emitted build configuration to rebuild without the generator. Developers MUST NOT need knowledge of Package Service internals. 2.11.7 Feature configuration Features are declared with defaults and constraints. Configuration crosses as structured data: Feature configuration MUST NOT depend on interactive prompts, environment variables, or ambient generator state. Lua gathers; the engine validates and applies. A feature whose constraints are unsatisfied MUST fail at resolution. 2.11.8 Offline availability Packages MUST be resolvable from declared offline sources. The Package Service MUST NOT implicitly require network access when an offline source is declared authoritative. If a required package is unavailable offline the engine MUST return a structured resolution error. Network acquisition MAY exist as an optional extension, but MUST NOT become an implicit requirement of the core generator 1.13 Repository invariant . 2.11.9 Integrity and validation Packages SHOULD declare an integrity digest, verified before entering the pipeline. Validation covers envelope and type block correctness, identity and version syntax, dependency availability and compatibility, framework/template/kit/platform compatibility, required engine capabilities, build declaration well formedness, feature declarations, and integrity. Invalid packages MUST NOT silently enter the pipeline. 2.11.10 Migrations A package version change requiring more than file replacement MUST declare migration rules, applied as part of the update transaction 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.11 . A required but unavailable migration MUST fail the update. 2.11.11 Reference package set Open questions Q 22 — build emission model, shared with 2.9 Kits . Related 2.7 Project generation model · 2.8 Templates · 2.9 Kits · 2.13 Dependency graph · 2.15 Error and transaction model

section: "2.12" title: Generated project boundary status: review tags: spec, architecture, boundary, ownership, invariant 2.12 Generated project boundary !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.11 Packages · Next: 2.13 Dependency graph !note Scope D 006a This section states the guarantee . The mechanism — ownership classes, provenance, conflict detection, ownership transfer — is 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.10 and §2.7.12 and is not restated here. Keeping the guarantee separate from the mechanism means it can be checked without reading the generation model. Purpose States, in checkable terms, what a generated project may never contain and may never require. This is the promise squared pg makes to every project it creates. Outline x the independence guarantee x the leakage prohibition x the preservation guarantee x the reproducibility guarantee x what the generator retains x how the guarantee is verified Content 2.12.1 Independence guarantee A generated project MUST NOT require squared pg to be present in order to: build; run; test; version control; relocate to another path, machine, or filesystem; share or distribute. Deleting squared pg entirely, or deleting the workspace's .squared/ metadata, MUST leave a fully working project. The only capability lost is the optional regeneration and update workflow. The generated project depends on the Squared framework. It MUST NOT depend on the generator that created it. squared pg creates the relationship. It is not part of it. 2.12.2 Leakage prohibition A generated project MUST NOT contain: generator implementation source; generator service interfaces, headers, or symbols; references to the generator repository layout; generator internal identifiers in build configuration; absolute paths to the generator installation; machine specific paths of any kind; resources from resources/generator/ ; generator internal state, handles, or temporary artifacts. A generated project MAY contain generator authored files. It MUST NOT contain generator coupled files. The distinction: an authored file works after the generator is deleted; a coupled file does not. 2.12.3 Preservation guarantee The generator MUST NOT destroy user work. A file the user authored is never overwritten. A file the generator seeded and the user then modified is never overwritten without explicit, per operation authorization. A path the generator did not create is never deleted. Any operation that would violate the above is reported as a conflict and requires explicit action. A blanket override mode MAY exist. It MUST be explicit, MUST NOT be the default, and MUST report every path it overwrites. 2.12.4 Reproducibility guarantee Given the recorded generation configuration and the same resource versions, the generator MUST resolve the same resource set and SHOULD produce byte identical output where no timestamp or ordering sensitive content is involved Spec conventions . The workspace records what produced it, so this is checkable rather than assumed. 2.12.5 What the generator retains After finalization the generator retains nothing : no lock, no handle, no reference, no background state, no requirement to be run again. The workspace metadata record is generator written but user owned . The user may delete it, edit it, or commit it to version control. 2.12.6 Verification The guarantee is testable and SHOULD be tested. A conformance check for a generated project: Check Method Independence build the project with the generator absent from the machine Leakage grep the workspace for the generator install path, repository paths, and internal symbol prefixes Relocatability move the workspace to a different path and rebuild Metadata optionality delete .squared/ and rebuild Preservation modify a seeded file, regenerate, assert the modification survives Reproducibility generate twice from the same configuration and diff the resolved set These checks belong in the generator's own test suite. An untested guarantee is a claim see 2.16 Architectural invariants . Related 2.7 Project generation model · 1.11 Dependency direction · 2.13 Dependency graph · 2.16 Architectural invariants

section: "2.13" title: Dependency graph status: review tags: spec, architecture, dependencies 2.13 Dependency graph !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.12 Generated project boundary · Next: 2.14 Extensibility model !success Unblocks §1.11 1.11 Dependency direction defers the authoritative graph to this section. D 026 resolves it. Purpose Defines the authoritative dependency relationships between every repository component, the resource tree, the Squared framework, and generated projects. Outline x authoritative direction x per component permitted dependencies x resources as inert data x third party constraints x generated projects as sinks x the framework's position x prohibited edges x acyclicity and justified cycles x enforcement and testing Content 2.13.1 Authoritative direction Arrows point from dependent to dependency. The graph is acyclic. 2.13.2 Per component rules third party/ — a leaf. Depends on nothing in the repository. May be depended on by engine/ only. lua/ MUST NOT depend on vendored C sources directly; it reaches Lua libraries through the runtime the engine embeds. Third party code MUST NOT define Squared project architecture. engine/ — depends on third party/ and on the C++ standard library. Depends on resources/ only as data , reached through the Resource Service by identity. MUST NOT depend on lua/ workflow code; it exposes a binding surface, it does not consume workflows. MUST NOT depend on generated projects. lua/ — depends on the engine public API through the binding layer. MUST NOT depend on engine internals, on third party/ sources, on resources/ layout, or on generated projects. Reaches resources by identity only. resources/ — inert data with no outgoing dependencies . Resources declare dependencies on other resources in their manifests, which the engine resolves; those declarations are data, not code coupling. A resource MUST NOT reference engine/ or lua/ implementation. hosts the CLI, embedding applications, tools — depend on engine/ , and on lua/ when they host workflows. Nothing in the repository depends on a host. Generated projects — sinks. Depend on the Squared framework and on their own declared external dependencies. Nothing in squared pg may depend on a generated project 2.12 Generated project boundary . Squared framework — external to this repository. Consumed by generated projects. The framework MUST NOT depend on squared pg . 2.13.3 Resource dependency sub graph Resources depend on each other through manifest declarations, resolved by the engine: Prohibited edges in this sub graph: package template — a package MUST NOT require a specific template as a dependency; it MAY declare template compatibility , which is a constraint, not an edge. asset anything — assets are leaves. An asset MAY declare package requirements as compatibility constraints, not as dependencies it pulls in. Any cycle. The resource dependency graph MUST be acyclic, and cycles MUST be reported with the full path. The distinction between a dependency pulls the target into the resolved set and a compatibility constraint restricts what the resolved set may contain is load bearing and MUST be preserved in manifests. 2.13.4 Prohibited edges, summarised From To Why engine/ lua/ the engine must be usable without any workflow engine/ generated project generated projects are outputs lua/ engine internals boundary violation lua/ third party/ sources reaches libraries through the engine runtime resources/ any code resources are inert data anything generated project outputs are never dependencies Squared framework squared pg the framework must stand alone 2.13.5 Acyclicity The graph MUST be acyclic. A deliberate cycle requires an explicit decision entry in Spec decisions naming the cycle, the justification, and the mechanism that prevents it from becoming load bearing. No such cycle currently exists. 2.13.6 Enforcement A dependency rule that is not tested decays. The following SHOULD be enforced automatically: Rule Mechanism engine/ does not include lua/ workflow code include path check in CI lua/ does not reach engine internals binding surface is the only registered API; audit registered symbols resources/ contains no executable code file type check over resource roots Resource graph is acyclic resolver rejects cycles at initialization; test with a deliberate cycle fixture No absolute host paths in generated output grep check in the generated project conformance suite Component build isolation engine/ builds and its tests pass with lua/ absent The last check is the strongest single guarantee: if the engine builds and tests green without the Lua layer present, the capability/orchestration split is real rather than aspirational. Related 1.11 Dependency direction · 2.1 Architectural model · 1.6 Third party dependencies · 2.12 Generated project boundary · 2.16 Architectural invariants

h: 2.14.1.1 How a resource demands a capability
x: section: "2.14" title: Extensibility model status: review tags: spec, architecture, extensibility, capabilities 2.14 Extensibility model !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.13 Dependency graph · Next: 2.15 Error and transaction model Purpose Defines how squared pg is extended without modifying core generator code — the mechanism behind the vision's requirement that the Lua layer remain programmable after release, and that the generator be embeddable in other tools. Outline x engine capability tokens x extension services x Lua workflows: discovery and loading x Lua trust model and sandboxing x custom resources x compatibility and versioning x what an extension may never do Content 2.14.1 Engine capability tokens !note Resolution of Q 05 D 023 , amended by D 053 This is the registry that gives a resource's capability requirements meaning. The original note said four manifest types declare requires capabilities as a cartridge envelope field; that stopped being true when cartridge format 2.0 trimmed the envelope. See §2.14.1.1. A capability token is a named, versioned engine feature. Rules: Tokens follow the identifier grammar of 2.8 Templates §2.8.1 with the type capability , and are versioned as SemVer. The capability set is compiled into the engine and MUST be enumerable through the control surface. Extensions MAY register additional tokens at initialization; they MUST NOT redefine an existing one. A resource declaring capability requirements is satisfied when every token is present at a version satisfying its constraint. Unsatisfied requirements MUST fail at resolution , never at materialization. The workflow must learn it cannot proceed before anything is written. 2.14.1.1 How a resource demands a capability A resource declares its requirements in its own consumer section §2.8.6, §2.9.2 : Each entry is name or name@range . A bare name is satisfied by any version. Nothing validates the token's grammar before the engine sees it. Cartridge format 2.0 carries the consumer section as opaque text §5.6 , so a malformed token arrives here rather than being refused at open. That is correct: this engine owns the capability. namespace and is the only party that can say which capability is missing and what provides it. A container reader could only ever have said that a string it did not understand looked wrong. 2.14.1.2 requires features is a different thing The cartridge envelope retains requires features , and the contrast is the reason it does: Guards Declared in Fails requires features the reader the cartridge envelope at open , before anything else requires.capabilities the consumer the consumer section at resolution A cartridge whose reader is too old cannot be opened at all — it may use a compression method or a signature scheme the reader does not implement, and only the container format can define what a reader must provide. A cartridge whose consumer is too old opens perfectly well and must be refused later, by that consumer, for reasons the container format has no opinion about. Stated as a rule: a newer sqcart satisfies requires features ; a newer generator satisfies requires.capabilities . They are not alternatives and a resource may need both. Capability versions are part of the public contract. Removing or narrowing a capability is a breaking change and MUST be documented. 2.14.2 Extension services Extension services expand engine functionality without modifying the core. They MAY provide additional template processors, package providers, platform integrations, validation systems, resource handlers, asset transformers, or build emitters. An extension service MUST declare its identity, version, compatibility requirements, the capability tokens it provides, and the ones it requires. It MUST expose explicit APIs, follow engine ownership rules, and register through the controlled mechanism. An extension service MUST NOT replace or modify a core service. A core service is part of the engine's contract; an extension that could swap one out would make that contract unverifiable. Extensions add; they do not substitute. A missing optional extension MUST be reported but MUST NOT prevent operation unless an active workflow requires a capability only it provides. Extensions participate in the shutdown lifecycle 2.4 Engine lifecycle §2.4.9 and MUST NOT prevent core cleanup. 2.14.3 Lua workflow discovery !note Resolution of Q 16, part 1 D 016 Workflows are discovered from an ordered search path: Each workflow directory contains workflow.json declaring: Discovery is deterministic: search paths in declared order, entries within a path sorted. A later path MAY shadow an earlier identity only when the host explicitly enables shadowing; otherwise a duplicate identity is an error. Workflow capability requirements are checked at load, so a workflow that cannot run fails before it starts rather than midway. 2.14.4 Trust model !note Resolution of Q 16, part 2 D 016 Two tiers: trusted — the repository's own workflows and workflows in the user's configuration directory. Full Lua 5.4 standard library. These are the user's own code, on the user's own machine. sandboxed — everything else, including project local workflows and anything obtained from a third party. Default for any workflow that does not declare otherwise, and the only tier a host may grant to downloaded content. Sandboxed workflows run without: os.execute , os.remove , os.rename , os.tmpname package.loadlib and C module loading the debug library raw io write access load / loadstring over arbitrary strings Sandboxed workflows reach the filesystem only through engine services, which is where provenance, validation, and transactions already live. They may read declared input paths supplied by the host. A workflow MUST NOT elevate its own trust tier. Trust is assigned by the host, not claimed by the workflow — a trust field in workflow.json is a request , and the host MAY refuse it. 2.14.5 Custom resources Users MAY author custom templates, kits, packages, and assets. A custom resource is an ordinary resource: same manifest envelope, same identity grammar, same validation. It is placed on a resource search path and indexed like any other. Custom resources SHOULD use a vendor segment kit.acme.raylib and MUST NOT use a reserved namespace 2.8 Templates §2.8.1 . Nothing about authoring a custom resource requires modifying the engine. If it does, that is a defect in the resource model, not a reason to modify the engine. 2.14.6 Compatibility and versioning Extensions declare an engine version constraint and capability constraints. The engine MUST refuse to load an extension whose constraints it cannot satisfy, and MUST report why. Breaking changes to the capability set, the manifest schema, the operation registry, or the binding surface are compatibility changes and MUST be documented with a migration path 2.6 Engine Lua boundary §2.6.15 . 2.14.7 Prohibitions An extension MUST NOT: replace or modify a core service; bypass the resource index, validation, or the transaction system; write to a workspace except through engine services; register a capability token that already exists; elevate its own trust tier; require network access in the core generation path; introduce non determinism into resolution. Related 2.4 Engine lifecycle · 2.5 Lua control layer · 2.8 Templates · 2.10 Assets and generator resources · 2.6 Engine Lua boundary

x: section: "2.15" title: Error and transaction model status: review tags: spec, architecture, errors, transactions 2.15 Error and transaction model !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.14 Extensibility model · Next: 2.16 Architectural invariants Purpose Defines how failures are detected, classified, and reported, and the transaction mechanics that make "leave the workspace unchanged" a guarantee rather than an intention. Outline x error structure, categories, codes x recoverable vs fatal x propagation and machine readability x logging vs errors x transaction model and staging strategy x the journal and crash recovery x durability policy x workspace locking x rollback failure x validation before mutation Content Part 1 — Errors 2.15.1 Error structure !note Resolution of Q 17 D 017 Two identifier fields: a coarse category for control flow, and a stable dotted code for diagnosis and documentation. category is closed so a workflow can exhaustively switch on it. code is open within its category so new specific failures can be added without a breaking change. 2.15.2 Categories internal means a defect in the engine. It MUST NOT be used for any failure the user could have caused, because a user cannot act on it. 2.15.3 Codes Codes are <category .<subject .<condition : Every code MUST be documented in docs/programmer/ . A code is part of the public contract: workflows branch on codes, so removing or repurposing one is a breaking change. Example: That diagnostic is actionable. "No compatible version found" is not. 2.15.4 Recoverable and fatal Recoverable — the workflow may reasonably continue by choosing differently: missing optional assets, unavailable optional packages, unsupported configuration options, validation failures the user can correct. The engine SHOULD supply enough information to choose an alternative. Fatal — execution cannot safely continue: corrupted resource metadata, invalid engine state, transaction failure, internal consistency failure. The operation MUST fail, dependent operations MUST NOT execute, the engine MUST remain in a defined state, and cleanup MUST remain possible. The engine classifies. Lua decides policy: retry, alternative, report, or abort. The engine MUST NOT enforce user facing behaviour. 2.15.5 Propagation Errors travel through the same result channel as successes 2.4 Engine lifecycle §2.4.7 . The engine MUST NOT terminate the host process, report failures only as console output, hide failures behind partial success, or let exceptions cross the Lua boundary. Internal exceptions MUST be converted before crossing; if conversion itself fails, the boundary emits internal with the operation identity attached 2.6 Engine Lua boundary §2.6.12 . Errors MUST be machine readable. IDE integrations, automation, and build systems MUST be able to determine failure without parsing human output. 2.15.6 Logging is not error reporting The engine MAY provide diagnostic logging. Logs are for debugging and troubleshooting. Results and errors are for control flow and automation. Logs MUST NOT replace structured errors, and a workflow MUST NEVER need to read a log to determine what happened. Part 2 — Transactions 2.15.7 Validation before mutation The complete resource set MUST be resolved and cross validated before the first workspace mutation 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.9 . Most failures should therefore occur before a transaction is ever opened — the transaction system exists for the failures that cannot be predicted, chiefly filesystem ones. 2.15.8 Staging strategy !note Resolution of Q 06 D 024 The hardest requirement here is Termux/Android, where /tmp is frequently on a different filesystem and cross device rename 2 fails. Staging therefore always occurs on the target filesystem , so cross device rename cannot arise. New project generation. Build the entire workspace in a sibling temporary directory, then land it with one rename: If anything fails, the temporary directory is removed and the target never existed. This is the simple case and MUST be used whenever the target does not yet exist. Regeneration. The workspace already exists, so a single rename is not available. Stage per file inside the workspace: Apply by renaming each staged file into place, recording progress in the journal. The engine MUST NOT stage in /tmp , TMPDIR , or any location not known to be on the workspace filesystem. 2.15.9 The journal The journal is a write ahead record making an interrupted transaction recoverable. States: Protocol: 1. Write every staged file. Write the journal in prepared . Flush the journal and its directory. 2. Transition to committing and flush. 3. Apply each operation in journal order, renaming staged content into place and moving replaced content to its backup path first. 4. Transition to committed and flush. 5. Remove staging and the journal. A file that is replaced MUST have its previous content moved to a backup path before the new content lands, so rollback never depends on regenerating anything. 2.15.10 Crash recovery On opening a workspace the engine MUST check for a journal. If one exists, the workspace is in an indeterminate state and the engine MUST NOT begin a new transaction. Journal state Meaning Action prepared nothing applied roll back: discard staging committing partially applied resolvable either way; default is roll back using backups committed fully applied complete cleanup: remove staging and journal rolling back rollback interrupted resume rollback Recovery MUST be idempotent — interrupting recovery and re running it MUST reach the same state. The engine MUST report the recovery to the caller as a diagnostic rather than performing it silently. A user whose generation was killed deserves to know their workspace was repaired. Recovery MUST NOT run automatically as a side effect of an unrelated operation unless the caller requested it; it is an explicit operation with an explicit result. 2.15.11 Durability policy Two modes, because Termux and a CI machine want different tradeoffs: Mode Behaviour durable default fsync staged content before rename; fsync the journal and its directory at each state transition fast fsync only the journal state transitions fast remains crash consistent — the journal still describes what happened — but may lose recently written content on power loss. It MUST be opt in and MUST be recorded in the operation result so the caller knows which was used. 2.15.12 Workspace locking !note Related to Q 15 D 015 Exactly one writer per workspace. <workspace /.squared/lock holds the process id, a start timestamp, and a generator version. Acquisition is exclusive; the lock is released at shutdown, including failure shutdown. A stale lock — the recorded process no longer exists — MAY be broken, and the break MUST be reported. A lock held by a live process MUST NOT be broken; the operation fails with transaction.locked . Read only operations, including producing a plan, do not require the lock. 2.15.13 Rollback failure Rollback can itself fail, typically on permission or space exhaustion. There must be a defined terminal state rather than undefined behaviour. On rollback failure the engine MUST: mark the journal damaged with the failing operation recorded; fail with transaction.rollback failed ; refuse further mutating operations on that workspace until the journal is resolved; leave the journal, staging content, and backups in place, since they are the only route to manual repair. The engine MUST provide an operation to inspect a damaged journal and report what was and was not applied. It MUST NOT silently delete a damaged journal — that would destroy the user's only recovery information. 2.15.14 Transaction invariants No workspace mutation occurs outside a transaction. Every replaced or deleted path has a backup before the change lands. A failed transaction leaves the workspace unchanged or restored. An interrupted transaction is detectable and resolvable on next open. Recovery is idempotent. One writer per workspace. The engine never leaves the workspace in a state its metadata does not describe. Staging never crosses a filesystem boundary. Open questions Q 24 — metadata format migration. .squared/ is versioned, but there is no rule for a newer generator opening an older record. Proposal: readers are forward compatible within a major version and refuse and report across one. Related 2.4 Engine lifecycle · 2.7 Project generation model · 2.6 Engine Lua boundary · 2.3 Generation pipeline

h: 2.16.1 The four that outrank the rest
x: section: "2.16" title: Architectural invariants status: review tags: spec, architecture, invariant 2.16 Architectural invariants !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.15 Error and transaction model Purpose States the properties that MUST remain true regardless of implementation change, names the section establishing each, and names how each is detected. This is the checklist a reviewer holds a proposed change against. Outline x invariant list x source section per invariant x detection mechanism per invariant x the four invariants that outrank the rest Content 2.16.1 The four that outrank the rest If a change forces a choice, these win: 1. User work is never destroyed. 2.12 Generated project boundary 2. Generated projects do not depend on the generator. 2.12 Generated project boundary 3. The engine provides capability; Lua provides orchestration. 2.1 Architectural model 4. Everything works offline from a clean checkout. 1.13 Repository invariant Everything else is a means to these. 2.16.2 Invariant register Invariant Established by Detection I 01 Capability and orchestration remain separate 2.1 Architectural model engine/ builds and its tests pass with lua/ absent I 02 The engine never decides workflow policy 2.2 Engine responsibility and role no engine symbol names a template, kit, or workflow; audited by grep over the public API I 03 Component boundaries are explicit 2.13 Dependency graph include path and registered symbol checks in CI I 04 The dependency graph is acyclic 2.13 Dependency graph resolver rejects cycles; deliberate cycle fixture in tests I 05 Resource resolution is deterministic 2.8 Templates resolve twice from one configuration, diff the resolved set I 06 Output is reproducible where not time sensitive Spec conventions generate twice, diff the workspace excluding declared volatile fields I 07 Resource identity is independent of filesystem layout 2.4 Engine lifecycle relocate a resource root, assert identical resolution I 08 Generation is offline 1.13 Repository invariant full generation suite in a network isolated environment I 09 No generated project dependency on generator internals 2.12 Generated project boundary build a generated project with the generator absent I 10 No undocumented global state 2.4 Engine lifecycle two engine instances in one process produce identical independent results; no non const namespace scope variables in engine/ , enforced by clang tidy I 11 Ownership and lifetime are explicit 2.4 Engine lifecycle ASan/LSan clean on the full suite; no raw owning pointers, enforced by clang tidy I 12 The public API is stable and versioned 2.2 Engine responsibility and role exported symbol and operation registry snapshot compared per release I 13 Workflows remain programmable after release 2.14 Extensibility model a custom workflow and custom resource load from the user path with no engine change I 14 Failure leaves a valid state 2.15 Error and transaction model fault injection suite: fail at each generation phase, assert workspace and engine validity I 15 Interrupted transactions are recoverable 2.15 Error and transaction model kill the process at each journal state, assert recovery reaches a consistent state I 16 User work is never destroyed 2.12 Generated project boundary workspace.verify reports a modified generated class file before a regeneration could overwrite it §2.16.5 ; and modify a seeded file, regenerate, assert survival I 17 Operations behave identically regardless of caller 2.4 Engine lifecycle same operation via C++ API, Lua, and CLI produces identical results I 18 Errors are machine readable 2.15 Error and transaction model every failure path in the suite yields a category and code; none require log parsing 2.16.3 On detection An invariant with no detection mechanism is documentation, not a guarantee. Every row above names one; where the mechanism is weak, that is visible rather than hidden. This register is the resolution of open question Q 25 Spec open questions , recorded as Spec decisions D 028 — Invariant register names a detection mechanism per invariant D 028 . I 16's mechanism was strengthened by workspace.verify §2.16.5 , which detects a threatened overwrite before it happens rather than asserting survival afterwards. The half it still lacks is checking a resource in isolation. I 10 is the weakest and deserves attention: "no undocumented global state" is only partially checkable. The two instance test catches state that affects results; clang tidy 's check on namespace scope mutables catches the obvious form. Neither catches state hidden behind a function local static. This is a known gap. 2.16.4 Changing an invariant An invariant may be changed, but not quietly. Changing one requires a decision entry in Spec decisions recording what is given up and why, and an update to every section that relied on it. 2.16.5 workspace.verify !note Resolution of AUD L 004 D 052, D 054 workspace.verify checks a generated workspace against its own provenance record . It is distinct from workspace.inspect , which reports what the record says; verify compares the record against the tree. It is the first reader of the provenance table . Every generation had written that table — path, ownership class, origin, sha256, one row per file — and nothing had ever read it back. Unread data drifts from correct without failing, so the table was true only by coincidence; verify makes it true on purpose, and its first assertion is that a freshly generated workspace verifies clean. What it checks, and what each finding means: Condition Result Because recorded generated file differs from its hash conflict a regeneration would overwrite the edit recorded generated file absent conflict recorded but gone; a different remedy, so a different finding recorded seeded file differs counted, not reported that is what seeded means recorded row carries no hash counted as unchecked copied assets are recorded without one; hiding this would overstate what verify proved It MUST NOT repair. Restoring a file would be the regeneration path §2.7.11 defers, arriving by a side door. It reports; the remedy is the author's. It exits non zero when there are findings, so it composes into a check target or a CI step. Not yet checked, and named so the gap is visible: Untracked files — present in the tree, absent from the record. Almost always the author's own work, and a useful number. No implementation offers directory listing on its filesystem service. A resource in isolation. Ownership overlaps §2.7.10 are detected during planning, so a defective template fails when someone generates from it, not before. sqcart performed this check until cartridge format 2.0 removed its jurisdiction format spec §6 , and it has had no successor since. This is the detection mechanism I 16 would want and does not have. Related 1.13 Repository invariant · 2.12 Generated project boundary · 2.13 Dependency graph · 2.15 Error and transaction model · Spec decisions

x: section: "2.2" title: Engine responsibility and role status: review tags: spec, architecture, engine 2.2 Engine responsibility and role !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.1 Architectural model · Next: 2.3 Generation pipeline Purpose Defines what the native engine is responsible for and what it is forbidden from doing. Outline x engine as Squared project domain engine x ownership of native resources x domain concepts the engine understands x public C++ API responsibilities x capability based API design x prohibited responsibilities x the pipeline analogy Content 2.2.1 Role engine/ is the native implementation layer. It exists to provide stable, reusable, testable APIs performing the computational and filesystem oriented work of generation. The engine MUST provide: deterministic operations; explicit state management; well defined input/output contracts; reusable APIs callable from Lua bindings and from C++ directly; platform independent functionality where possible. 2.2.2 The pipeline analogy The engine SHOULD be structured like a programmable pipeline: 1. Engine initialization creates the generator execution environment. 2. Initialization exposes the available control surface. 3. Lua configures and sequences engine operations. 4. Engine operations execute the requested actions. 5. Results return through the Lua boundary. This is the shape described in the project vision: fixed, well tested capability with programmable sequencing on top. 2.2.3 Domain model The engine MUST understand the core data models required to manipulate Squared projects: SquaredProject Template Kit Package Asset Configuration Generated project metadata !note Resolution of Q 14 D 014 These are the engine's native domain model, not workflow logic. The earlier draft's "the engine MAY contain knowledge of Squared project domain concepts" is deleted; understanding the domain model is a MUST. 2.2.4 Engine responsibilities The engine SHOULD contain: project filesystem operations; transactional file generation; template expansion; package and asset processing; archive handling; metadata processing; dependency resolution primitives; validation systems; build configuration emission; resource management. 2.2.5 Prohibitions The engine MUST NOT contain: command line argument parsing; interactive prompts; user specific workflow logic; assumptions about a single generation workflow; hidden filesystem paths; user facing presentation policy. The engine MUST NOT decide which template a user should select, which kit should be applied, which packages should be included, or how a project should be structured for a specific workflow. Those decisions belong to 2.5 Lua control layer . 2.2.6 Capabilities, not workflows The engine API MUST expose capabilities rather than workflows. The engine MAY provide: Lua decides when they are called, in what order, which template is selected, which kit is applied, and what project type is generated. This separation is what allows squared pg to serve command line usage, automated build tools, IDE integrations, custom generators, and third party tooling from one implementation. 2.2.7 API stability The public C++ API MUST be documented and versioned. Changes to the control surface MUST preserve compatibility where possible and MUST document breaking changes where they cannot. Public API documentation belongs in docs/programmer/ ; implementation detail belongs in docs/developer/ see 1.8 Documentation . Related 2.4 Engine lifecycle · 2.6 Engine Lua boundary · 1.3 Engine

section: "2.3" title: Generation pipeline status: review tags: spec, architecture, pipeline 2.3 Generation pipeline !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.2 Engine responsibility and role · Next: 2.4 Engine lifecycle !note Scope D 027 This section is the conceptual, workflow facing pipeline: the stages a workflow author thinks in. The normative engine phase order is 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.9. Where the two are compared, §2.7.9 governs. Purpose Describes the conceptual sequence transforming user input into a generated project, and which side of the boundary owns each stage. Outline x conceptual stage list x ownership of each stage x stage dependency relationships x reference to the normative phase order x transaction boundary reference Content 2.3.1 Conceptual stages Stage Owner 1 Input acquisition Lua 2 Configuration loading Lua 3 Configuration validation engine, invoked by Lua 4 Workflow selection Lua 5 Template resolution engine Template Service 6 Kit resolution engine Kit Service 7 Package resolution engine Package Service 8 Asset resolution engine Asset Service 9 Squared framework integration engine 10 Project generation engine 11 Generated project validation engine 12 Finalization engine Workflows MAY add, remove, or reorder stages provided they preserve the architectural invariants — in particular, resolution before mutation. 2.3.2 Input acquisition Inputs MAY originate from command line arguments, standard input, streams, configuration files, embedded application APIs, or automated systems. Input acquisition belongs to Lua. The engine MUST NOT parse command line syntax or define interaction behaviour. Lua converts external input into structured data for engine APIs. 2.3.3 Configuration loading and validation Lua locates and loads configuration. The engine MAY provide parsing and validation services but MUST NOT decide how configuration is obtained. Validation SHOULD cover required fields, resource availability, template compatibility, kit compatibility, package compatibility, platform requirements, and dependency availability. Invalid configuration MUST prevent generation from proceeding. 2.3.4 Workflow selection Workflow selection belongs entirely to Lua. The engine MUST NOT select workflows; it executes operations requested by the selected workflow. 2.3.5 Resolution stages For each of template, kit, package, and asset resolution: Lua determines what is requested; the engine determines whether it can be resolved and reports the result. The engine MUST NOT substitute an alternative resource when resolution fails. If an alternative is appropriate, Lua selects it. Detailed resolution semantics are defined per resource type in 2.8 Templates , 2.9 Kits , 2.11 Packages and 2.10 Assets and generator resources . 2.3.6 Generation, validation, finalization Lua initiates generation. The engine performs filesystem operations, template expansion, resource materialization, file creation, and transaction management. After generation the workflow MUST validate the generated project. The engine provides validation capability; Lua determines validation policy and the response to failures. Finalization commits the transaction and transfers ownership to the user. 2.3.7 Transaction boundaries Generation workflows MUST define transaction boundaries. Before modifying a user visible project directory the workflow MUST establish one. On failure: incomplete output MUST NOT be presented as a valid generated project, rollback MUST occur, and errors MUST be reported through the engine error system. Mechanics are defined in 2.15 Error and transaction model ; the engine guarantees transactional correctness for the operations it performs, and Lua determines recovery behaviour. 2.3.8 Pipeline invariants Generated projects MUST NOT depend on squared pg internals. Engine operations MUST be deterministic. Lua MUST remain responsible for orchestration. Engine capabilities MUST remain usable outside the CLI. Workflows MUST use documented engine APIs. The resolved resource set MUST be reproducible from equivalent inputs. Related 2.7 Project generation model · 2.15 Error and transaction model · 2.5 Lua control layer

section: "2.4" title: Engine lifecycle status: review tags: spec, architecture, engine, lifecycle 2.4 Engine lifecycle !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.3 Generation pipeline · Next: 2.5 Lua control layer Purpose Defines how the engine is created, initialized, operated, and destroyed, and who owns what at each stage. Outline x 2.4.1 Engine creation x 2.4.2 Initialization sequence x 2.4.3 Service registration x 2.4.4 Resource loading x 2.4.5 API exposure x 2.4.6 Operation execution x 2.4.7 Result handling x 2.4.8 Error handling x 2.4.9 Cleanup and shutdown x 2.4.10 Resource ownership x 2.4.11 Lifecycle states and legality matrix x 2.4.12 Concurrency model x 2.4.13 Lifecycle invariants Content 2.4.1 Engine creation The engine MUST be an explicit runtime object with a well defined ownership boundary. The instance represents the active squared pg execution environment. Creation MUST: allocate the engine instance; initialize internal state containers; establish default configuration state; prepare service registration; prepare resource management; prepare error reporting. Creation MUST NOT parse arguments, read user configuration, select resources, generate files, modify the filesystem, or execute workflows. The component creating the engine MUST also be responsible for initiating shutdown, directly or through a controlled ownership mechanism. Implementation note: the engine instance is created through a factory returning std::unique ptr ; there is no global instance and no singleton. 2.4.2 Initialization sequence Initialization is explicit and separate from creation. It MUST be deterministic: given the same configuration, resource set, and dependency versions, it MUST produce the same runtime state. Order: 1. Validate engine startup configuration. 2. Initialize internal subsystems. 3. Register engine services. 4. Build the resource index. 5. Initialize Squared project model support. 6. Initialize template, kit, package, and asset systems. 7. Expose the control surface. 8. Mark the engine Ready. Initialization MUST NOT select a template, modify a project directory, apply a kit, install packages, materialize assets, or execute workflow logic. If initialization fails the engine MUST NOT enter the operational state, and MUST remain in a state where cleanup can be performed safely. 2.4.3 Service registration Services are the capabilities exposed by the control surface. Each MUST have a well defined API with explicit ownership, lifecycle, and error behaviour. Core services, all registered during initialization: Service Responsibility Filesystem controlled filesystem operations, workspace management Resource discovery, indexing, manifest loading, integrity Template template resolution, validation, instantiation Kit kit resolution, compatibility, integration Package package resolution, dependency graph, materialization Asset asset indexing, resolution, transformation, materialization Project SquaredProject model creation and management Validation configuration, resource, and workspace validation Transaction staging, journaling, commit, rollback, recovery Metadata workspace metadata and provenance A missing required core service MUST prevent the engine from entering Ready. Extension services are optional and are defined in 2.14 Extensibility model . A missing optional extension MUST be reported but MUST NOT prevent operation unless an active workflow requires it. Service registration MUST be deterministic. The registry MUST remain independent from Lua workflow logic: Lua selects and sequences services, it does not define them. Pattern: Service Locator, scoped to the engine instance rather than global. 2.4.4 Resource loading !note Resolution of Q 11 D 011 Initialization builds an immutable resource index mapping identity to manifest, version, and location. Lazy loading may only fetch payloads for already indexed identities. The index MUST NOT change during a session. Eager, at initialization: resource discovery and indexing; manifest loading and envelope validation; identity, version, dependency, and compatibility metadata; integrity information. Lazy, on demand: template file trees; package contents; asset payloads; archives; platform specific resources. This is what makes hybrid loading deterministic: the set of resources is fixed at initialization; only payload retrieval is deferred. A resource failure discovered during lazy loading MUST be reported through the same error system as an initialization failure. !note Resolution of Q 12 D 012 The Resource Service validates the manifest envelope — well formedness, identity syntax, version syntax, integrity. The owning typed service validates the type block — what a template, kit, package, or asset manifest means. Resource identity is manifest based. Filesystem paths are never canonical identity: Lua MAY request resources by identity. Lua MUST NOT scan resource directories, modify manifests, bypass validation, or access internal resource storage. Development repositories MAY use predictable layouts for maintainer convenience, but those layouts MUST NOT become part of the public contract. 2.4.5 API exposure The control surface has two layers. Service layer — low level reusable capabilities. This is the fundamental control surface. Operation layer — named, coordinated actions built from services. !note Resolution of Q 08 D 008 Operations MUST be documented compositions of service calls. No capability may exist only at the operation layer. The operation layer exists for convenience, consistency, and reduced boilerplate — never as a second source of truth. Service APIs MUST have documented contracts, defined ownership and lifetime rules, deterministic behaviour, and structured error reporting. Lua workflows MAY use either level: The choice of abstraction belongs to the workflow author. The API boundary MUST prevent direct access to internal engine state. Internal implementation details remain private unless intentionally promoted. 2.4.6 Operation execution !note Resolution of Q 07 and Q 09 D 007, D 009 The earlier draft carried two competing models. Unified here: execution is synchronous , and a typed C++ operation registry is canonical . The Lua table form is binding sugar over that registry. An optional job wrapper MAY exist but MUST NOT change the contract. Registry Every operation is registered with: operation identity a stable dotted name, e.g. project.generate ; a typed parameter structure; a typed result structure; required services; required engine capabilities; transaction requirements; possible error codes. The registry is compiled in and enumerable through the control surface, which is what allows Lua, tooling, and documentation generation to discover operations without hardcoding them. Pattern: Command. Operations are reified, which is what makes the generation plan in §2.7.9 possible. Synchronous execution The default and normative execution model is synchronous. A synchronous operation: 1. receives a complete request; 2. validates operation availability against lifecycle state; 3. validates inputs; 4. acquires required services; 5. establishes transaction boundaries if required; 6. executes; 7. commits or rolls back; 8. returns a result or error. An operation MUST NOT return before its state changes are complete. This gives deterministic behaviour, simple ownership, predictable Lua integration, easier testing, reliable CLI behaviour, and suitability for lightweight environments such as Termux. Invocation forms Both MUST map to the same registry entry and produce identical behaviour. Operation context Each operation executes within an explicit context containing the engine instance, registered services, the resource index, resolved resources, the filesystem abstraction, transaction state where applicable, and diagnostic facilities. Operations MUST NOT depend on global mutable state, hidden filesystem paths, environment specific assumptions, or undeclared external resources. Rejection The engine MUST reject operation requests when initialization has not completed, required services are unavailable, shutdown has started, the lifecycle state forbids the operation, or prerequisites are unsatisfied. Invalid operations MUST fail before performing any partial modification. Service boundaries Operations MUST NOT bypass service boundaries. An operation requiring template access MUST use the Template Service; one requiring filesystem modification MUST use the Filesystem and Transaction Services. The engine MUST NOT expose internal service sequencing as part of the public contract. project.generate may internally perform template expansion, kit application, package installation, asset materialization, and file generation, but callers depend only on the documented operation contract. Optional job wrapper The synchronous model MAY be wrapped by a job layer providing progress reporting, cancellation, background execution, and integration with graphical or remote tools. The wrapper MUST NOT change the operation contract. The same operation MUST behave identically whether executed directly or through a job. 2.4.7 Result handling All operations MUST return a structured result. Results MUST NOT rely on implicit global state, filesystem inspection, parsing console output, or undocumented side effects. The engine owns creation and lifetime of results. Lua receives a representation across the boundary. The engine MUST ensure returned data remains valid during Lua access and that ownership and memory lifetime rules are explicit. Lua MUST NOT manage internal engine memory. Results MUST be machine readable and usable by non interactive consumers. The presentation format belongs to the consumer; the engine provides information, not user interface policy. New result fields MAY be added without breaking existing workflows. Existing fields MUST NOT change meaning without a documented compatibility change. 2.4.8 Error handling Errors are part of the result system. The engine reports failures; Lua decides policy. The engine MUST NOT terminate the host process because of an operation failure, report errors only as console output, hide failures behind partial success, or allow exceptions to cross the Lua boundary. Internal C++ exceptions MAY exist but MUST be converted into structured errors before crossing the boundary. A failed operation MUST leave the engine in a valid state with resources correctly owned, transactions resolved, cleanup possible, and error information available. Full error taxonomy, categories, codes, and transaction interaction are defined in 2.15 Error and transaction model . 2.4.9 Cleanup and shutdown Shutdown is the controlled transition from an active instance to a released, invalid one. The engine MUST support shutdown after successful execution, failed execution, interrupted workflows, cancellation, and partial initialization failure. The engine MUST NOT rely on host process termination to release resources. Order: 1. Stop accepting new operations. 2. Complete or cancel active operations. 3. Commit or roll back pending transactions. 4. Release temporary operation state. 5. Release extension services. 6. Release core services. 7. Release loaded resources and the resource index. 8. Release the workspace lock if held. 9. Destroy the engine instance. A failed initialization MUST still permit cleanup; the engine MUST track partially initialized state. Extension shutdown failures MUST be reported but MUST NOT leave the engine undefined, and MUST NOT prevent core cleanup. Lua MAY request shutdown explicitly. Operations attempted after shutdown MUST be rejected. A host application MUST be able to create an engine, execute workflows, destroy the engine, and continue running. The engine MUST NOT assume ownership of the host process. 2.4.10 Resource ownership The engine owns service instances, resource managers, loaded metadata, resolution state, validation state, transaction state, temporary generation resources, and internal caches. It MUST release all of them during shutdown. Lua owns command line arguments, user input, workflow state, selected options, script state, and workflow scoped temporary data. Lua MUST NOT own or manipulate internal engine resources. Ownership MUST NOT be transferred implicitly, MUST NOT depend on execution order, MUST NOT depend on filesystem location, and MUST NOT depend on process termination. Cleanup MUST occur in reverse dependency order, and a resource MUST NOT be destroyed while an active consumer depends on it. Generated projects become user owned at finalization see 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.12 . 2.4.11 Lifecycle states and legality matrix The engine MUST always be in exactly one defined state. State Meaning Created object exists, not initialized Initializing startup sequence executing Ready control surface available, no operation running Operating an operation is executing Failed initialization or operation failure requiring shutdown Shutdown releasing resources Destroyed resources released, instance unusable Legality: Call Created Initializing Ready Operating Failed Shutdown Destroyed initialize yes no no no no no no enumerate capabilities no no yes yes yes no no resolve resource no no yes yes no no no execute operation no no yes no no no no produce plan no no yes no no no no inspect last result no no yes yes yes yes no shutdown yes no yes no yes no no Rules: Operations MUST NOT execute before initialization. Initialization MUST NOT occur after shutdown. Shutdown MUST be safe from any valid state. A destroyed instance MUST NOT be reused. Nested operation execution MUST be rejected: an engine in Operating accepts no new operation. Pattern: State. Transitions are explicit and centrally enforced rather than scattered across service entry points. 2.4.12 Concurrency model !note Resolution of Q 15 D 015 An engine instance is not thread safe and has affinity to the thread that created it. All control surface calls MUST occur on that thread. Multiple engine instances MAY coexist in one process, provided no two target the same workspace. Exactly one lua State per engine instance. Lua state MUST NOT be shared between instances. Exactly one writer per workspace, enforced by an advisory lock see 2.15 Error and transaction model . The optional job wrapper MAY execute an operation on a worker thread, but only one operation per engine executes at a time, and results MUST be marshalled back to the owning thread before Lua observes them. Any future relaxation MUST be an explicit, documented compatibility change. 2.4.13 Lifecycle invariants The engine is always in a defined state, and invalid operations are rejected. Initialization is deterministic and free of hidden global state, machine paths, and undocumented external resources. Every engine owned resource has a defined owner, lifetime, and cleanup responsibility. Boundaries between engine internals, public API, Lua, and generated projects remain explicit. The engine provides capability; Lua provides orchestration. Resource identity is stable and independent of filesystem layout. Operations behave identically regardless of caller. Failure leaves the engine valid, resolvable, and cleanable. Shutdown is deterministic from any valid state. The whole lifecycle works offline from a clean checkout. Related 2.2 Engine responsibility and role · 2.6 Engine Lua boundary · 2.15 Error and transaction model · 2.14 Extensibility model · 2.7 Project generation model
