p: docs/spec/02 Generator architecture/2.5 Lua control layer.md
x: section: "2.5" title: Lua control layer status: review tags: spec, architecture, lua 2.5 Lua control layer !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.4 Engine lifecycle · Next: 2.6 Engine Lua boundary Purpose Defines Lua as the programmable orchestration layer: what it decides, what it owns, and what it may not touch. Outline x 2.5.1 Architectural role x 2.5.2 Lua lifecycle x 2.5.3 Workflow orchestration x 2.5.4 Command line interface control x 2.5.5 Input handling x 2.5.6 Configuration handling x 2.5.7 Engine API interaction x 2.5.8 Result driven workflows x 2.5.9 Filesystem scope x 2.5.10 Ownership model x 2.5.11 Invariants Content 2.5.1 Architectural role Lua is the orchestration layer above the native engine. The engine provides capabilities; Lua provides decisions. Lua is responsible for acquiring user input, loading configuration, selecting workflows, invoking engine APIs, processing results, handling workflow decisions, and controlling generation order. Lua MUST NOT implement low level generator capabilities, and MUST NOT replace engine services such as filesystem management, template processing, package resolution, resource management, project generation, or transaction handling. The separation is what allows one implementation to serve command line generation, custom workflows, embedded tools, IDE integration, automated project creation, and user defined pipelines. 2.5.2 Lua lifecycle The Lua lifecycle follows the engine lifecycle: Lua MUST NOT execute engine operations before the engine reaches Ready . Lua MUST ensure engine shutdown occurs before the host exits. 2.5.3 Workflow orchestration Lua defines the order and relationship between operations. Workflows MAY select templates, kits, packages, and assets; define generation options; execute conditionally; and implement entirely custom sequences. The engine MUST NOT determine workflow order. The engine executes requested actions. Lua decides why and when. 2.5.4 Command line interface control !note Resolution of Q 01 D 025 The earlier draft stated the engine must only receive requests through the Lua boundary, which contradicted the embedded use guarantees elsewhere. Restated: The CLI MUST NOT implement generation policy in native code. The CLI is a thin host: it starts a Lua runtime, creates and initializes an engine, hands control to a workflow, forwards I/O, and reports the final result. Lua is responsible for parsing command arguments, interpreting switches, loading command configuration, selecting workflows, and formatting user facing output. This does not make Lua a mandatory intermediary. An embedding application MAY call the engine C++ API directly see 2.1 Architectural model §2.1.6 . What is prohibited is baking workflow policy into the native layer. 2.5.5 Input handling Lua provides the input abstraction. Supported sources MAY include command line arguments, standard input, configuration files, streams, embedded application data, and tool requests. The engine receives structured data. The engine MUST NOT parse command line syntax, user prompts, interactive responses, or shell conventions. 2.5.6 Configuration handling A workflow MAY supply no platforms at all, and SHOULD by default. An empty platform set means no restriction , not "unknown". Three spellings mean the same thing and all are accepted: the resource declares no platforms, the resource declares all , or the request names none. A workflow MUST NOT detect the host platform and supply it as a default. The generation host is not necessarily the target — a workspace for Android is routinely generated on a desktop, and on Termux the two happen to coincide, which makes the mistake invisible exactly where it would be made. Detection would also make generation depend on ambient state, which §2.7.2 forbids. Where a platform genuinely matters, it is the caller's to name. Lua locates configuration sources, combines values, and selects workflow behaviour. The engine validates configuration data, reports compatibility issues, and processes validated values. Precedence between configuration sources is a workflow decision and MUST be documented by the workflow, not assumed by the engine. 2.5.7 Engine API interaction Lua MUST interact with the engine through the public API only. Lua MAY call services, execute operations, inspect results, handle errors, and control workflow state. Lua MUST NOT access C++ internal objects, manipulate engine memory, bypass service boundaries, or reach private engine state. The binding layer MUST preserve ownership rules, lifetime rules, error semantics, and result semantics see 2.6 Engine Lua boundary . 2.5.8 Result driven workflows Workflows MUST be driven by engine results. The engine reports success, failure, warnings, diagnostics, and data. Lua decides whether to continue, retry, amend configuration, or abort. The engine MUST NOT contain workflow recovery policy. 2.5.9 Filesystem scope !note Resolution of Q 13 D 013 The earlier prohibition on Lua filesystem access was too broad — Lua must load configuration files and streams. Scoped as follows: Lua MAY read and write user space input and output: configuration files, streams, standard I/O, and paths the user explicitly supplied. Lua MUST NOT : read, scan, or modify generator owned resources directly; mutate a generated workspace except through engine services; bypass the resource index, manifest validation, or the transaction system; depend on the repository's directory layout. Any path that will become part of a workspace MUST be written through the Filesystem and Transaction Services, so that provenance and rollback remain correct. 2.5.10 Ownership model Lua owns workflow state, user interaction, command interpretation, script execution state, and workflow decisions. The engine owns native resources, services, resource handles, generation state, and transactions. Ownership MUST NOT cross the boundary implicitly. All cross boundary resources use explicit APIs. 2.5.11 Invariants Lua controls workflow, not engine internals. Lua selects operations, not implementation details. Lua owns decisions, not native resources. Engine results drive workflow decisions. CLI behaviour is separate from engine capability. Workflows remain programmable after release see 2.14 Extensibility model . Lua execution is deterministic given identical inputs. The engine remains usable without any particular Lua workflow. Related 2.6 Engine Lua boundary · 2.14 Extensibility model · 1.4 Lua · 2.4 Engine lifecycle

section: "2.6" title: Engine/Lua boundary status: review tags: spec, architecture, boundary, lua, engine 2.6 Engine/Lua boundary !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.5 Lua control layer · Next: 2.7 Project generation model !note Filename Stored as 2.6 Engine Lua boundary because / is not permitted in filenames. The section title remains "Engine/Lua boundary". Purpose Defines the contract between the native engine and the Lua control layer: the narrow, explicit surface through which they communicate. Outline x 2.6.1 Boundary responsibilities x 2.6.2 Architecture model x 2.6.3 Binding layer x 2.6.4 Public API exposure x 2.6.5 Data crossing the boundary x 2.6.6 Handle model x 2.6.7 Resource identity across the boundary x 2.6.8 Configuration representation x 2.6.9 Ownership and lifetime rules x 2.6.10 Operation invocation x 2.6.11 Result representation x 2.6.12 Error propagation x 2.6.13 Filesystem and path abstraction x 2.6.14 Streams and I/O x 2.6.15 Versioning and compatibility x 2.6.16 Boundary invariants Content 2.6.1 Boundary responsibilities The boundary MUST define callable APIs, supported data representations, ownership transfer rules, resource lifetime rules, result representation, error propagation, filesystem abstraction, configuration representation, and operation invocation rules. The boundary MUST NOT expose internal C++ classes, internal memory ownership, private engine state, service implementation details, filesystem implementation details, or compiler specific data structures. It exists to provide controlled communication, not to expose internals. 2.6.2 Architecture model The binding layer translates between Lua representations, engine API contracts, and native types. The binding layer MUST NOT become a workflow layer : it MUST NOT select templates or kits, determine generation order, implement generation policy, or bypass engine services. 2.6.3 Binding layer The binding layer exposes approved engine APIs, converts Lua values into engine input types, converts results into Lua values, preserves ownership rules, and translates errors. It MUST be generated from or validated against the operation registry 2.4 Engine lifecycle §2.4.6 , so that the set of callable operations cannot drift from the set of registered ones. It MUST NOT implement workflows, make resource decisions, modify engine behaviour, access private state, or bypass service boundaries. 2.6.4 Public API exposure Lua accesses engine functionality only through documented public APIs. Lua MUST NOT access internal C++ objects, service implementation classes, private resource managers, filesystem internals, or native memory ownership. The public API MUST remain independent from command line behaviour and MUST support Lua workflows, embedded applications, IDE integrations, automated systems, and test environments. 2.6.5 Data crossing the boundary Supported representations: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, maps, structured configuration objects, resource identifiers, operation requests, operation results, and diagnostic information. The boundary MUST NOT expose raw memory addresses, unmanaged pointers, internal object layouts, or compiler specific structures. Numeric care: Lua 5.4 distinguishes integers and floats. Version components, counts, and sizes MUST cross as integers. The binding layer MUST NOT silently narrow or coerce values; conversion loss MUST be a structured error. Representations MUST remain stable across compatible engine versions. 2.6.6 Handle model Engine objects exposed to Lua MUST use controlled references — opaque handles, identifiers, or managed references — never raw pointers or addresses. Handles MUST have explicit ownership and lifetime rules, become invalid after destruction, and be validated by the engine before use. Using a stale handle MUST produce a structured error, never undefined behaviour. Lua MUST NOT directly manage native object lifetime. 2.6.7 Resource identity across the boundary Resources cross the boundary as identities. Lua MUST NOT reference resources by physical path. The Lua layer MUST remain independent from repository layout. Identity grammar is defined in 2.8 Templates D 022 . 2.6.8 Configuration representation Configuration crosses as structured data. Lua converts external input into engine compatible configuration. The engine MUST validate configuration and MUST NOT parse user facing command syntax. Command line policy belongs to Lua. 2.6.9 Ownership and lifetime rules Lua MUST NOT manually destroy engine owned resources. The engine releases native resources according to 2.4 Engine lifecycle . Temporary objects exposed to Lua MUST have explicitly documented lifetime. Values crossing into Lua SHOULD be copied rather than referenced where the copy is cheap; where a reference is necessary, its validity window MUST be documented. 2.6.10 Operation invocation An operation request MUST carry operation identity, required parameters, optional parameters, and execution context where required. The engine validates operation availability, parameters, required services, resource availability, and compatibility. Lua determines which operations execute, in what order, under what conditions, and how to recover. The engine determines how operations execute, how resources are accessed, internal sequencing, and result generation. 2.6.11 Result representation Lua MUST be able to determine whether execution succeeded, what data was produced, what warnings occurred, what errors occurred, and whether recovery is possible. The representation MUST remain stable across compatible engine versions. 2.6.12 Error propagation Errors cross as structured results. The engine MUST NOT throw unmanaged exceptions into Lua, terminate the host process, require log parsing, or hide failures behind partial success. Internal C++ exceptions MAY exist but MUST be converted into engine error results before crossing. If conversion itself fails, the boundary MUST produce a generic internal error with the operation identity attached rather than propagating an unknown exception — the boundary is never allowed to leak. Lua decides retry behaviour, alternate workflows, user messaging, and termination. Categories and codes are defined in 2.15 Error and transaction model . 2.6.13 Filesystem and path abstraction Filesystem interaction affecting generator resources and generated workspaces MUST be performed by the engine. Lua MAY supply requested output locations, user workspace locations, and configuration paths, and MAY perform user space I/O for its own inputs and outputs D 013, see 2.5 Lua control layer §2.5.9 . The engine determines resource locations, staging locations, transaction paths, and generated file handling. Resource identity is based on manifests, not paths. 2.6.14 Streams and I/O Lua owns user facing input and output: stdin, stdout, stderr, command streams, and interactive prompts. The engine SHOULD provide structured information — diagnostics, logging, progress events, execution status — rather than writing to user interfaces. Presentation belongs to Lua or the embedding application. 2.6.15 Versioning and compatibility The boundary MUST expose an API version and the set of supported capabilities. Lua workflows MAY query them and MAY declare a required version. Changes breaking existing workflows are compatibility changes and MUST be documented with a migration path. 2.6.16 Boundary invariants Lua controls workflow; the engine controls capabilities. No direct access to internal state. Explicit ownership and lifetime. Stable data contracts. Structured results and structured errors. Resource identity independent of paths. Deterministic behaviour. Support for CLI, embedded, and automated use. Related 2.4 Engine lifecycle · 2.5 Lua control layer · 2.15 Error and transaction model · 2.14 Extensibility model

x: section: "2.7" title: Project generation model status: review tags: spec, architecture, generation, ownership 2.7 Project generation model !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.6 Engine Lua boundary · Next: 2.8 Templates Purpose Defines how squared pg transforms configuration, templates, kits, packages, and assets into a complete, buildable, user owned Squared project workspace — and who owns what, when. A generated project is not a collection of files. It is a developer workspace : application code, framework integration, platform support, build configuration, resources, and the metadata required to understand how it was produced. This section defines composition and ownership. Resource definitions — manifest schema, identity grammar, versioning, discovery — are 2.8 Templates , 2.9 Kits , 2.10 Assets and generator resources and 2.11 Packages D 006 . The boundary guarantee is 2.12 Generated project boundary ; the mechanism behind it is §2.7.10 here D 006a . Error taxonomy and transaction mechanics are 2.15 Error and transaction model . Outline x 2.7.0 Terminology x 2.7.1 Generated project definition x 2.7.2 Generation inputs x 2.7.3 Workspace model x 2.7.4 Template integration x 2.7.5 Kit integration x 2.7.6 Package integration x 2.7.7 Asset integration x 2.7.8 Squared framework integration x 2.7.9 Generation phases x 2.7.10 Generated file ownership and provenance x 2.7.11 Regeneration and update model x 2.7.12 Ownership transition x 2.7.13 Project generation invariants Content 2.7.0 Terminology The following terms are used with fixed meaning throughout this section. Canonical cross project definitions live in Spec glossary ; this table fixes the meaning of each term within this section and stays in sync with the glossary per the glossary's drift rule . Term Meaning Workspace The complete generated directory tree, including all layers. Synonymous with generated project . Working directory The user working directory: the subtree the user authors code in. A subset of the workspace; see §2.7.3 The user working directory . Resource Any generator owned, manifest identified unit: template, kit, package, or asset. Materialization Writing a resolved resource's content into the workspace. Provenance The recorded relationship between a generated path and the resource that produced it. Ownership class The regeneration policy attached to a generated path §2.7.10 . Finalization The commit point at which workspace ownership transfers to the user. SquaredProject refers to the engine's in memory project model. Squared project refers to the generated artifact. 2.7.1 Generated project definition A generated Squared project is the primary output of squared pg . A generated project MUST be: self contained — buildable from its own tree plus its declared external dependencies; independent — free of any runtime or build time dependency on squared pg internals; reproducible — derivable again from its recorded generation configuration; legible — understandable by a developer with no knowledge of the generator's implementation; continuable — suitable for ongoing development, version control, and relocation. Project identity Every generated project MUST have a stable project identity established at generation time. Project identity MUST include: project name; project type derived from the template ; target platform set; generator version; Squared framework version. Project identity MUST NOT be derived from the workspace's filesystem location. Moving a workspace MUST NOT change its identity. Generator responsibility boundary The engine performs generation capabilities. Lua selects and sequences them. The engine MUST NOT decide: what kind of project the user wants; which template is selected; which kits are applied; which packages are included; which assets are materialized; the order in which generation stages execute. Those decisions belong to Lua or an embedding application §2.5 . Relationship to the generator squared pg establishes the relationship between the project and the framework. It does not participate in it. After finalization, squared pg MUST NOT be required to build, run, test, or distribute the generated project. The single permitted exception is the update workflow defined in §2.7.11, which is opt in and MUST NOT be required for normal development. 2.7.2 Generation inputs All generation inputs MUST be explicit. Generation MUST NOT depend on: ambient environment variables; the current working directory; host specific filesystem layout; interactive prompting from within the engine; network availability; the location of the generator installation. Required inputs A generation request MUST supply: project name; output workspace location; template identity; Squared framework version constraint. Optional inputs A generation request MAY supply: kit identities; package identities and version constraints; asset identities; target platform set; template parameters; package feature configuration; build configuration options; workflow specific options. Input assembly Lua is responsible for assembling generation inputs from command line arguments, configuration files, streams, or an embedding application §2.5.5, §2.5.6 . The engine receives structured configuration data and MUST validate it against the resolved template, kit, and package contracts before any workspace mutation occurs. If required inputs are missing, the engine MUST return a structured validation error identifying each missing input. The engine MUST NOT supply defaults for identity bearing inputs project name, template, output location , and MUST NOT prompt. Lua MAY then request additional input, amend the configuration, select an alternative workflow, or terminate. Input normalization The engine MUST normalize inputs before validation: resource identifiers to canonical form; version constraints to canonical form; paths to absolute form; platform names to the declared platform vocabulary. Normalization MUST be deterministic and MUST NOT consult the filesystem for anything other than path resolution. 2.7.3 Workspace model Structural variance The engine MUST NOT assume a single workspace layout. Workspace structure is determined by: the selected template; the applied kits; the resolved packages; the target platform set; project configuration. The template defines the workspace foundation. Kits, packages, and assets populate declared extension points within it. The user working directory Every generated workspace MUST designate exactly one user working directory — the subtree in which the user authors application code. The generator MUST guarantee that: the user never needs to edit files outside the working directory to develop the application; no generated class file §2.7.10 is written inside the working directory; the working directory's location is declared in project metadata. Templates MAY name this directory conventionally. The reference convention is sq app/ . Example layouts template.headless may generate: template.android.cpp may generate: Layouts MAY differ. The layer model below MUST NOT. Workspace layers A generated workspace MUST be organized into the following logical layers. A layer MAY be a single directory, several directories, or a set of declared paths, but each layer MUST have a declared, discoverable location. Application layer Contains user authored code: application behaviour, game logic, user interfaces, domain systems. MUST be the user working directory or contained within it. MUST NOT contain generator implementation detail. MUST NOT contain files the generator will overwrite. Framework integration layer Connects the workspace to the Squared framework and to applied kits. MAY contain framework initialization, adapters, middleware bridges, and platform integration code. Generated and maintained according to template and kit rules. Platform layer Contains platform specific project components — Android manifests and resources, terminal launchers, desktop packaging. MUST remain isolated from application logic where practical. Build layer Contains everything required to compile: CMake files, Gradle files, toolchain configuration, dependency declarations. Build files MAY be fully generated or seeded, and a seeded file MAY include a generated fragment. The ownership class of every build file MUST be declared by the template §2.7.10 . Resource layer Contains project resources: textures, audio, shaders, fonts, configuration, localization data. The workspace MUST distinguish framework resources, kit resources, and user authored application resources. Generator owned resources MUST NOT silently become user editable application assets §2.7.7 . Workspace metadata Every generated workspace MUST contain a metadata record. The metadata record MUST be: machine readable; located at a declared, stable path reference convention: .squared/ ; generator owned; versioned. The metadata record MUST contain: generator version; template identity and version; kit identities and versions; package identities and resolved versions; asset identities and versions; Squared framework version; resolved platform set; the normalized generation configuration; the working directory location; the layer location map; the file provenance table §2.7.10 . The metadata record MAY contain a generation timestamp. It MUST NOT contain: absolute host paths; temporary filesystem locations; user account information; generator internal state or handles. Metadata exists to support project maintenance, reproducibility, update workflows, and debugging. A user MUST be able to delete the metadata record and retain a working project — losing only update capability. Workspace initialization files Templates MAY seed project documentation and development configuration: These SHOULD establish project conventions, build instructions, development workflow, and the generated/user ownership boundary. They are seeded class §2.7.10 unless the template declares otherwise. Workspace generation rules The generator MUST: create all declared directories; materialize all required files; apply selected kits at declared integration points; integrate resolved packages; resolve framework dependencies; record provenance for every path it creates; preserve declared ownership boundaries. The generator MUST NOT: place generated files outside declared layer locations; mix generator internals into the application layer; require the user to understand generator implementation to build the project; create any dependency on the generator repository layout. Workspace structure invariant The workspace is the developer facing product of squared pg , not an exposed implementation detail of the generator. Its structure MUST communicate ownership, responsibility, and extension points without reference to generator documentation. 2.7.3b Metadata record versioning !note Resolution of AUD L 005, partial answer to Q 24 D 054 The workspace metadata record carries record version , currently 1 . A reader MUST NOT infer an absent field's value. Where a later version adds a field, the honest reading of an earlier record is unknown , never the new version's default. The case that produced this rule: a tier field would take the record from v1 to v2, and reading a v1 record as tier: sandbox would mean a workspace silently acquiring restrictions it never agreed to. tier: unknown is both true and safe, and a tool that needs the answer can ask. A reader encountering a record version newer than it implements MUST report that and MUST NOT proceed on the fields it recognises. The unknown fields may change the meaning of the known ones. Q 24 metadata format migration remains open for the harder half: whether an older record is ever rewritten forward, and by what. This section settles only how one is read. 2.7.3a The environment !note Resolution of AUD L 001, AUD L 002, AUD L 003 D 054 Specified after implementation rather than before, which is the pattern AUD L 001 was filed to prevent. Recorded so the register is honest about it. An environment is a host directory holding the tool and the workspaces made with it. Called an environment, not a workspace: a workspace is one generated project §2.7.3 and the word is taken. .sqpg/ mirrors a source layout exactly, so the marker search of §2.1.5a finds it with no configuration. It holds both binaries: a workspace whose deliverable is a cartridge shells out to sqcart , so a tool directory without it cannot support cartridge authoring. !note Named .sqpg , not .squared D 055 A generated workspace keeps its own record at <workspace /.squared/metadata.json . One name meaning "the installed tool" in one place and "this workspace's provenance" in another was already confusing enough to produce a defect: workspace detection tested for a .squared pg directory that has never existed, and the mistake survived because a fallback caught it. .squared now means one thing. The tool directory is the newer of the two and had one installation to migrate. A workspace is recognised by its metadata record and by nothing else. Not by a build file, and not by a build file beside a conventional directory — that describes half the C projects in existence, and a generator that treated one of them as its own would run workflow verbs in a tree it never made. A workspace MUST NOT be generated inside another workspace. A nested tree cannot be promoted, since tier movement takes a name in a tier and not a path, and it sits inside the outer workspace's provenance scope. A conforming implementation MUST refuse, checking every ancestor of the target rather than only its parent. Discovery boundary The engine never discovers; the control layer may. §2.7.2 forbids ambient inputs to generation, and an environment located from $SQSYSROOT or from $HOME is ambient by definition. The prohibition is preserved by where the lookup happens: the control layer resolves an environment root and passes explicit absolute paths to the engine, which has no concept of an environment and cannot be made to acquire one. So sqpg promote demo may resolve demo against a discovered root, while project.generate receives a path and nothing else. Generation remains a pure function of its stated inputs; convenience lives one layer up, where a wrong guess costs a clear error rather than a wrong workspace. Tiers Two tiers, distinguished by one invariant: Nothing in sandbox is irreplaceable. Everything there is regenerable from a template or discardable. Every other rule derives from that: it is why an agent may be pointed at the sandbox, why version control is expected in project/ and not required in sandbox/ , and why demotion is the dangerous direction. State the invariant, not its consequences. "Sandbox has no git" is a consequence, and stating a consequence as a rule invites relitigating it case by case. The tier is the location. ls ~/sqsysroot/sandbox tells the truth without consulting anything. A metadata field could disagree with the filesystem; a directory cannot disagree with itself. Most of this is documentation, not enforcement. The engine does not know about tiers and MUST NOT be taught: it would have to refuse work based on where a path sits, which is exactly the ambient dependency §2.7.2 forbids. What the tiers buy is a shared vocabulary and a legible layout, and that is enough to be worth having. Tier movement promote sandbox → project , demote project → sandbox and quarantine outside → sandbox mutate an existing workspace, which §2.7.11 does not cover and the engine refuses. They are a narrower path , and specified as distinct from regeneration rather than folded into it: rename , then additive writes only, then provenance checked replacement where an existing file must change. Rename first, and rename back on failure. Rename is the only filesystem operation with a perfect inverse, which buys atomic enough semantics without the write ahead journal §2.15.9 specifies and no implementation has. A cross device move MUST be reported rather than degraded to copy and delete: a silent copy is the one thing that must not happen to a tree being promoted. quarantine is not demotion and MUST NOT share its path. A tree from outside has no provenance record, so workspace.verify cannot check it, provenance checked replacement does not apply, and no file has a known ownership class. It copies rather than moves — the source belongs to someone else — synthesises a record in which everything is unknown, marks the tree unreviewed, and deletes nothing. What demotion may never do Demotion moves a tree from precious to not precious. It MUST NOT: delete a .git directory, or any other history. Removing the only copy of a history to satisfy a tier rule is the worst thing this tool could do; delete anything else it did not create; proceed silently. It MUST report that the tree has entered a tier whose invariant is that nothing in it is irreplaceable. !note Divergence: dirty trees D 054 The design proposal required demotion to refuse on a tree with uncommitted changes. The implementation moves and warns, and that behaviour is normative here. The reasoning: refusing would make git a hard dependency of the tier system, and would refuse most sandbox trees, which have no repository to be dirty. Moving loses nothing — the rename is reversible and the working tree is carried intact — so the stricter rule would buy protection against a failure that cannot occur while costing a legitimate operation. 2.7.4 Template integration The template is the first project specific structural component applied to the generation context. It defines what kind of project is being created . Template role A template provides: workspace directory structure; the working directory designation; the layer location map; initial application source files; build system foundation; platform integration points; kit and package integration points; default project conventions; declared file ownership classes. A template MUST be reusable across generated projects. A template MUST NOT contain environment specific or user specific data. A template MUST NOT contain generator logic. Behaviour belongs to the engine and to Lua; templates are declarative resources. Template selection Template selection is a workflow decision. Lua MUST determine the requested template from user input, configuration, workflow logic, or embedding application policy. The engine MUST NOT select a template, MUST NOT infer one from filesystem layout, and MUST NOT substitute an alternative when resolution fails. Template resolution The Template Service MUST resolve templates by manifest defined resource identity, never by path. Resolution MUST verify: template existence; manifest validity; template version against the requested constraint; engine capability compatibility; declared dependencies; required parameter definitions; platform support for the requested platform set. An unresolvable template MUST produce a structured error. If an alternative is appropriate, Lua decides. Template parameters Templates MAY declare required and optional parameters — project name, package name, namespace, application name, target platform, build configuration, optional feature flags. Parameters MUST be structured configuration data §2.6.8 . Lua acquires parameters. The engine validates them against the template contract. The engine MUST NOT obtain missing parameters by prompting; it MUST return a structured validation error naming each missing or invalid parameter. Template instantiation Instantiation converts a resolved template into workspace structure. Instantiation MAY: create directories; materialize template files; expand template variables; generate configuration files; establish the declared workspace structure; record initial provenance entries. Instantiation MUST occur inside the generation transaction 2.15 Error and transaction model . Failed instantiation MUST NOT leave a partially populated workspace visible as a project. T

x: section: "2.8" title: Templates status: review tags: spec, architecture, resources, templates 2.8 Templates !info Navigation Index: Specification Index · Parent: 2 Generator architecture Prev: 2.7 Project generation model · Next: 2.9 Kits !abstract Scope This section defines what a template is and, because it is the first resource section, the manifest envelope and identity grammar shared by all resource types . How a template is composed into a project is 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.4. Purpose Defines the template resource: manifest, identity, parameters, processing, composition, and validation — plus the resource conventions all four resource types share. Outline x resource identifier grammar shared x version and constraint grammar shared x manifest envelope shared x manifest location and discovery shared x what a template represents x template manifest block x workspace structure and layer declaration x working directory declaration x parameter declaration x ownership class declaration x template processors and substitution syntax x composition rules x validation x reference template set Content 2.8.1 Resource identifier grammar !note Resolution of Q 04 D 022 Rules: Identifiers are lowercase. Case is significant and uppercase is invalid. A segment MUST start with a letter. Hyphens MAY appear inside a segment but MUST NOT start or end it, and MUST NOT be doubled. An identifier MUST have at least one segment after the type and MUST NOT exceed 128 characters. Identifiers MUST be unique within their type across the active resource environment. A duplicate identity is an initialization failure, not a silent override. template.android.cpp is therefore valid: type template , segments android and cpp . Dots separate segments; they do not appear inside one. Reserved namespaces: package.squared. — first party Squared framework packages. .squared pg. — reserved for generator internal use. Third party resources SHOULD use a vendor segment, for example kit.acme.raylib . An identity names the artifact, not the host A resource identity MUST describe what the resource is or produces , never where it happens to run or be built. Platform applicability belongs in platforms , which is data a resolver can act on; an identity is a name and a resolver cannot reason about it. template.termux.cpp was renamed template.terminal.cpp for this reason: it produces a terminal application, and that Termux is a convenient place to build one is a property of the host, not of the artifact. Nothing about the template is Termux specific, and the name was the only thing claiming otherwise. template.android.cpp keeps its name under the same rule. Android is what it produces — an APK, a NativeActivity, a specific packaging model — not where it is built. kit.termux is likewise correct: the thing it wraps is the Termux:API toolset. A kit that wraps a platform's facilities may name that platform, because the platform is its subject. 2.8.2 Version and constraint grammar Versions are SemVer 2.0.0 . Pre release and build metadata are permitted; build metadata is ignored for ordering. A resource is referenced as identity or identity@constraint : Constraint Meaning 1.2.3 exactly 1.2.3 ^1.2.3 =1.2.3 <2.0.0 ~1.2.3 =1.2.3 <1.3.0 =1.2 <2.0 explicit range or omitted any available version Selection policy, which MUST be deterministic: 1. Collect all indexed versions of the identity. 2. Discard versions failing any accumulated constraint. 3. Sort descending by SemVer precedence. 4. Select the highest remaining version. 5. If none remain, fail with .version.unsatisfiable . Where dependency resolution requires backtracking, candidates MUST be visited in that same descending order, so that resolution is reproducible. Pre release versions MUST NOT be selected unless explicitly requested by a constraint naming a pre release. Partial operands A range operand MAY omit trailing components. ^1.0 , =0.1 and ~1.2 are all legal and pad with zeros to three components: ^1.0.0 , =0.1.0 , ~1.2.0 . A manifest's own version is not padded. An identity is exact and a resource that cannot say which version it is has a defect, not a default. The padding is not a convenience. Callers write: so a range that fails to parse yields an empty optional and the constraint silently never applies — a resource declaring ^1.0 would accept every version in existence rather than failing to load. The failure mode of not padding is not an error message; it is a constraint that quietly evaporates. 2.8.3 Manifest envelope !note Resolution of Q 03 D 021 Manifests are JSON , in a file named manifest.json at the resource root, parsed with the vendored yyjson. JSON is already a build dependency, is fully offline, has an unambiguous grammar, and — unlike Lua tables — is inert data that can be validated statically and read safely from a sandbox. Every resource manifest, regardless of type, MUST contain this envelope: Envelope rules: schema version is an integer. An engine MUST refuse a manifest whose schema version it does not support, with a structured error. id MUST match §2.8.1 and its type prefix MUST equal type . version MUST be valid SemVer. requires engine constrains the engine version. requires capabilities lists engine capability tokens see 2.14 Extensibility model . dependencies entries are resource references; optional defaults to false . The type specific block is named for the type: template , kit , package , or asset . Exactly one MUST be present and it MUST match type . Unknown envelope keys MUST be preserved and ignored, so newer manifests remain readable by older engines within the same schema version . The Resource Service validates the envelope: JSON well formedness, identity and version syntax, required keys, and integrity. The owning typed service validates the type block D 012 . 2.8.4 Discovery and indexing Resources are discovered by scanning declared resource roots for directories containing manifest.json . Discovery produces the immutable resource index described in 2.4 Engine lifecycle §2.4.4. Directory layout beneath a resource root is a maintainer convenience and MUST NOT form part of any contract. A resource MUST be locatable solely through the index. Discovery MUST be deterministic: roots are scanned in declared order, and entries within a root in sorted order, so that duplicate identity conflicts are reported consistently rather than depending on filesystem enumeration order. 2.8.5 What a template is A template defines what kind of project is being created . It provides: workspace directory structure; the working directory designation; the layer location map; initial application source files; build system foundation; kit, package, and platform integration points; default project conventions; the declared ownership class of every path it produces. A template MUST be reusable across projects, MUST NOT contain environment or user specific data, and MUST NOT contain generator logic. Templates are declarative resources; behaviour belongs to the engine and to Lua. 2.8.6 Template manifest block A template's declarations live in its cartridge manifest under consumers.squared pg cartridge format §5.6 . This section is the only normative definition of that schema. The container format carries the section as opaque text and validates nothing inside it, so no rule below is enforced by sqcart . Members Member Type Absent Read by working directory string no working directory; every path is generator visible resolution platforms array of string admits every platform resolution layers object of arrays no layer mapping planning integration areas array of string the template offers no anchors resolution integration arity object every area is single planning parameters array of objects no declared parameters planning, validation processor string substitute planning executable array of glob nothing is marked executable planning requires.engine range unconstrained indexing requires.framework range unconstrained resolution requires.capabilities array of token demands nothing resolution requires.packages array of identity none validation requires.kits.required array of identity none validation requires.kits.optional array of identity none not read ownership object every path is seeded planning project types array of string — not read Malformed values fall back; processor does not A member whose value is of the wrong shape is treated as absent and takes the default in the table above. It is not an error. This is deliberate and it is the consequence of §5.6: no reader validates the section, so a manifest can carry anything, and a generator that refused to run over an unrecognised value would be unable to open a cartridge written for a newer version of itself. processor is the exception. An unrecognised processor MUST fail with capability.unsatisfied rather than falling back to substitute . The other members describe what to generate ; processor describes how to transform content , and silently substituting the wrong transform would produce a workspace that looks correct and is not. ownership The three pattern lists MUST NOT overlap one another §2.7.10 . default is the class taken by any path no pattern matches; where default is absent, an unmatched path is seeded . The manifest's vocabulary is not the engine's. user here means the author owns this file , which the engine records as seeded — written once and never rewritten. OwnershipClass::user describes a file the generator never writes at all, which no manifest can enumerate. shared is §2.7.10's reserved merged and is also recorded as seeded in v1 D 020 . Members read by nothing project types and requires.kits.optional appear in every shipped template and no code reads either. They are recorded here rather than quietly omitted, because an author copying a shipped manifest will copy them and be entitled to assume they do something. They are reserved: an implementation MUST accept them and MUST NOT rely on them. Removing them is a decision for the version that gives them meaning or deletes them. Rules: working directory MUST name exactly one path D 001 . It MUST appear in the application layer. No generated class path may fall inside it. layers MUST declare a location for each layer the template uses. A layer with no content MAY be omitted. integration points names the anchors kits and packages may write to 2.9 Kits . files entries MAY use glob patterns. The most specific matching entry wins; where two patterns are equally specific the manifest is invalid, not resolved by order. A path matching no entry defaults to seeded D 004 . 2.8.7 Parameters Parameters are declared with a name, a type, and whether they are required. Parameter types are drawn from a closed vocabulary — string , identifier , java package , path , bool , integer , enum — so that validation is performed by the engine rather than by template logic. The effective parameter set Validation is performed against the effective set, not against the declared one. Three layers contribute, and every step is put if absent, so precedence runs: workflow value engine built in declared default The layers are applied in the opposite order from that precedence: 1. Workflow values. Whatever the invocation supplied. Present first, so everything below can only fill gaps. 2. Engine built ins. Contributed by the engine, never declared by the template. 3. Declared defaults. The template's own default and default from , applied last . Defaults come last so that "default from": "project name" resolves: the built in it references must already be present when the default is evaluated. Applying them first — the ordering a reader would assume, and the one this section stated before D 053 — would make every default from referencing a built in silently produce an empty value. The order costs nothing else. Because each step is put if absent, a workflow value still wins over both, and a template default for a name the engine also provides is redundant rather than in conflict. Engine built ins Name Value project name the requested project name namespace the project name, unless overridden working directory the resolved working directory generator version the running engine's version template id the resolved template's identity template version the resolved template's version framework version the requested framework version, or 0.0.0 kit list the resolved kit identities, comma separated, or none Every built in derives from the request or from the engine. None derives from the environment or the clock : §2.7.2 forbids ambient inputs, and §2.7.13 requires byte identical output from equivalent inputs, which a timestamp would destroy. A template MAY declare a parameter that shares a built in's name. Doing so has no effect unless the built in is absent, which for the eight above it never is. Lua acquires parameter values. The engine validates them against the declared contract. The engine MUST NOT prompt; missing or invalid parameters produce a structured validation error naming each one. A parameter MAY declare a default or a default from referencing another parameter. Defaults MUST be pure derivations, never environment lookups. 2.8.8 Processing A template declares a processor. The engine MAY provide several; each is an engine capability token. Processor Behaviour copy direct materialization, no substitution substitute variable substitution plus conditional file inclusion Substitution syntax is {{ parameter name }} . A literal brace pair is escaped as {{"{{"}} . An unknown parameter reference is an error, never an empty string — silent substitution failure produces broken projects that look generated correctly. Conditional inclusion is declared in the manifest, not embedded in file content, so that the file set is knowable before any file is read: Processing MUST be deterministic and MUST NOT depend on undocumented global state. Pattern: Strategy. Processors are selected by manifest declaration; adding one requires no change to the Template Service core. 2.8.9 Composition Templates MAY support composition. Where supported: each composed template retains its own identity and version; composition order MUST be declared and deterministic; circular composition MUST be rejected; the composed result MUST declare exactly one working directory and one layer map; conflicting files entries between composed templates MUST be an error, not a silent last wins. Where composition is not implemented, a template MUST provide its complete workspace foundation directly. 2.8.10 Validation Before use a template MUST be validated for: envelope correctness, type block correctness, identity and version syntax, referenced files existing, parameter declarations well formed, ownership classes assignable, processor availability, declared kit and package references resolvable, layer map completeness, and working directory validity. An invalid template MUST NOT enter generation. 2.8.11 Reference template set These are the templates the first release targets, drawn from the project vision. Open questions Q 21 — is composition implemented in v1? The four reference templates share substantial structure, which argues for it; self contained templates are simpler and cannot produce composition order bugs. Decide when the reference templates are authored. Related 2.7 Project generation model · 2.9 Kits · 2.10 Assets and generator resources · 2.11 Packages · 1.5 Resources · 2.14 Extensibility model

How a kit is applied is 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.5. The manifest envelope and identity grammar are 2.8 Templates §2.8.1–2.8.4. Purpose Defines the kit resource: the bridge connecting Squared to an external framework, middleware system, or platform. Outline x what a kit represents — the bridge chain x kit manifest block x integration points and conflict semantics x external framework declaration x dependencies x composition x ownership class declaration x validation x migration rules x reference kit set Content 2.9.1 What a kit is A kit is the bridge layer. It connects Squared to an external system, and that system to the platform: This is the chain described in the project vision: Squared talks to SDL3 through a bridge, and SDL3 to Android. A kit MAY provide adapters, framework bridges, platform integration, initialization and lifecycle code, event/input/rendering translation, build configuration fragments, dependency declarations, platform specific sources, kit resources, and compatibility metadata. A kit MUST integrate through documented Squared public interfaces and MUST NOT modify Squared framework internals. A kit MUST NOT define the overall project structure — that is the template's role — and MUST NOT assume it owns the workspace. The external framework itself remains an external dependency, conceptually distinct from the kit that bridges it. 2.9.2 Kit manifest block A kit's declarations live under consumers.squared pg cartridge format §5.6 . As with templates §2.8.6 , this section is the only normative definition of the schema and nothing validates it. Members Member Type Absent Read by external.id string the kit wraps nothing diagnostics external.version range unconstrained resolution external.acquisition string not acquired resolution platforms array of string admits every platform resolution compatible templates array of identity admits every template resolution integration areas array of string the kit fills no anchors resolution conflicts with array of identity conflicts with nothing validation requires.engine range unconstrained indexing requires.framework range unconstrained resolution requires.packages array of identity none validation ownership object every path is seeded planning runtime.model none / polled / callback — not read provides array of string — not read Malformed values fall back to the "absent" column, for the reasons given in §2.8.6. Field names corrected against the implementation Version 1.0 of this section named six members that no implementation has ever read: This section said The engine reads supported templates compatible templates supported platforms platforms supported framework requires.framework requires packages requires.packages writes integration points integration areas files , migrations nothing; both unimplemented A kit written to the old text would have resolved as though it declared nothing: unconstrained platforms, every template compatible, no integration areas. It would not have failed — §2.8.6's fallback rule would have absorbed every one of those names as absent — which is exactly the failure mode a normative document is supposed to prevent, and why the divergence went unnoticed until this section was checked against the code. files and migrations are removed rather than corrected. Per file ownership is ownership §2.7.10 , and migrations belong to the regeneration path §2.7.11 defers. runtime.model Declares which side of the kit's main loop calls the other: none the kit contributes no loop , polled the application drives the kit , callback the kit's runtime drives the application . Nothing reads it. It was added during the cartridge format 2.0 bump against a kit.sfml that does not exist, and every shipped kit declares none . It is recorded here as reserved so an author who copies it knows it currently does nothing. 2.9.3 Integration points An integration point is a named anchor a template declares 2.8 Templates §2.8.6 that kits and packages may contribute to. Points are named, not positional, so contributions are comparable without inspecting file content. Rules: A kit MUST declare every integration point it writes. A kit MUST NOT write to a point the active template does not declare. Two kits writing the same point MUST both declare it; whether that is a conflict is determined by the point's declared arity. Point arity, declared by the template: Arity Meaning single exactly one contributor; a second is a conflict multi many contributors; contributions are emitted in resolution order Conflicts MUST be detected during cross validation, before any workspace mutation, and reported as a structured compatibility error. Lua then removes a kit, selects an alternative, amends the workflow, or terminates. conflicts with declares a known incompatibility independent of integration points, and MUST be honoured even if no point collides. Who owns an integration point's substrate An integration point has two parts: the substrate that makes the point exist at all, and the filling a kit contributes to it. The substrate belongs to whoever cannot be absent. A template is always present; a kit is optional by construction. So anything the workspace needs in order to build without a given kit belongs to the template, even when it looks like that kit's concern. The concrete case: NDK detection and native app glue belong to template.android.cpp , not to kit.opengl . The template promises a workspace that builds and runs with no rendering kit at all — a NativeActivity that opens a window and does nothing is still a working Android application. If the glue arrived with the rendering kit, that promise would be false, and removing the kit would break the build in a way the template's own tests could not see. The rule generalises: if removing a kit would leave the workspace unable to build, the thing that broke was never the kit's to provide. A kit contributes to a host toolchain; it does not reorganise one A kit adds to the build configuration of a workspace that already builds. It MUST NOT reorder, replace or take ownership of the host toolchain's existing search paths. Two corrections stand as evidence, both found by on device build failure rather than by review: Additional sysroots are added with idirafter , never I . I prepends , so an NDK sysroot added that way displaces the host's own C headers and libc++ stops finding them. idirafter appends, so the sysroot serves only the headers nothing else provides. The failure is not a missing header; it is the wrong header found first, which surfaces far from its cause. Libraries are named by path, not by l with an added L . An added L changes resolution for every l in the link, including ones the kit knows nothing about. Naming the file directly affects exactly the library intended. The general rule: a kit's contribution must be additive and order insensitive . If it only works when it comes first, it is reorganising the toolchain rather than adding to it. 2.9.4 External framework acquisition external.acquisition declares how the external framework reaches the generated project: Value Meaning package supplied by a named generator package offline system expected to be present on the build host vendored vendored into the generated project by the kit A kit using system MUST declare the detection mechanism the generated build will use, so the generated project can find the dependency without the generator. Offline generation MUST be possible for every kit whose acquisition is package or vendored . A system kit MAY require host software at build time, but MUST NOT require network access at generation time. 2.9.5 Dependencies Kits MAY depend on packages, other kits, and platform components. All dependencies MUST be declared in the manifest and MUST NOT be discovered through filesystem convention. The engine MUST validate the complete kit dependency graph before application. The graph MUST be acyclic. 2.9.6 Composition Multiple kits MAY be applied where compatibility permits: Composition MUST be deterministic. Application order is the resolution order of the kit set, which is itself deterministic 2.8 Templates §2.8.2 . 2.9.7 Ownership and updates Kit contributed paths declare an ownership class exactly as template paths do 2.7 Project generation model §2.7.10 . The generator MUST NOT overwrite a user authored file merely because a kit originally provided a file at that path. Kit versions MUST be recorded in workspace metadata. A kit update MUST NOT silently alter an existing project; updates occur only through the explicit workflow in §2.7.11. Where a version change requires more than file replacement — moved paths, renamed targets, changed configuration — the kit MUST declare migrations . A required migration that is unavailable MUST fail the update rather than proceeding partially. 2.9.8 Validation Before application a kit MUST be validated for: envelope and type block correctness, template compatibility, framework version compatibility, package requirements, platform requirements, dependency availability, integration point declarations, conflict declarations, and required parameters. An invalid kit MUST NOT partially modify the workspace. 2.9.9 Reference kit set Open questions Q 22 — build emission. This section assumes kits contribute build fragments that a per build system emitter assembles. The alternative is each kit emitting its own build files directly. Confirm when kit.android is authored, since Gradle plus CMake is the case that will decide it. title: Spec conventions tags: spec, meta Spec conventions Back to Specification Index . Normative language The keywords MUST , MUST NOT , SHOULD , SHOULD NOT , and MAY in this specification are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119 https://www.rfc editor.org/rfc/rfc2119 : they mark requirements MUST/MUST NOT and recommendations SHOULD/SHOULD NOT, which a conforming implementation may ignore only with documented justification and permissive options MAY . They are always uppercase. Lowercase "must"/"should" in prose is non normative and is avoided — if it is a requirement, uppercase it. The specification is a strong guideline that is weakly enforced : it describes the intended design and the repository is the authoritative statement of what currently exists. Where a specification statement and the repository disagree about a fact of the repository's present state, the repository wins and the specification is amended to match. Normative requirement keywords are aspirational for the design and binding on implementations that aim to conform, but nothing in the specification overrides the authority of the repository as the ground truth of the current implementation. Rules: The same property MUST NOT be stated as MUST in one section and SHOULD in another. A MAY MUST NOT be followed by a contradicting MUST. Prohibitions are MUST NOT, never "should avoid". Determinism vocabulary Property Level Meaning Resolution determinism MUST Same inputs → same resolved resource set. Output reproducibility SHOULD Same inputs → byte identical files. Byte identity is SHOULD because timestamps and archive member ordering are not worth mandating. Resolution determinism is MUST because everything depends on it. Status values Status Meaning stub Outline only. outline Outline agreed, content not written. draft Content written, incomplete. review Content complete, awaiting review. final Reviewed and settled. blocked Cannot progress until a dependency exists. Note structure 1. YAML frontmatter — section , title , status , tags 2. <number <title 3. Navigation callout — index, parent, prev, next 4. Purpose 5. Outline — checkbox list, retained after writing as the completeness checklist 6. Content 7. Open questions omitted when none remain 8. Related Formatting One second level section per note. Third level subsections are headings within, addressable as 2.4 Engine lifecycle 2.4.3 Service registration . ASCII diagrams always inside fenced code blocks. Never nest fenced blocks. No chat residue. Code examples are illustrative unless labelled normative. Cross references Wikilinks are the canonical form: 2.15 Error and transaction model . A bare §N.M reference is permitted when the target note is named on the same line or is otherwise unambiguous for example a self reference within the note, or a range expressed in the notes tree . When a cross note reference is the first mention of that note on a line, prefer the wikilink form. This keeps dense tables readable without requiring a full link at every call site; it is a weak style rule, not a compliance gate. When section A defers to section B, both say so: A under Open questions or inline, B under Related . Naming inside the vault This vault lives at squared pg/docs/spec/ . Note names are prefixed Spec in meta/ to avoid collision with docs/edu/ notes of the same name notably Glossary if docs/ is opened as a single Obsidian vault. Audit cadence D 054 No new audit is opened until the previous one is closed. audit 02 sat with 22 unmarked findings for long enough that two of them described a cartridge format that had been superseded in the interval. An amendment written against a version of the system that no longer exists cannot be applied; it can only be closed or rewritten, and discovering which costs more than the amendment saved. The bottleneck is the marking pass, which is human and does not scale with how fast findings can be generated. Capping the number of open audits at one puts the constraint where it actually is. An amendment is checked against the code before it is applied. Applying audit 02 found three amendments that were wrong: the parameter layering order was stated backwards, §2.9.2 named six kit fields no implementation reads, and §1.1 asserted a directory was unprovisioned that had been populated for months. All three had survived a full prior audit, because every audit until this one compared the specification against intent . A question added during implementation is triaged when the audit that would have caught it closes. Not later. Q 26 through Q 29 accumulated untriaged because no step in the process owned them.

It is a consumer of the engine §2.1.6 , not part of it; placing it under engine/ would blur the line §2.2.5 draws. engine/lua/ — the binding layer. §2.6.3 requires it to be generated from or validated against the operation registry, which makes it engine side. It builds as a separate target so an embedder may link the engine alone and never pay for a Lua runtime. Rejected: putting the binding in lua/ , which is Lua source by §1.4 and would have put C++ there; putting the CLI in engine/ , which §2.2.5 forbids in spirit. Amend §1.1 to list both. D 030 — Resources are cartridges; the manifest envelope is the cartridge format's 2.8 Templates · 2.10 Assets and generator resources §2.8.3 defines an envelope schema version , type , requires engine , requires capabilities and §2.8.1 an identifier grammar a z a z0 9 a z0 9 + , unbounded segments . The repository already contains manifests in the cartridge format format version , kind , engine , requires features ; segments a z a z0 9 , two to eight , a tested reader for them, and a CLI that writes them. The engine implements the cartridge form and opens every resource through sqcart . ResourceId::parse accepts both and as segment separators so that identities written against either document validate. Rationale: a second manifest reader would be a second chance to disagree about what a manifest means, and disagreement between the tool that packs cartridges and the tool that consumes them has the worst possible symptoms. Rejected: implementing §2.8.3 alongside the cartridge envelope two readers ; rewriting sqcart to §2.8.3 discards a tested, shipped implementation . Amend §2.8.1–2.8.3 to state that generator resources are cartridges and inherit the container format's envelope and identity grammar. D 031 — Resource payload root 2.8 Templates · 2.9 Kits · 2.10 Assets and generator resources Templates declare their payload root as template.tree . The cartridge format gives kits, packages and asset bundles no equivalent field, so the engine's convention is: tree/ when the cartridge has entries beneath it, the cartridge root otherwise. SQ INF/ is never payload. Amend §2.9 and §2.10 to state the convention, or add a tree field to those bodies in the format. D 032 — Architecture fields absent from the cartridge format are read from raw JSON 2.7 Project generation model · 2.8 Templates · 2.9 Kits The generator architecture needs manifest fields the container format does not model: working directory , integration areas , integration arity , processor , parameter default / default from , executable , external.acquisition , conflicts with . These are read from Manifest::raw json , which format §5.4 guarantees is preserved verbatim. This keeps the divergence one directional: the engine knows more than the format, and the format never learns about generation — which is the scope rule sqcart/AGENTS.md already states. Where such a field is absent or malformed the engine falls back to a documented conservative default working directory → sq app , processor → substitute , arity → single . An unknown processor is a hard capability.unsatisfied failure, because §2.14.1 requires an unsatisfied capability to fail at resolution. D 033 — v1 implements new workspace generation only 2.7 Project generation model · 2.15 Error and transaction model project.generate refuses an existing workspace with filesystem.workspace.exists . Regeneration §2.7.11 requires the write ahead journal §2.15.9 , per file staging, crash recovery across the four journal states, and the damaged terminal state §2.15.13 . Refusing loudly is the correct failure: a half implemented journal would corrupt user work in exactly the situations the journal exists to protect. Already in place for it: provenance hashes written on every generation, a reified plan the same type an update plan needs , and enforced ownership classes. Missing: the journal and the apply in place loop. Package and asset materialization are deferred on the same principle — resolution is implemented and reported, materialization is not, and there is no package or asset in the repository to design it against. D 034 — The engine supplies built in substitution parameters 2.7 Project generation model · 2.8 Templates The template parameter contract is validated against the effective parameters: the template's declared defaults, then engine built ins derived from the request, then the workflow's values. Built ins: project name , namespace , working directory , generator version , template id , template version , framework version , kit list . Every one derives from the request or the engine — never from the environment or the clock, because §2.7.13 requires byte identical output from equivalent inputs. Without this, every workflow would have to restate project name = name to pass a check the engine was about to satisfy itself. §2.8.7 should say that the engine contributes built ins and that validation sees the effective set. D 035 — requires capabilities is an opaque array in the cartridge envelope 2.8 Templates · 2.14 Extensibility model · supersedes part of D 030 §2.14.1 requires an unsatisfied capability to fail at resolution. Until now a manifest had nowhere to state one: the capability registry was enumerable and undemandable, and eight of the nine tokens could not be required by anything. The cartridge format gains requires capabilities : an array of opaque tokens in the envelope, beside requires features . sqcart validates shape only — name or name@range , dotted lowercase, no duplicates — and exposes it as Manifest::requires capabilities . It never interprets a token and must not: a reader that vetted the vocabulary would need teaching every consumer's, and every new generator capability would become a sqcart release. The parallel with requires features is deliberate, and so is the distinction: Guards Fails at Fixed by requires features the reader open a newer sqcart requires capabilities the consumer resolution a newer consumer The precedent is a jar manifest's vendor specific attribute sections: the archiver carries them and never reads them, which is what keeps it a general tool. This is the mechanism that lets sqcart stay one. Rejected: adding a generator specific requires capabilities field that sqcart understands puts generator vocabulary in a general format ; reading it from raw JSON as D 032 does for the structural fields a mistyped token would silently pass, and silent passing is the worst failure mode for a mechanism whose entire purpose is failing loudly . Note the limit: this shape works because a capability requirement is a flat list of strings. It does not generalise to the D 032 fields, two of which are maps and one of which carries arbitrary JSON values. Those stay in the kind body, read from raw JSON. Validating them, if it becomes worth doing, is a generator side JSON Schema — generator semantics checked by the generator. D 036 — Version range operands may be partial 2.8 Templates ^1.0 , =0.1 and ~1.2 now parse, padding to ^1.0.0 , =0.1.0 , ~1.2.0 . A manifest's own version field is not padded: "version": "1.0" remains a defect. This was a latent bug, not a feature request. Callers write if range && range satisfied by v , so an unparsed range meant the constraint silently never applied — and the repository's own manifests wrote requires engine: "^0.1" , so the engine compatibility warning had never once fired. A compatibility check that quietly does nothing is worse than one that errors, because nothing signals it. D 037 — NDK detection belongs to the template, not the rendering kit 2.8 Templates · 2.9 Kits template.android.cpp locates the NDK, exports SQ NDK INC / SQ NDK LIB , and compiles android native app glue.c from it. kit.opengl consumes those and adds only lEGL lGLESv3 plus its own header. An earlier draft put detection in the kit. That is wrong for a reason worth recording: the template requires no rendering kit — that is what makes kit.opengl and a future kit.sfml alternatives rather than one being baked in — so a project with no kit would have had no glue and could not build. NativeActivity is the template's architecture; EGL is the kit's contribution on top of it. The general rule: an integration point's substrate belongs to whoever cannot be absent. A second rendering kit inherits a working NativeActivity build rather than re solving detection, and there is one copy of the detection logic rather than one per kit. D 038 — Declared parameter defaults are applied after engine built ins 2.8 Templates · amends D 034 effective parameters layers workflow values, then engine built ins, then the template's declared defaults — each put if absent, so an earlier layer still wins. Built ins first is what lets a template write "default from": "project name" , where project name is engine supplied rather than workflow supplied. template.android.cpp uses exactly that for app label , and with the previous order the reference resolved against nothing and substitution failed. A template default for a name the engine also provides is now redundant rather than in conflict, which is the right relationship: the engine's built ins are facts about the request, and a template cannot know better. D 039 — SDK levels are build settings, not generation parameters 2.7 Project generation model AndroidManifest.xml carries no <uses sdk . minSdkVersion , targetSdkVersion and the ABI are make variables in mk/squared generated.mk , passed to aapt2 link at package time. Baking them at generation time would mean regenerating a project to retarget it, which §2.7.11's absence makes worse than it sounds: with no in place update, regenerating means losing the workspace. Declaring them in both places would create two sources of truth, and aapt2 takes the manifest's. The general test: if a value can change over a project's life without changing what the project is , it belongs in the build, not in the generated content. D 040 — A kit adds an external sysroot with idirafter , never I 2.9 Kits kit.opengl reache

title: Spec glossary tags: spec, meta Spec glossary Back to Specification Index . Terms with fixed meaning. Drift between these is a defect. Project and workspace Term Meaning Workspace The complete generated directory tree. Synonymous with generated project . Generated project Same as workspace. Preferred when contrasting with the generator. Working directory The subtree the user authors application code in. Reference convention sq app/ . SquaredProject The engine's in memory project model a C++ type . Squared project The generated artifact, not the model. Resources Term Meaning Resource Any generator owned, manifest identified unit: template, kit, package, or asset. Template Defines the project foundation — what kind of project . Kit Bridges Squared to an external framework or platform. Package Reusable Squared framework functionality. Asset Data consumed by the generated application. Manifest manifest.json at a resource root; gives the resource its identity and metadata. Resource identity The manifest declared identifier. Never a filesystem path. Resource index The immutable identity→manifest map built during engine initialization. Engine Term Meaning Capability Something the engine can do. Provided, never decided. Orchestration Deciding which capabilities run, when, in what order. Lua's job. Service A registered, persistent engine capability provider. Operation A named, typed, coordinated action composed from services. Control surface The public engine API. Preferred term; "public API" is a synonym. Engine capability token A declared, versioned engine feature a manifest may require. Generation Term Meaning Resolution Identifying and validating a resource without writing anything. Materialization Writing a resolved resource's content into the workspace. Instantiation Converting a resolved template into workspace structure. Generation plan The complete ordered operation and path list, produced without mutation. Provenance The recorded relationship between a generated path and the resource that produced it. Ownership class The regeneration policy attached to a generated path. Finalization The commit point at which workspace ownership transfers to the user. Regeneration Applying generator operations to an existing workspace. Journal The on disk record enabling crash recovery of an interrupted transaction. Ownership classes Defined normatively in 2.7 Project generation model . generated · seeded · user · metadata · merged reserved, not implemented in v1
