x: Lint How make lint works, what it checks, and why each check is there. Programmer side: none. Lint checks the framework's own source; a project's code in sq app/ and sq android/ is the project's business. Related: code style.md code style.md the format rules , tools.md tools.md the script , priority audit.md priority audit.md the findings the rules track . Three layers layer catches tool status 1. clang tidy owning raw pointers, missing special members, copies, oversized enums, bugs squared/.clang tidy in make lint 2. source rules what clang tidy has no check for: std::function , exceptions, RTTI, any new / delete tools/lint rules.txt and tools/lint baseline.txt in make lint 3. frame allocation counter a heap allocation inside the frame loop the dev module, in DEV LOG builds reports on the device No static check can prove the frame loop does not allocate: a std::vector::push back is fine at load time and a bug at frame time, and the code is the same. Layers 1 and 2 keep ownership honest; layer 3 measures the loop. A format check runs first, so make lint is the one command for all of it. Running it LINT ARGS and not LINT : GNU make predefines LINT as a program name. Progress prints as it goes: a line per 40 files for the format step, a line per rule, a line per translation unit for clang tidy. The report is build/release/lint/report.txt ; clang tidy's full output, with its notes and fix it hints, is in build/release/lint/tidy/<file .log . exit meaning 0 no findings 1 findings; the report lists them 2 usage error, a named file that does not exist, changed or since outside git, an unknown commit for since , record baseline with a file list A step whose tool is missing says so and is skipped. It does not fail the run: a machine without clang tidy can still run the rules. Engine and data The root Makefile holds one line for lint: bash tools/lint.sh $ LINT ARGS . Everything else is in two kinds of file: the engine , tools/lint.sh : finds files, runs tools, compares with the baseline, prints progress, writes the report. the data : .clang tidy which checks and tools/lint rules.txt which patterns , plus tools/lint baseline.txt which matches are accepted . The split is there so the engine can be replaced in Lua, with PEG matching instead of regular expressions, say without touching the Makefile or the rules. A replacement must keep: the command line above, since make lint passes LINT ARGS through; the rules format below and the baseline format, rule file count , one per line, starting a comment or a reason; the report path and the exit statuses; the stripping contract for rules: a pattern is matched against code with comments removed and string and character literal contents blanked, line for line. A PEG engine can read match as it likes, but the five rules today are written as POSIX extended regular expressions plus \b , which GNU grep what Termux ships and BusyBox grep both accept with E . Layer 1: clang tidy squared/.clang tidy enables checks by group. Each group serves a priority: group checks priority ownership cppcoreguidelines owning memory , no malloc , modernize make unique , make shared 1: memory is owned by a type that frees it class hygiene cppcoreguidelines special member functions , slicing , virtual class destructor , rvalue reference param not moved , missing std forward 1: no accidental copies, no leaks through a base pointer size and copies performance , including performance enum size 1, then 3 bugs bugprone except easily swappable parameters fires on every two float function and narrowing conversions the build's Wconversion already reports it ; exception escape ignores three standard library exception types triage triage round 1 sprint 2 task 23 correctness ODR and includes misc definitions in headers , header include cycle , unused using and alias declarations the self containment invariant modern spelling nullptr , override , using , = default , = delete , no void 2 readability only checks that prevent a bug or a slow path 2, 3 static analysis clang analyzer core , cplusplus , deadcode , unix correctness Not enabled, on purpose: cppcoreguidelines avoid magic numbers , readability identifier length , modernize use trailing return type and the other style checks. They produce volume, not safety, and the style is clang format's job. HeaderFilterRegex: '/squared/ a z +/' reports findings in squared's own headers and never in third party/ the underscore stops a z + or system headers. The squared pg repository has its own, broader .clang tidy at its root; squared/.clang tidy does not inherit it, so the framework's checks are the same in the package, in an example and in a generated workspace. What is analysed Exactly what the build compiles, with the build's flags. The engine asks the Makefiles, through a helper makefile that adds a print <variable target and builds nothing: 1. the root Makefile 's MODULES ; 2. each module's SOURCES , STANDARD , OPTIMISE , SQUARED ABI and INCLUDES . OPTIMISE matters: DNDEBUG decides which asserts exist. Warning flags are not passed; the build already reports those, and clang tidy would report them again as clang diagnostic . There are two configurations: host : whatever local.mk selects by default the null backend and the POSIX platform ; android : added when the NDK's sysroot headers are found $PREFIX/opt/android sdk/ndk/ /toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/<host /sysroot/usr/include , or under $ANDROID NDK HOME . It sets SQUARED GRAPHICS BACKEND=gles , SQUARED PLATFORM=android and compiles for API 22 against the NDK target=aarch64 linux android22 sysroot=<sysroot stdlib++ isystem <sysroot /usr/include/c++/v1 , the way the Android template builds an application since 3.3, and contributes only the sources the host configuration does not compile gles/ , the GLES backend, the Android asset file system . A selected .cpp that neither configuration compiles is named as skipped, never analysed with guessed flags. Each progress line says which configuration a file was analysed in. Since 7b.4 every module interface .cppm is a unit of its own, analysed as the implementation units are; clang tidy reads the BMIs of what a unit imports, so tools/lint.sh builds first make : quick when the build is current , and for the Android units a build of its own in build/lint android/ , its objects from the build cache when the same were built before. That build is given the target in CXX as well CXX=clang++ target=aarch64 linux android22 sysroot=... , as the package mk gives it: the std BMI is made from CXX and the flags, not the includes, so without it the std BMI was Termux's own API 24 and every Android unit refused it 2026 11 03, the first Android units changed since C++23 . The few headers left a test's stub are analysed through the files that include them; findings are deduplicated by place and check. A tree without Makefiles a test fixture falls back to every <module /src/ .cpp with std=c++23 and the layout's include paths. Versions Written against clang tidy 21 Termux and checked with 18. The file uses no option either rejects; in particular not ExcludeHeaderFilterRegex , which 18 does not have. Findings can differ slightly between versions: a check gains cases. Layer 2: source rules tools/lint rules.txt holds the rules, one block each: The default file set is every .hpp , .cpp and .cppm outside third party/ , build/ , docs/ and any test/ directory. Tests may do what the framework may not: files/test/asset stub.cpp stands in for the NDK's C API, which hands out raw pointers. rule matches why std function std::function heap capture and an indirect call; priority audit.md priority audit.md item 5 exceptions throw , try , catch the move to fno exceptions ; items 1 and 3 rtti dynamic cast , typeid the tree builds with fno rtti and has to keep doing so; item 2 raw new a new expression, placement new included ownership goes through a type raw delete a delete expression, not = delete the same Matching runs on a stripped copy of each file: comments removed and the contents of string and character literals blanked, line for line, so a match's line number is the source's. A comment that says "do not throw" and the string "try again" do not match. Raw string literals are not understood; squared has none. The baseline Code that already breaks a rule is not fixed in one go. tools/lint baseline.txt records, per rule and file, how many matches are accepted: A file may match a rule as many times as its entry says; a file without an entry may not match at all. The report quotes every matching line of a file over its count, since the engine cannot tell which match is the new one. After fixing, tools/lint.sh record baseline writes the smaller counts; commit that file with the fix. Recording also accepts any increase, and it says so accepted exceptions gui/src/ui.cpp: 9 11 : raising a count is a decision, made in a commit a reviewer sees. A reason written after on an entry's line survives re recording. Recording needs the whole tree, so it refuses a file list and changed . Heap allocation is not the problem; unowned allocation is The rules and the ownership checks do not forbid the heap. A texture atlas's pixels are megabytes and belong on the heap. What they forbid is memory nobody owns: make unique for overwrite C++20 skips the zero fill a pixel buffer is about to overwrite: priority 3, at no memory cost. std::vector adds 16 bytes for its size and capacity: acceptable once per resource, not per sprite. Where allocation happens is a separate rule load time, not frame time , and layer 3 is what checks it. A pool that constructs objects in its own storage needs placement new . That is the one legitimate raw new match: accept it in the baseline with a reason on the entry's line. Layer 3: the frame allocation counter A development build make DEV LOG=1 apk in the Android template replaces the global operator new with one that counts, and the template brackets each frame's update and render with sq::dev::frame begin and frame end . Frames that allocate are reported over the log sink: Each site is named once, as library offsets; addr2line f C i e build/libdemo.so <offsets turns them into functions and lines. Only the frame thread is counted, and a release build contains none of it. Unlike layers 1 and 2 it does not fail make lint : it runs on the device, so its result is read from nc klu 5555 . How it works: dev.md dev.md the frame allocation counter ; how to use it: ../programmer/dev.md ../programmer/dev.md frame allocations . Memory and cost None of this is in the application: priority 1 does not apply to it. What it costs is time and the phone's RAM while it runs. step processes notes format one clang format per 40 files about a second for the tree rules one awk to strip every file, one grep per rule, one awk per file over its count under a second tidy one make per module per configuration, one clang tidy per translation unit minutes on a phone jobs defaults to the number of CPUs, at most 4. One clang tidy on a large file can take a few hundred megabytes; four is the most a phone should run next to an editor. Scratch files go to $TMPDIR and are removed on exit. The engine needs bash 4.3 or newer wait n ; Termux and current Linux distributions have bash 5. It uses no GNU only option of find , grep , sed , awk , split or sort . Known limitations Rules are textual. A new inside a macro defined elsewhere is not seen, and a pattern cannot tell a type from a variable. clang tidy's ownership checks cover the cases that matter. clang tidy cannot see a header that no .cpp includes, and a changed header pulls in its direct includers only, not the sources that reach it through another header. The android configuration needs the NDK. Without it, the GLES and Android sources are skipped, and the run says so. changed compares with HEAD : committed work is not re checked. For that, since <commit compares with an earlier commit, so since HEAD~1 checks what the last commit touched. h: Names, addresses and the name table (Sprint 6.1)
x: messaging — internals The Telegraph's parts, rebuilt in Sprint 6 to the app model: names and addresses 6.1 , keys 6.1b , the 32 byte telegram and its text form 6.2 , the ring between two threads 6.3 , the latest value cache 6.4 , both ends of a virtualized list 6.5 , the Telegraph 6.6a and the model's thread with its wakes 6.6c . Nothing here allocates but std::thread 's state, once at start. Programmer counterpart: ../programmer/messaging.md ../programmer/messaging.md Layout The old dispatcher was removed 2026 10 20 , 34 files: MessageDispatcher , Subscription , EndpointId , MessageId , the receipts, the providers the module's extension surface, which the old header check listed and a 208 byte Telegram carrying a JsonValue and two std::string ids. Nothing outside the module used it, it had no tests, and the new Telegram needed its name. Its fates, as the app model decided: scheduled delivery is the model's timers time::DeadlineQueue , moved to the module root, since nothing in src/ reached it any more ; correlation ids are in the envelope; providers become the latest value cache; snapshots become persistence in background ; receipts are dropped; JSON payloads are for saves and the network only. The module no longer depends on time or data . Since 6.6b it depends on time again: the model's runner measures its ticks with time::Timepiece and reads time::now ; one 24 byte value, no code of the old hierarchy. Names, addresses and the name table Sprint 6.1 The first part of the new Telegraph, as the app model specifies it an address is a name plus a uid . Three types, two translation units, no allocation. Name is a 64 bit FNV 1a hash offset basis 0xcbf29ce484222325 , prime 0x100000001b3 . name hash takes a seed so a name can be hashed in pieces: item 17 .name is parsed by hashing item , then .name continuing from it, with nothing copied. The literal constructor is consteval ; an invalid literal calls detail::not a valid name , which is declared and never defined or constexpr, so the program does not compile no throw , which the source rules count . 64 bits, decided in Sprint 5: one in about 37 trillion for 1,000 names to collide, where 32 bits gives one in 8,600, and mods register names on users' phones. Address is a Name and a std::uint32 t uid: 16 bytes with padding. The envelope 6.2 packs it into 12. NameTable is one span of bytes its owner supplies. Entries 16 bytes: id, text offset, length sit sorted by id at the front; text grows from the back; they meet in the middle, and full is the gap closing. Lookup is a binary search, O log n ; add is O n for the shift, fine for a few thousand names registered at start. Entries are read and written with memcpy , so the storage needs no alignment. A collision same id, other text is refused and the first name kept; it can only be tested through a friend NameTableProbe , since no two real names are known to collide. Text form: the uid goes after the first segment item 17 .name , as the app model's list protocol writes it. An unregistered name is and 16 hex digits, so a line can always be written and read back. Standard library: std::span , std::string view , std::from chars , std::to chars , std::optional for the parse result; none allocates. A hash map was passed over for the sorted array: smaller no buckets, no load factor and the lookups are not on a per frame path. Patterns: the table is a Flyweight store for name text: every telegram carries 8 bytes, and the text exists once. Memory: sizeof Name 8, sizeof Address 16, sizeof NameTable 24, plus the storage it is given TELEGRAPH NAMES , 8 KB by default, when the Telegraph owns it . Measured: 203 names in 5,649 bytes, about 28 bytes each. Tested test/address test.cpp : the published FNV 1a vectors and hashing in pieces at compile time; valid and invalid names; parsing 9 forms and refusing 16; registration added, known, invalid, collision, full, nothing half written ; 200 names in no order all found again; every address written and read back to itself; a buffer too small; and no allocation in add , text , format or parse address . An invalid literal was checked by hand not to compile, with g++ and clang. Keys 6.1b Key<T, Verbs, Uid is a name, a const char to the literal for the name table: the text is already in the binary, so registering a key copies nothing until the Telegraph does it once , and three things only the compiler sees. 16 bytes; keys are constants and never travel. Verbs is a structural struct of four bits, so it can be a template argument and be combined with state set . sendable<K, Verb, Value is the concept every sending call will be constrained by: the key carries the verb, and the value converts as the type says. Deliberately narrow: an integer takes any integer but never a bool; a number takes any arithmetic type but a bool; text takes anything a string view can be made from. A narrower concept makes the compile error the place a mistake is found. decltype of an inline constexpr key is const Key<... , so the concept strips cv and references first the first build's tests caught it . Pattern: none beyond a type tag. Nothing virtual, nothing at run time. The telegram 6.2 Bytes Field 0–7 name id 8–11 uid 12–13 correlation 14–15 kind: verb in bits 0–1, value type in bits 2–5, the rest 0 16–31 value No padding, so the 32 bytes are the telegram: memcpy in, memcpy out, and operator== is the bytes. The value is a std::array<std::byte, 16 read and written with memcpy , not a union, so there is no type punning to argue about. The factories zero the bytes a type does not use, which is what makes "equal" mean "equal bytes"; valid checks it for bytes that arrive from a file, along with the spare bits, the type range, a bool being 0 or 1, no NaN, and a uid list being whole uids. The class is trivially copyable, which the rings 6.3 rely on. Why no NaN: the text form must give back the same bits, and NaN has many bit patterns and one word. A NaN is a programmer error asserted in the factories ; read telegram refuses nan . Text and uid lists live in a data area, and the telegram holds where DataRef : 32 bit offset and length . TelegramData is the simple one, a span filled from the front, for reading lines and for tests; the Telegraph's rings keep their own data rings 6.3 . "Bit for bit" for these types means everything but the offset, which depends on where the data area put them; the tests compare the bytes instead. The text form 6.2 write telegram and read telegram , in telegram text.cpp , and write value 7.5a : the value alone, which a bound label shows. Both writers go through one put value , so a label shows a value exactly as the line writes it; the test checks write value against each exact line's tail. Numbers: std::to chars and std::from chars , so no locale and the shortest form that reads back to the same bits doubles and floats . A double always shows a . , an exponent or inf , or .0 is added, so 2.0 is a number and 2 an integer. 0.0 survives. Text: escapes for \ , " , newline and tab, \xNN for other control bytes and 0x7F; bytes from 0x80 up are written as they are, so UTF 8 stays readable. Reading decodes in two passes: the first checks and counts, the second writes straight into the data area at its final place TelegramData::reserve , writable , so nothing is copied twice and nothing is allocated. Refusal leaves nothing behind: a line that fails after its text or uids were read rewinds the data area TelegramData::rewind . Cost to note: to chars for doubles carries tables Ryu into any app that writes telegrams as text; to be measured when the dev log uses it. Tested test/telegram test.cpp : the key concept both ways 7 sends that compile, 8 that must not, with static assert , so a regression is a build failure ; the telegram's layout, byte equality, and valid refusing a stray value byte, a spare bit, an unknown type; 16 exact lines, each read back; 8 non canonical lines read and written canonically; 25 lines refused, 3 of them after their data was read, with the data area left empty; a data area too small; 20,000 random telegrams every type, random uids, correlations, text bytes 0–255, floats including infinities, −0 and denormals, doubles from random bits written, read and written again, identical; 20,000 damaged lines, read or refused but never crashing, and every one read written canonically and read again to the same line; no allocation in reading or writing. Four planted bugs no .0 on a whole double, 0x7F unescaped, the spare bits unchecked, no rewind on failure each fail it. g++ and clang. The ring 6.3 TelegramRing , in telegram ring.cpp : a bounded single producer, single consumer queue of telegrams with a data ring beside it, as the app model specifies one each way, sized at init, no lock, no allocation, a full ring returns full . Header placement: at the module root, beside TelegramData , though apps will reach it only through the Telegraph. A header in src/ must be reachable from a workhorse header make headers , until 7b.4 , and nothing reaches it until the Telegraph exists 6.6 ; listing it as extension surface would be wrong. When the Telegraph includes it, it can move to src/ or stay; to be settled then. Slots: a power of two of 32 byte slots, so an index is a free running 32 bit counter masked; the capacity divides 2^32, so the counters wrap harmlessly, and head tail is the fill. Telegrams go in and out with memcpy TelegramBytes , so the storage needs no alignment. Full is head tail == capacity : no slot is wasted to tell full from empty. The data ring: push copies a text or uids value in and rewrites the telegram's DataRef to where it went. A value never crosses the end of the ring: when it would, the rest of the ring is skipped and it starts at 0. The consumer does not need the producer's position to follow: values are popped in the order they were written, so a value starts where the last one ended, unless its offset is not that place, which means the end was skipped. Empty text takes no room. A value over a quarter of the data ring is too large decided 2026 10 20 . With the skip, a value can need almost twice its size, so anything up to half the ring would always fit in an empty one and the ring could never be stuck; the quarter also keeps room for a second value of the largest size while one waits, so one big value never holds up the next throughput, not safety; corrected 2026 10 20, the first text said a larger value could block the ring . The spec makes an oversized value a programmer error, asserted in debug builds; that assert belongs to the Telegraph's send 6.6 , because the ring's own test has to see too large come back. Memory order: the producer writes the data and the slot, then stores head with release; the consumer loads head with acquire, reads, then stores tail and data tail with release; the producer loads both with acquire before reusing room. The producer's and the consumer's counters sit on separate 64 byte lines, so the two threads do not take one cache line from each other at every telegram priority 3, for 128 bytes . No cached copies of the other side's counter: one acquire load a call is cheap at the spec's rate about 50 telegrams a turn , and it keeps stats exact. Stats: the highest number of telegrams and data bytes held at once the skipped end included , seen by the producer as it pushes; relaxed atomics, so the Console's telegraph command can read them from another thread. The spec sizes the knobs from these. Waiting is not here. Neither side waits. The UI drains at the start of a frame; waking the model thread when a telegram arrives, and the model's bounded wait for room, are the model thread's 6.6 . Standard library: std::atomic<std::uint32 t lock free on arm64 and x86 64 , std::span , std::optional , std::memcpy . Passed over: std::deque and std::queue they allocate , std::mutex the UI thread must never block , std::hardware destructive interference size g++ warns that its value may differ between compilers; 64 is right for both targets . Patterns: none from the catalogue; a ring buffer bounded queue . Tested test/telegram ring test.cpp : every value type in order, with correlations; empty text; full slots nothing written, room after a pop ; a full data ring other telegrams still sent ; a value that skips the end, the consumer following it, and the room after; too large , also on a ring with no data ring; no allocation over 2,000 pushes and pops; 200,000 random steps against a std::deque model, every telegram and byte checked, and never full when the ring is empty; and two real threads, 200,000 telegrams integers, text and uid lists up to a quarter of a 256 byte data ring, 16 slots, so it is full most of the time , each checked for order and bytes. Clean under ThreadSanitizer g++ . Four planted bugs each fail it: head stored relaxed ThreadSanitizer , the consumer ignoring the skip, the producer forgetting the skip when it checks for room, and the size limit at a half. g++ and clang. The latest value cache 6.4 ValueCache , in value cache.cpp : the last value of each address, on the UI side, so a screen built later shows current values at once the app model's cache . Decided 2026 10 20 "yes to all your suggestions" , from the choices the spec left open: how an entry is found, and how text room comes back. Entries: a dense array of 32 byte entries, laid out as a telegram's bytes with the correlation's two bytes used for a bound count and flags 0–7 name, 8–11 uid, 12 bound, 13 flags, 14–15 kind, 16–31 value . Read and written with memcpy , so the storage needs no alignment. A power of two of them, 2 to 32,768. New entries are handed out in order fresh ; after that, an entry is reused only through the clock. Finding one: an open addressed index beside the array, two 2 byte slots an entry, so it is at most half full and probes stay short. The slot is the name's hash with the uid mixed in and the bits spread a multiply xorshift , so the low bits depend on all of them. Linear probing; a removed entry's slot is closed by a backward shift, not a tombstone, so lookups never slow down with age. Priority 1 chose the separate index: the entries in the table itself at a safe fill would leave about 4 KB of spare entries at the defaults; the index is 2 KB. Passed over: a sorted array with binary search, like the name table smaller, but adding an address shifts up to 16 KB, and virtualized lists add uids at every scroll: priority 3 ; std::unordered map a node per entry, §2.1 . Eviction, the clock: one "recently written" bit an entry and a hand going round. A bound entry is passed; a marked one loses its mark and is passed; the first other is taken. Two turns see every entry unmarked, so if none is taken every entry is bound, and the value is dropped and counted. Roughly oldest first, not strictly: an entry written once long ago can outlive one written twice since. Chosen over a 2 byte timestamp an entry and a scan of all 512 for the oldest, which a full cache would pay on every new value while a list scrolls. unbind marks the entry, so one just shown is passed once more. Binding: a count, 255 at most; bind makes an entry with no value yet when the address has none, so the first value lands in it. Text and uid lists: up to 16 bytes in the entry's value the flags byte holds the length plus one; no text area room, nothing to reclaim . Longer ones in the text area, each after a 4 byte header its entry, its room . A longer value replacing one is rewritten in place when it fits the old room; otherwise appended. When the end is reached, the area is compacted: walked front to back, a text kept only if its entry still points at it, slid down, its room shrunk to its length, its entry's offset updated. No sort, at most the area moved, and only when it fills. Still short: the text being replaced is dropped, but only once that is enough so a store that fails keeps the old value ; then unbound entries holding text give theirs up, by the clock; then the value is dropped and counted. A value over a quarter of the text area is too large , as in the ring. Passed over: fixed blocks with a free list a long text would span blocks, so it could not be read as one piece ; a ring a replaced text in the middle could never be freed . A view's life: find 's data points into the cache, valid until the next store or bind compaction moves text, eviction reuses entries . The cache is used on the UI thread only, so that means within the frame; a caller keeping it longer copies it. dropped keeps the old value. The spec: "the new value is dropped". An actor then shows the value before; the drops are counted for the Console's telegraph command, which is how the knobs are set. Standard library: std::span , std::optional , std::memcpy , std::memmove , std::fill . No container allocates. Patterns: none from the catalogue; the clock is the textbook second chance page replacement. Tested test/value cache test.cpp : every value type back as it went in, the correlation dropped; text of 0, 8 and 16 bytes in the entry, 17 and 100 in the text area; uid lists of 3 and 5; a value replaced by another type and back; in place shorter, then back to its size, nothing appended ; 2,000 random growing values on three addresses, every value right after each store, compaction always enough; the clock's exact order on 4 entries bound passed, marks cleared, the rewritten one kept ; every entry bound dropped, counted, bind refused , unbound again and taken; 255 binds; a full text area an unbound text holder gives way, bound ones do not, a dropped value keeps the old one ; too large; no allocation over 2,000 rounds; 300,000 random steps over 120 addresses and 32 entries against a model every value found is the latest stored, a value stored while bound is never lost, drops only for want of room, the counts agree; the last third only binds, so the full paths run too: 152,107 stored, 58,320 dropped, 127,885 evicted ; 8 rounds of 1,024 addresses on 1,024 entries, each round all found. Clean under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. Five planted bugs each fail it: the backward shift's condition inverted, compaction not moving the offset, the clock taking bound entries, a rewrite in place ignoring its room, and the old text dropped before the new one is sure to fit. g++ and clang. Virtualized lists 6.5 The app model's list protocol count , view , a row's uid, fields by uid , both ends, without a Telegraph: 6.6 wires them in. Decided 2026 10 20 "memory is a priority, but i am willing to spend it on large speed gains. This is a hot path" : the four suggestions below. A row source, ListRows<Source, Out : count , uid at row , publish out, uid , checked by a concept, so a missing member is a compile error at t.list . list source<Out source turns it into a ListSource : a void and three captureless lambdas converted to function pointers. No virtual, no std::function §2.1 , nothing allocated; the Telegraph can hold lists of different types in one table. Chosen over a base class with virtuals inheritance for extension, a vtable call a row . ModelList , the model's end: keeps the uids it last sent for the rows in view window , 4 bytes a row and where the view is. show first, rows reads the new rows' uids into a scratch area, sends state name row uid for each row whose uid is not the one sent for it, then publish uid for each item not in the old view. Scrolling keeps an item at its row, so that is checked first; only the others search the old view at most 128 compares each . So a scroll of k rows costs k rows and k items; a sort of 10,000 with the same items on screen costs their rows only; nothing changed costs nothing. Chosen over resending every row and field in view on each change: no memory, but 30 rows of 5 fields is 150 telegrams into a 256 slot ring, the burst that makes the model wait priority 3 bought with priority 1 on a hot path: about 8 KB

x: Priority audit The project's priority order is RAM efficiency, then API ergonomics, then speed, then extensibility. This page records where the tree as it stands contradicts that order, or contradicts the language rules the project sets for itself. None of these were changed during the file split : every one is a behavioural or API change, and hiding those inside a mechanical refactor would make both impossible to review. Counts are measured against this tree, not estimated. 1. Exceptions are live — contradicts the no exceptions rule 23 throw statements, plus std::unordered map::at in the style lookup path style or default falls back to styles.at "default" , which throws std::out of range when a skin has no default style . Affected: FontResource , Skin::add font , ButtonGroup , NinePatchDrawable , Ui::set tooltip config , Ui::update , the skin loader. The framework rule is a Result style return for recoverable failure, an assert for programmer error, and hard failure only at startup. Every throw site here is one of the first two. 2. RTTI — resolved Closed. All 17 dynamic cast expressions are gone and the tree builds clean with fno rtti : They were three distinct questions, answered three ways: Was Sites Now : Actor → Widget 11 gui::actor cast<Widget Actor → Group 3 gui::actor cast<Group Widget → TextField 3 Widget::wants text input actor cast is a one virtual call downcast built on Actor::actor interface ActorInterfaceId : each derived interface publishes a constant and answers for it, delegating to its base otherwise. It costs no storage — Actor already had a vtable — and is cheaper than dynamic cast was. See gui.md gui.md downcasting without rtti . The third replacement is an improvement rather than a translation: only TextField could raise the soft keyboard before, and a virtual lets any custom text entry widget opt in. 3. fno exceptions does not build fno rtti is clean as of the RTTI pass. fno exceptions is not: 21 remaining errors , all exception related. What is left, by kind: Kind Count Work : throw std::invalid argument on a precondition 20 assert instead; one line each catch ... rollback against bad alloc 6 blocks dead under fno exceptions ; delete catch std::bad alloc converted to an error code 2 blocks pre check limits and reserve instead FontResource constructors validating external data 3 throws static factories returning a status styles.at "default" in style or default 1 return a static default constructed style The 20 precondition throws are null unique ptr arguments 9 , reversed min/max limits 2 , empty resource names 2 , out of range nine patch splits, an empty input listener, an already parented actor, a non finite tooltip config, and a tooltip factory returning a parented widget. Every one is programmer error, which the framework rules say is an assert. FontResource is the only genuine API change on the list. It does not need a new Result type: BitmapFont::parse ..., BitmapFontError& already establishes the idiom this codebase uses for recoverable failure. Since 3.1c, 2026 10 16, that idiom is a returned error: BitmapFont::load returns a BitmapFontError , true on failure. See graphics.md . External blocker: gui/src/skin loader.cpp wraps the whole load in catch const std::exception& , and inside it calls data::parse json from a module outside this archive. That translation unit cannot build with fno exceptions until sq::data is exception free. 3b. Context::present discarded surface loss — resolved Closed. It returned void ; it now returns nodiscard bool . The only signal some devices give that the rendering surface has gone was being thrown away, and the symptom is an application frozen on its last frame after a phone call. Found by comparing the framework's declaration against kit.opengl , which had it right. 4. Skin is the largest resident cost sizeof Skin is 688 bytes, and that is before any content: ten std::unordered map<std::string, T members, each of which heap allocates a control block on first insert and one node per entry, with a 32 byte std::string key per node. A skin with 40 drawables and 8 styles per widget kind pays roughly 100 allocations and several kilobytes of pointer chased nodes, resident for the life of the application. Priority 1 says this is the first thing to fix. Shape of the fix: intern names to a 32 bit handle at load time and index a dense std::vector per style kind. Lookup becomes an array index; the string table exists once instead of once per map. 5. std::function on interaction paths Seven std::function members across the public API: Button::Callback , ToggleButton::ChangeCallback , Slider::ChangeCallback , Widget::TooltipFactory , gui::InputListener , and both skin resolvers Dialog::ResultCallback went with Dialog in 7.7 . 32 bytes each, plus a heap allocation for any capture past the small buffer size, plus an indirect call. None of these are per frame in the strict sense — they fire on input, not on tick — but Widget::TooltipFactory sits in the 136 byte Widget base, so every widget in the tree pays 32 bytes for it whether or not it has a tooltip. That is the cheapest real win available: move it to a side table keyed by widget, and Widget drops to 104 bytes. 6. Style names are std::string members std::string style {"default"} appears in Label , Panel , Button , TextField , Slider and ProgressBar Window 's went in 7.7: a pane frame keeps a std::string view to a literal . 32 bytes per widget to store a name that is almost always the same short literal, and it is compared by value on every lookup. An interned handle is 4 bytes and compares as an integer. 7. Virtual dispatch on the layout and paint path minimum size , preferred size , maximum size , layout , paint , and pointer event are all virtual and all called per frame per widget through Ui::layout and Ui::paint . This is the ergonomic model libGDX users expect, and the priority order does put ergonomics above speed — but it also says ergonomics must not cost memory, and the vtable pointer is already paid for by gui::Actor . Recorded here as a known cost, not as a defect. 8. Other standard library choices std::deque<Cell in Table , std::shared ptr behind DrawablePtr and FontPtr 16 bytes plus an atomic control block per resource , std::unordered map<std::int64 t, Widget for pointer captures in Ui . See standard library deviations.md standard library deviations.md . What the file split changed Nothing on this list. That refactor moved text between files and adjusted include sets. Every declaration and every definition was byte identical to its input, verified by a round trip check in the tooling. What the RTTI pass changed Item 2 only. Nine files: a new ActorInterfaceId header, the interface query on Actor and Group , the same on Widget plus wants text input , the TextField override, and the 17 call sites in ui.cpp , widget.cpp and stack.cpp . ui.cpp also drops its text field.cppm include, which is no longer named there. Behaviour is unchanged. actor cast was tested against the cases dynamic cast used to answer: a plain Group is a Group and not a Widget ; a Widget answers both identifiers and returns the same Group subobject dynamic cast produced; an Actor that is neither answers neither; null in, null out; and the const overload agrees with the mutable one.

Paths and module names below are as they were then: <module /include/squared/<module / has since become the module root and src/ , graphics2d is part of graphics , and scene2d is part of gui . The current layout is in file layout.md file layout.md . What changed The archive's flattened layout was restored to <module /include/squared/<module / , which is what every include in the tree already expected. Headers were moved to the module matching their namespace. gui/include/ had been holding headers for four namespaces: graphics , graphics2d , scene2d and gui . gui/module.cppm 2,719 lines, 55 types and gui.cpp 3,281 lines were split into one file per type, along with bitmap font.cppm 13 types , texture.cppm 7 , input.cppm 9 , skin loader.cppm 6 and timepiece.cppm 3 . Anonymous namespace helpers shared by several now separate translation units moved to src/detail/ as inline entities in a detail namespace. A make/g++ build and two bash scripts were added; there was no build system in the archive. What did not change No declaration and no definition was rewritten, reordered within its own body, reformatted, or renamed. Behaviour is identical. This is verified rather than asserted. The splitting tools parse each original file into namespace scope segments and re emit each segment verbatim; a round trip check reassembles every segment and compares against the original namespace body. All 19 headers and 10 sources round trip exactly. Files kept whole gui/src/skin loader.cpp and gui/src/skin atlas resolver.cpp are copied byte for byte. They contain free functions and one 781 line single translation unit helper namespace, not classes, so there is nothing to split. How the include sets were proved The forward declare or include rule is a heuristic and cannot be sound on its own, so the compiler decides. tools/converge.py generates the tree, compiles every header standalone and every source, parses the errors, records each demotion the compiler rejected, and re runs. It converged in two passes and found four pairs that need a definition despite naming the type only by reference; they are listed in file layout.md file layout.md . Final state: 113 public headers compile standalone and 40 translation units compile, with std=c++20 Wall Wextra Wpedantic , zero failures and zero warnings. Verification performed Check Result Segment round trip against originals 19 headers, 10 sources, 0 mismatches Every public header compiled standalone 113 headers, 0 failures Every translation unit compiled 40 sources, 0 failures Full make build 5 archives, 0 warnings fno rtti build clean, 0 errors, 0 warnings fno exceptions probe 21 errors, catalogued by kind RTTI removal pass A separate pass after the split, touching nine files: new scene2d/include/squared/scene2d/actor interface id.hpp Actor gains actor interface and the actor cast templates Group and gui::Widget publish identifiers and override the query Widget gains wants text input ; TextField overrides it 17 dynamic cast call sites replaced across ui.cpp , widget.cpp and stack.cpp ui.cpp drops import sq.gui; , now unused Verified: make SQUARED ABI= fno rtti builds all five archives with zero warnings, 114 headers remain self contained, and a behavioural test links under fno rtti and asserts actor cast answers exactly what dynamic cast answered. No dynamic cast or typeid remains in the tree. Not done clang format and clang tidy were not run. Neither tool was available. The priority order findings in priority audit.md priority audit.md are reported, not fixed. Each one is an API or behavioural change and belongs in its own reviewable commit. No test suite was present in the archive, so behavioural equivalence rests on the round trip check and the compiler, not on tests.

t: Shims: generated classes Android calls into
h: Shims: generated classes Android calls into
x: Shims: generated classes Android calls into !important The rule for every shim All behaviour stays in C++. The dex only tells Android "these classes exist, and their methods live in that library." Programmer counterpart: ../programmer/tools.md ../programmer/tools.md dexgensh the tools only; shims have no API of their own . Why they exist JNI lets C++ call any Android API. It cannot give Android a class of ours to call into: a second activity, a service, a receiver. Those must be classes in a dex. squared generates them instead of compiling Java: no javac, no d8, no JDK Sprint 4, decided 2026 10 15; see the app model spec, "Generated shims" . A shim method is one of two kinds, and dexgen can express nothing else: Kind Bytecode Use constructor invoke direct {v0}, Parent.<init V then return void : 4 code units every shim native none; bound by RegisterNatives from C++ every behaviour a shim has A shim that would need a branch, a loop or a field is the wrong shim: its logic moves into C++ behind a native method. The service was expected to need a third kind, a static initializer that calls System.loadLibrary ; it does not 12.6 : its natives are registered from C++ as the activity is made, through the activity's class loader the app's; FindClass there would ask NativeActivity's, the system's . The dex then names no app's library, and stays one dex for every app. The cost: a service Android started by itself, in a process where no activity has registered them, would find no natives; so it is never sticky START NOT STICKY , and only the app starts it. The shims Class Extends Methods For dev.squared.ConsoleActivity android.app.NativeActivity the constructor the monitor process, CONSOLE=monitor 4.7 . NativeActivity reads android.app.lib name from the activity's own manifest entry, so a second entry with its own android:process and library needs no code dev.squared.ModelService 12.6 android.app.Service the constructor; native onStartCommand Intent, int, int , onBind Intent , onDestroy running in the background app.keep running : the template's sq android/background.cpp registers the three and does everything the notification, the wake lock, Exit . Packed by BACKGROUND=1 , with the manifest entry The names are fixed and do not depend on the app's package, so the dex is the same for every app: generated once, committed as tools/dexgen/shims.dex . The file tools/dexgen/shims.dex : 812 bytes since 12.6 432 with the Console's activity alone , dex version 035, which every Android release from 5.0 reads. sha256 079d5dae1775a6335813898224e8926bb94930fce2b08cd300b6380ef79113cd . Section Contents header 0x70 bytes: magic dex\n035\0 , Adler 32 of everything after it, SHA 1 of everything after the signature, sizes and offsets string ids the method names, the class and parameter descriptors, the shorties type ids the classes, their parents, the parameter and return types proto ids V , Intent IBinder , Intent, int, int int , ordered as the format requires method ids the parents' <init and the shims' methods class defs 2: public, no interfaces, no source file, no annotations data two code items the constructors: registers 1, ins 1, outs 1 , a type list, the string data, the class data the natives have no code , the map How dexgen writes it tools/dexgen/dexgen.cpp , one file, written from the published format source.android.com, "Dalvik executable format" . A host tool: the standard containers are used freely, as the framework rules allow outside resident code. 1. Collect every string, type, prototype and method reference the shim table names. 2. Sort each table the way the format requires and Android's verifier checks: strings by code point all ASCII here, so byte order , types by string index, prototypes by return type then parameters, methods by class, name, prototype; class definitions by descriptor a shim's parent is a framework class, so no definition order is forced . 3. Lay out : header, then the id tables in their fixed order, so the data section's offset is known before any of it is written; then code items 4 aligned , type lists 4 aligned , string data, class data, and the map last. 4. Sign : SHA 1 over everything after the signature field, then Adler 32 over everything after the checksum field, signature included. dexgen dump reads any dex back: it verifies the checksum, signature, size and endian tag, and prints the strings, methods, classes, flags, register counts and every instruction invoke direct , invoke static and return void ; anything else is named by opcode . How it is checked Byte for byte. tools/dexgen.sh regenerates the dex and compares it with the committed file. Identical from clang 18 and g++ 13 here, and expected from clang 21 on the phone: nothing in it depends on the compiler. Since C++23 dexgen.cpp is import std; : the script builds it through the framework's make make dexgen , as the tests are , which gives it the std module; until 12.6 it compiled it alone, and failed. Independently. The checksum and signature were recomputed with Python's zlib and hashlib , and the file was parsed by androguard 3.3.5's DalvikVMFormat , a dex reader that shares no code with dexgen : one class, the right parent, flags 0x10001 public constructor , registers 1, invoke direct then return void . androguard is not part of the tree; it was the sandbox's check. The 12.6 dex was read back by a second small reader written for it in Python no network for androguard that day : the checksums, sorted string and method tables, both classes and their parents, the constructors' code items, the three natives with 0x101 public native and no code. The paths no shipped shim uses yet. tools/dexgen.sh self test builds dexgen with a test service three native methods, parameter lists, a second class , writes it and reads it back; androguard parsed that file too. On the device : Android's verifier is the last word on the file. 12.6 is the first time a dex reaches one sqterm, BACKGROUND=1 : the 4.0 spike with ConsoleActivity was never run, the Console having moved into the app's own process first. What it costs Nothing in a build without a shim: a build without BACKGROUND=1 ships no dex and keeps android:hasCode="false" . With it: 812 bytes in the APK; ART compiles the dex on install a few KB ; the APK gets a class loader, as every Java app has. The C++ is untouched: Android does nothing more to machine code. Adding a shim 1. Add it to shims in tools/dexgen/dexgen.cpp , as a constructor plus native methods. 2. tools/dexgen.sh write , then tools/dexgen.sh dump to read what you wrote. 3. Commit the dex with the change. The byte for byte check then guards it. 4. Register its natives from C++ RegisterNatives before Android can call them: through the activity's class loader, as sq android/background.cpp does for ModelService .

assets One place to ask for an asset. The manager loads it once, hands out shared immutable references, records what each asset pulled in, and drops the lot on unload. Developer counterpart: ../developer/assets.md ../developer/assets.md Type Header Purpose AssetManager squared/assets/asset manager.cppm Typed asset cache over one file system AssetManagerOptions squared/assets/src/asset manager options.cppm Resource limits fixed for one AssetManager AssetHandle squared/assets/src/asset handle.cppm Shared immutable reference to one loaded asset AssetLoader squared/assets/src/asset loader.cppm Callback that turns a path into one asset of type T AssetLoadContext squared/assets/src/asset load context.cppm The restricted view of the manager a loader is given AssetLoadResult squared/assets/src/asset load result.cppm One loaded asset, or the failure that prevented loading it AssetTypeId squared/assets/src/asset type id.cppm Stable per type identifier used to key the loader and cache tables AssetError squared/assets/src/asset error.cppm Structured asset loading failure information AssetErrorCode squared/assets/src/asset error code.cppm Stable error categories produced by asset loading The shortest call site A second load of the same path and type returns the cached handle without calling the loader again. Writing a loader A loader gets an AssetLoadContext , not the manager. It can read bytes and ask for typed dependencies, and nothing else: Every dependency asked for through the context is recorded, so unloading the skin drops the atlas with it. One loader per type. Registering a second for the same type returns LoaderAlreadyRegistered rather than replacing it. Reload and unload Reload does not disturb handles already handed out. They keep pointing at the old asset until their last holder drops them, which is what makes reload safe to call while a frame is in flight. Unload cascades to the dependencies the loader recorded. Anything still held elsewhere — by another asset or by you — stays alive through its handle; only the cache entry goes. Limits Every limit is a precondition: zero is a programmer error and is asserted, not reported. Exceeding one at run time is an ordinary failure — CacheFull , SourceTooLarge , DependencyTooDeep — and comes back in the result. An asset that depends on itself, directly or through a chain, returns DependencyCycle rather than recursing until the stack runs out.

Building squared builds with clang and GNU make. No CMake, no generator step, no network access, and nothing that assumes a desktop. squared is modules, in C++23 include layout.md include layout.md , which it builds the way clang does: CXX is clang++ by default, and another compiler stops the build at once. On Termux, g++ and c++ are clang already. The standard library is libc++, everywhere: Android's and Termux's already; on a desktop, install it Debian and Ubuntu: apt install libc++ dev libc++abi dev . Desktop Linux and Termux Or drive make directly: Archives land in build/<release debug /lib/libsquared <module .a . What a build prints. One short line as each step starts, and the flags once: cc compiles one file its path from squared/ , ar makes a module's archive, bin builds a test or tool, and test runs one: ok or FAIL is the line after. The first line says the flags are what they were; when they are not another CXX , SQUARED ABI , BUILD 's optimisation, or a first build it lists every flag, one to a line, marking each new or gone , and everything they affect is rebuilt. Warnings and errors print in full, as the compiler wrote them. A failed test prints its whole output after FAIL ; a passing test's output is in build/<release debug /<test .log . Tests run only when something they cover changed. A test binary is rebuilt when its sources, the archives it links, the files and module interfaces it reads or the flags change, and make test runs it only when it was rebuilt since it last passed. A module whose tests were all kept says how many: gui: 4 unchanged since they passed . With nothing changed make test takes about a second; make retest or make test RETEST=1 runs all of them. A failed test is run again next time, changed or not. Modules outside this tree Every squared module is in this tree, and so is the one third party dependency. Unpack it once after checkout: That reads third party/yyjson .tar.gz and puts yyjson.c and yyjson.h in third party/yyjson/ . It is idempotent, and it leaves an already unpacked dependency alone, so it is safe to re run and safe to delete the tarball afterwards. data/Makefile compiles yyjson.c into libsquared data.a , so an application links one library rather than two, and local.mk is not needed for it. Why vendored rather than a system package. This tree is built with the NDK toolchain for an APK. pkg install yyjson under Termux gives you a header and a library built for the host sysroot — the wrong target. It may even link and then fail on a device. The source is compiled by your build, for your target, or not at all. local.mk still exists for anything else you need on the include path, and is still picked up automatically. build/common.mk picks it up automatically. local.mk is per checkout and should not be committed. Setting the variable on the command line still works for a one off: For Android A project made from the Android template builds squared for you, for the project's target: make in the project compiles the vendored squared/ with the same compiler, API level and NDK sysroot as your own code. You do not build the framework separately. The API level is SQ MIN SDK in the project's mk/squared generated.mk , default 22 Android 5.1 . It is what the code is compiled and linked for, not only what the manifest claims, so one APK runs on Android 5.1 and on every release after it. The log sink sends each log line, and a backtrace if the app dies, to a UDP port on the same device. You read it in a terminal on that device. It uses the loopback address only: no network, no Wi Fi, and nothing leaves the device. The shortest use In the Android template, one flag does everything: Open the app in another window. LogSinkOptions open log sink Opens the socket and, unless catch crashes is false, installs handlers for SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, SIGBUS, SIGFPE, SIGILL and SIGTRAP. Returns Meaning Opened Ready. AlreadyOpen A sink is already open; nothing changed. SocketFailed The OS refused the socket. On Android this is almost always the missing INTERNET permission. Failure is a returned value; nothing is thrown. log line Sends one line to the sink, if one is open; lines over 1000 bytes are cut. Also hands it, whole and with its level, to the listener, if one is set and this is the thread that set it. It never blocks; if nothing is listening the line is dropped. Lines written on other threads go to the sink only, so the listener needs no lock; the crash handler's lines never reach it. The listener must not call log line itself. The sink must be async signal safe write , sendto . The dev log's crash report and the Console's crash file both use it. close log sink Closes the socket and restores the signal handlers it replaced. Frame allocations A frame should not touch the heap: squared allocates at load time and reuses during frames. Static checks cannot tell a load time push back from a frame time one, so a development build counts them. The Android template does it for you in DEV LOG builds: every frame's update and render are counted, and frames that allocate are reported over the log sink. frame and summary lines. The first arrives the first time any frame allocates. After that, at most one summary every 120 frames two seconds at 60 frames a second , and only when a frame in that window allocated. A program whose frames never allocate prints nothing. site lines name each place that allocates, once, the first time it does. A site is the four innermost frames above operator new , innermost first: the code that called new often a container growing , then what called that. The number is the site's id for the rest of the run. by site follows each summary: the window's busiest sites as id:allocations , most first. Turn a site into function names and source lines with the unstripped library from your build, one offset or several at once: i matters. It shows the functions inlined at that address, which is where std::vector and std::string growth usually is. The C++ library is linked into your library, so its frames resolve the same way, from the same unstripped build/libdemo.so ; the APK's copy is stripped. A frame inside libc++ is usually a container growing: look one frame further out to see who asked it to. To count something else, bracket it yourself: FrameAllocations frame begin Starts counting allocations made by the calling thread. Calling it again before frame end restarts the count. frame end Stops counting and returns the count. Reports through the log sink as above when one is open. Returns zeros when frame begin was not called on this thread. report allocations Reports every frame counted so far through log line : one summary line; what operator new holds now, on every thread squared's and your own heap, apart from the GPU driver's and the C library's direct malloc ; then a site line for every site found. The Console's alloc command runs it. Call it on the thread that counts frames. What it counts Every operator new the counted thread makes, including the ones inside the C++ library a std::string growing, a std::vector reallocating . Not other threads: a loader or audio thread allocating meanwhile is not a frame allocation. Not malloc called directly, and not the GPU driver. At most 64 distinct sites are named per run. Later ones are still counted and show as unnamed in the by site line. Linking this part of the module replaces the global operator new and operator delete for the whole process. That is why it exists only in a development build. Lua Not bound. These are native debugging aids. A crash that happens before open log sink runs is not reported. The Android template opens the sink when the library loads, to cover startup.

Two attributes interleaved in one buffer share a stride and differ in offset. Seeing what the program actually is The linker removes anything a shader declares but never reads. That is the usual reason a uniform "does not work", and these two queries make it visible: glsl type name gives the spelling you would write in the shader — vec4 , mat3 , sampler2D . gl enum name gives the GL identifier when you want the raw form. Nothing is cached. Both fill a caller owned vector, so a program that is drawn with a thousand times a second costs nothing for lists that are read once. Errors Every failing call returns a GlesError . Nothing throws. For CompileFailed and LinkFailed , message is the driver's own log, verbatim . Drivers say genuinely useful things there and squared does not paraphrase them. check gl errors drains the GL error queue and reports the first failure. Draining matters: GL hands errors back one at a time, and leaving any queued makes the next unrelated check report a failure that already happened. After context loss Every object has invalidate , and you must call it rather than destroy : destroy calls glDelete on a name that belonged to a context which no longer exists. At best that is a no op; at worst it frees an unrelated object in the new context, and the corruption looks like a driver bug. invalidate forgets the name without touching GL. Building gles is built only when the graphics backend is gles , because it needs the NDK's GL headers: A null backend build skips the module entirely, so the rest of squared still builds on a machine with no GL headers at all.

A layout made fresh for every call allocates twice, every time: clear empties the layout and keeps that storage. Assign sq::graphics::GlyphLayout{} to give it back. reserve glyphs, lines makes the room up front, where allocating is expected at load, not in a frame , so a text that fits lays out with no allocation. A failed set text leaves the previous layout as it was. Errors BitmapFont::load and GlyphLayout::set text return a BitmapFontError . It is empty on success and true when something failed, so the failure path reads as one line: A failed load leaves the font as it was; a failed set text leaves the layout as it was. Nothing is thrown. Field Meaning code The category, a BitmapFontErrorCode ; none on success message What failed, in words, such as "missing required field" . Never null; empty on success field The descriptor field involved, such as "lineHeight" ; empty when none is line The descriptor line, counted from 1; 0 when the failure is not about one line byte For invalid utf8 : the offset of the first bad byte in the text; 0 otherwise Code Returned by When invalid argument both The parse limits include a zero; or the font is not valid, or the options are out of range limit exceeded both The descriptor, a line, a name or a count is over its parse limit; the text expands past 2^24 glyphs; out of memory malformed load A record or field cannot be read, or the records disagree unsupported load A record BMFont text does not define; line says which duplicate load A record, page, glyph or kerning pair appears twice missing required load A required record or field is absent; field names a missing field invalid utf8 set text The text is not valid UTF 8 and reject invalid utf8 is set, which is the default; byte says where The error owns nothing, so making, copying and returning one never allocates. The texts in message and field live in the library for the life of the program; keep the pointers or print them, but don't free them. Creating a context The platform layer owns the Context . Application code receives higher level objects and never presents the window itself. Leave native window null on a backend that creates its own window. Per frame present is nodiscard on purpose. Ignoring it is how an application ends up frozen on its last frame after a phone call. Surface loss Android takes the rendering surface away when your application goes to the background, and may or may not keep GPU objects alive when it comes back. Atlases and sprite batches each have an invalidate and restore pair for this; see below. Choosing a backend The null backend draws nothing and succeeds at everything. A project builds and runs before a real backend exists, and graphics and gui can be tested without a GPU. Loading an atlas Pages are resolved next to the atlas file, so the .png the atlas names is found wherever the atlas came from: inside the APK or on disk. find region name returns the first region with that name. find region name, index selects among regions packed under the same name. Both return nullptr when there is none. Filtering is taken from the atlas file. A pixel art skin that asks for Nearest gets it, and nothing you pass can override that. After context loss: restore reloads every page and re validates every region for you. Any AtlasRegion you're holding is usable again afterwards, without being re fetched. Drawing begin returns false if the batch has no GPU objects: after context loss, before restore . end draws whatever is left queued. Which way is up comes from the camera. draw region, x, y, w, h places the image's top edge at the top of the quad under either orientation: camera.origin x, y is the quad's y grows CoordinateOrigin::TopLeft default top left corner downwards CoordinateOrigin::BottomLeft bottom left corner upwards The GUI, glyph layout and GlyphPlacement all measure from the top, so use a TopLeft camera for them. A Sprite 's rotation is counter clockwise under a BottomLeft camera, so it appears clockwise under a TopLeft one. Draw sprites that share a texture together. The batch issues one draw call per run of sprites from the same texture. Ten sprites from one atlas cost one call; alternating between two textures six times costs six. Regions from the same atlas page share a texture, which is most of why atlases exist. A region whose texture was discarded or reloaded is skipped rather than drawn, so a stale region leaves a gap instead of showing the wrong pixels. After context loss: invalidate abandons anything queued, so you don't need to call end first.

An import is not text: the module was compiled once, when squared was built, and your file reads from it only what it uses. That is why it is quicker than the headers were. What still needs an include C macros. A module carries no macros. assert , errno and its codes, va start , UINT32 MAX , SIGSEGV , offsetof , stdout : include the C header that defines them, above the imports: Every include above every import. libc++'s C headers <stdio.h , <stdlib.h , <string.h , <math.h , ... bring in parts of the C++ library too, and read after the standard library came in by import they clash with it: "type alias template redefinition". So a file includes first system headers, then your own headers, which may import , and imports last. Nothing else needs an include: the std module is the whole standard library, std::isdigit and the other <cctype functions included on Android, with D BIONIC CTYPE INLINE=inline , which the build passes . Your flags The build compiles your code the way the framework was compiled where it matters: C++23, libc++ and pthread . A file compiled with another standard, or without RTTI or exceptions when squared has them, cannot read squared's modules "configuration mismatch" : keep CXXSTD at c++23 . A generated project's build does all of this mk/pkg squared core.mk , and builds the framework first: the modules are read from squared/build/release/modules/ , std among them made once per compiler and flags, and shared by your projects: building.md building.md . There are no exceptions, so you never have to search for where something is declared. Each module keeps the types you will use at its root, and the rest one level down in src/ : Both come with the module's import. The module pages list every type with its file. struct Runtime Defined at app/runtime.cppm:35 ../../../../app/runtime.cppm L35 brief The services only the platform layer can construct. Handed to Application::create once, at startup. The application keeps references to whichever members it uses. Admission rule. Something belongs here only if its lifetime is the whole process and only the platform layer can build it. The rendering context needs the native window. The file system needs the asset manager and the app's private storage path, which only the platform knows. The asset manager needs that file system. All three pass. A sprite batch, a skin or a UI does not pass: the application can make its own, and putting them here would turn this into the object every subsystem reaches into. That rule is what keeps a bundle of three references from becoming a Service Locator. Non owning. Every member is a reference to an object the platform layer owns for the life of the process, so this is three pointers wide and cheap to pass. It holds references rather than owning because the file system is polymorphic a POSIX one in Termux, an asset backed one on Android and owning it would mean a heap allocation or a template on the platform type. Not global. Nothing reaches in by type. It is passed explicitly, once. Members public graphics::Context & graphics public files::FileSystem & files public assets::AssetManager & assets

class Bridge Defined at console/bridge.cppm:85 ../../../../console/bridge.cppm L85 brief The Console, reachable from Termux on the same device: every line it prints goes out, and every line that comes in is run as a command. A TCP port on 127.0.0.1, so nothing off the device can reach it, and a secret, so another app on it cannot either without reading this app's APK, which holds the secret. Dev builds only the Android template opens it in CONSOLE builds . One client at a time: a newer one that gives the secret takes over. It waits on events, never on a timer: open asks the owner, through watch , to tell it when a socket is ready, and ready is how the owner does the template uses Android's looper . Nothing allocates. Output waits in a fixed 16 KB buffer; when the client reads slower than lines arrive, lines are dropped and counted, and the client is told how many once there is room. Files travel both ways, one at a time each way, in 4 KB chunks read and written as the socket is ready, so a large one neither fills memory nor stalls the frame: send file sends one the pull command, file commands.hpp , and a client's push is written into BridgeConfig::push directory. Wire format: console/src/bridge protocol.hpp. Not thread safe: one thread. class SnapshotChannel Defined at messaging/src/snapshot channel.cppm:21 ../../../../../messaging/src/snapshot channel.cppm L21 Three buffers between one writer the model's thread and one reader the UI's : the writer fills its own, then trades it for the middle one; the reader, when the middle one is newer than its own, trades its own for it. Neither ever waits, and the reader always gets the newest whole snapshot: a publish the reader never saw is simply replaced.
