x: {{project name}} {{description}} Generated by squared pg {{generator version}} from {{template id}}@{{template version}} . Build, package, install No Gradle, no Android Studio, no classes.dex , no Java in the build. A compiler, make , and the NDK and SDK command line pieces. It works on a phone. A build prints one short line as each step starts and says the flags once: When the flags changed another SQ MIN SDK , DEV LOG=1 , CONSOLE=app it lists every one, a line each, marking what is new or gone , and rebuilds what they affect. Warnings and errors print in full. make V=1 prints every command instead. adb on the phone itself Without adb, make install hands the APK to Android's installer, which asks every time, and nothing in Termux can read the app's log an app reads only its own . With Wireless Debugging Android 11 and later, on Wi Fi , Termux's adb reaches the phone it runs on: The pairing dialog closes when you leave it, so keep Termux beside it split screen or a floating window while you type the code. Wireless Debugging turns itself off when Wi Fi does. make install uses adb only for this phone : the attached device whose build fingerprint matches the one Termux reads, and only when adb's server is already running it never starts one to look . Anything else, a tablet on USB included, is used only when named: make install DEVICE=<serial , with the serial make devices shows SQ ADB=termux adb for a USB device reached through termux adb . run as needs a debuggable build: DEV LOG and CONSOLE builds are. Layout Who owns what Path Owner On update sq app/ you never touched sq android/ you never touched Makefile , README.md , .gitignore you never touched mk/ , sq kit/ generator rewritten .squared/ generator rewritten sq android/ is seeded rather than generated on purpose. The manifest, the resources and the platform entry point are all yours to change — that is the expert escape hatch. You should not normally need it, because the defaults work. Where to start sq app/src/main.cpp and sq app/layouts/landing.json : a screen that says Hello and has a Quit button. squared main pushes it; the build compiles the layout file into layouts::landing . Add a screen by adding a layout file, a model with app.run<YourModel . sq app/README.md has the rest. Note what sq app/ does not include: no <android/... , no EGL, no GLES. The platform layer runs your app through sq::App ; the same code compiles under other templates with a different platform layer. Keeping Android out of sq app/ is worth defending as you add code. Rendering The renderer is chosen when the framework is linked: sq::graphics::Context always exists, and with no GLES backend the null one draws nothing, so this project builds and runs without one — you get a black window and a log line saying so. With kit.opengl you get sq::gl : EGL context management and GLES 3.0. Shaders are GLSL ES 3.00 version 300 es , which needs explicit precision qualifiers in fragment shaders. Why the SDK version is not in the manifest AndroidManifest.xml deliberately carries no <uses sdk . The levels are passed to aapt2 by the build, so retargeting never means editing a file: SQ MIN SDK is more than a manifest entry. The code is compiled for that API level and linked against that level's system libraries from the NDK, so a call to anything newer fails the link instead of the device. The default, 22 Android 5.1 , gives one APK that runs on that and on everything after it. The C++ runtime is linked into your library; the APK carries no libc++ shared.so . One ABI This host builds for arm64 v8a . Termux's clang targets aarch64 only, and building four ABIs on a phone is not the use case. A desktop NDK can do more — make android help explains how. Independence This workspace does not depend on squared pg. The generator is not on the build path, is not referenced by the Makefile, and does not need to be installed to build, run or ship what it produced.

sq android — the platform layer How this project meets Android. Everything here is yours ownership class: seeded — the generator wrote it once and will not overwrite it. This is the expert escape hatch. You should not normally need it. entry.cpp Runs the android native app glue event loop, translates lifecycle and input events into calls on your App , and brings up a rendering surface if a rendering kit was applied. The renderer import is guarded, so this file compiles with no kit at all. That guard is what makes kit.opengl and a future kit.sfml alternatives rather than one of them being baked in. What the device lacks is decided from its API level , read once at start from the configuration NativeActivity already holds AConfiguration getSdkVersion and logged with the process's name as device: API <n , process <name an app with a :console process logs each separately ; the GL driver is logged once as driver: <version ; <renderer ; <vendor when the first context is current. Both reach logcat make logcat , through adb , which is how a device without Termux is read. Each such check costs a comparison, cheaper than reading a cached answer from storage, so nothing is cached. The UI thread. Everything here runs on the glue's thread, but a window's views belong to Android's main thread, so hiding the bars must happen there. The manifest names squared on create as the activity's entry android.app.func name : it runs on the main thread, adds a pipe to that thread's looper, then starts the glue as its own entry would. The glue's thread writes one byte, a job, into the pipe hide bars , show bars , to the background and the main thread runs it: a few JNI calls on the thread they belong to, no Java. Without the manifest line the glue starts alone: the bars stay up, and the rest works. The system bars are hidden immersive unless your app says app.stage.hide bars false : through WindowInsetsController from API 30, the system UI flags from 19. A swipe from the edge shows them for a moment. They are asked for again after each focus a dialog may bring them back . Back at your root screen sends the app to the background moveTaskToBack , as Home does; only a quit quit , app.quit ends it. What Android keeps. When Android asks its save instance state , the App hands it the screen stack, a few hundred bytes; the log says saved state: N bytes, for Android to keep with the activity . At the next start the log says what came back: saved state: N bytes: Android brings the activity back when Android ended the process itself memory, the freezer , and the App shows the screens again; saved state: none: a new launch after a swipe from the recent apps, a quit, a force stop or a reboot, and the App starts fresh. Your model's own save save comes back either way. The safe area the camera cut out, the keyboard, the bars when shown is measured from the window's insets from API 23. Below that, those methods do not exist, and the window's visible frame getWindowVisibleDisplayFrame , API 1 answers instead: some older devices lay the window out under translucent bars, and the Android 5.1 tablet does found 2026 10 19: its clock and battery drew over the Console's x . It is measured on events, never on a timer: for a few frames after a new window, a rotation, the bars hidden or shown, and the keyboard shown or hidden, and every 30 frames while the keyboard is up it can be closed without a word to the app . Typing. NativeActivity gives native code key codes, never characters. android text.cpp turns a key press into the character it types through Java's KeyCharacterMap one JNI call per key press, never per frame , and shows and hides the soft keyboard. entry.cpp hands your App a sq::app::TextInputService set text input service : when a text field takes focus the keyboard shows once every finger is up: one shown while the touch is still going, Android puts away when it ends , tapping it again brings the keyboard back after it was put away, Enter asks for it again some keyboards, CleverKeys among them, put themselves away after Enter with no text view behind them , and each key arrives as a KeyDown event and, if it types something, a TextInput event with Ctrl, Alt or Meta held, the character without them and the modifiers . What does not arrive: an input method's composition accents built from two keys, CJK input, emoji , which needs a Java InputConnection . The volume keys are left to Android. Running in the background BACKGROUND=1 in the Makefile; background.hpp/.cpp . For an app whose work goes on with the app off the screen a shell, a download : app.keep running {.title = ..., .text = ...} in squared main starts a foreground service, dev.squared.ModelService , with a notification saying so, so Android neither freezes nor ends the process; and a swipe from the recent apps no longer starts the app afresh. The notification opens the app when tapped, and has Exit the app gets QuitRequested and quits; with no activity left, the service stops and the process ends and Acquire / Release wakelock the CPU stays on with the screen off . Quitting stops it, as does app.stop running . The service is a shim from squared's tools/dexgen a constructor and three native methods, 812 bytes with the Console's : BACKGROUND=1 packs it as the APK's classes.dex , and gives the APK a copy of your manifest with the service, android:hasCode="true" and the permissions it needs FOREGROUND SERVICE , FOREGROUND SERVICE SPECIAL USE , WAKE LOCK , POST NOTIFICATIONS ; your manifest is not edited. The service is declared android:foregroundServiceType="specialUse" , with the subtype property Android 14 asks for: an app that targets SDK 34 or later the template's default is stopped with MissingForegroundServiceTypeException when it starts a foreground service whose type the manifest does not declare. A specialUse service has no time limit, unlike dataSync from Android 15; an app published on Google Play explains its use in the Play Console. The natives are registered as the activity is made, through its class loader. Android 13 and later ask for the notification permission the first time, while the app is on screen; without it the service still runs, its notification hidden. Without BACKGROUND=1 , keep running returns false and the log says why. The clipboard. entry.cpp also hands your App a sq::app::ClipboardService set clipboard service , after create : sq android::Clipboard , Android's ClipboardManager through the same JNI code. text out reads the whole clip 512 UTF 16 units at a time, on the stack and says its size in UTF 8; set text writes one, labelled with the app's name. An sq::App passes it to its Stage, where a widget reaches it as stage.clipboard . The Console make CONSOLE=app ; see squared's docs/programmer/console.md . A three finger tap anywhere, or on a keyboard, opens and closes it; the gesture is taken before your App sees it fingers already down are released far off screen, so nothing is clicked . While it is open, a gesture that starts on it is its own: tap to type the keyboard shows , drag to scroll back, hold the input row for half a second to paste, x or Back to close. copy puts lines on the clipboard. Every other touch, and every key while it is closed, reaches your App as before. app stop disposes your App and puts a fresh, uncreated one in its place; app start creates it and hands it the surface again, as at launch; app restart does both. The process, the window, the graphics context and the Console stay, so this recovers from a stuck screen or bad state, not from a crash. While stopped, no method of your App is called and the screen is cleared under the Console. In a Console build a create that fails no longer leaves a black window: the Console opens and app start tries again. quit finishes the activity, the same way your quit requested does. From Termux. A Console build also listens for Termux on this phone 127.0.0.1 , a port made from the package name, and a secret your build makes : make console in the project shows the Console's lines as they are written and runs what you type, make console CMD='mem' runs one command. Declaring them here too would create two sources of truth, and aapt2 would take this one. SQ MIN SDK default 22 is also what the code is compiled and linked for, so the manifest cannot claim a level the library was not built for. No android:debuggable . The build sets it for DEV LOG and CONSOLE builds aapt2 link debug mode , read back from the linked manifest to check , so run as reaches their private files; plain builds never carry it. SQ DEBUGGABLE= turns it off for one build, SQ DEBUGGABLE=1 on. Committing it here would ship a debuggable release. android:hasCode="false" and android.app.NativeActivity are what let this project have no Java: the APK carries no classes.dex , and the build needs a JDK only for signing.
